units.english_text: St. John Chrysostom calleth this acclamation "the common preface in all ecclesiastical actions: when the primate entereth into the church, he immediately saith: **'Peace be unto all'**; when he ariseth for the sermon, he beginneth not to speak unto the people before he imparteth peace unto all; when the priests perform the blessing (at Matins and Vespers before the prayer), they preface it with this; when he biddeth greeting to be given—**'Peace be unto all'**; when the Sacrifice is accomplished—**'Peace be unto all'**" [^806]. In the West likewise, judging by Blessed Augustine, this greeting was pronounced by the bishop before the readings. Describing a service whereat a miracle of healing took place, Blessed Augustine saith: "joy was complete, joyful voices sounded forth: 'Thanks be to God, praise be to God' (*Deo gratias, Deo laudes*); no one kept silence; on every side they cried aloud; I greeted the people, and again they exclaimed (*clamabant*) with the same ardent voice; and when at last silence was restored, there took place the solemn reading of the divine scriptures" [^807]. That this "greeting" of the bishop unto the people upon entering the church before the reading consisted in the imparting of peace is evident, besides the cited passage of Chrysostom, also from several other passages of his homilies, which indicate likewise the response of the people unto the greeting: "Upon entering the church, we immediately *(Orig. p. 170)* according unto this law (in conformity with the Savior's commandment concerning reconciliation with one's neighbors before prayer) say: **'Peace be unto you'**, and you reply: **'And with thy spirit'**" [^808]. "What is more perverse and senseless," Blessed Augustine reprehendeth the Donatists, "than for lectors and those who read the Epistles to say 'peace be unto thee' (*pax tecum*), and yet to separate themselves from the peace of those churches unto which these Epistles were written?" [^809] From these passages it is evident at the same time that the practice of the Eastern and Western Churches on this point was identical: in both places the reading was preceded by the imparting of peace; the formula, apparently, was not yet firmly fixed and everywhere uniform. Peace was imparted by the primate of the assembly, that is, for the most part by the bishop. But from the fact that the Council of Carthage of 419 forbiddeth lectors to "greet (*salutent*) the people" [^810], one may conclude that originally this peaceful greeting was pronounced by the lector himself [^811], and only when there was attached unto it a sacramental-intercessory significance was the right unto it transferred unto the bishop or presbyter.

Августин донатистов, — как говорить чтецам и читающим послания мир ти (pax tecum), и отделяться от мира тех церквей, к которым эти послания написаны» [225]. Из этих мест вместе с тем видно, что практика Восточной и Западной Церкви по этому пункту была одинакова: там и здесь чтение предварялось преподанием мира; формула, по-видимому, не была еще твердо установлена и всюду однообразна. Преподавал мир предстоятель собрания. т. е. большей частью епископ. Но из того, что Карфагенский Собор 419 г. запрещает чтецам «приветствовать (salutent) народ» [226], можно заключать, что первоначально это мирное приветствие произносил сам чтец [227], и только когда ему усвоено было сакраментельно-молитвенное значение, право на него передано было епископу или пресвитеру.
units.english_text: St. John Chrysostom mentioneth the acclamation **"Let us attend"** (*«Вонмем»* / *Proschomen*) before the reading: "There stands the deacon, the common minister, crying aloud and saying: 'Let us attend'; and this frequently... after him the lector begins: 'The prophecy of Isaiah'; then he pronounceth aloud (*eis epekoon*): **'Thus saith the Lord'** [^812], while the standing deacon stoppeth the mouths of all by the imposition of silence (evidently by the acclamation: 'Let us attend'), he speaketh this, rendering honor not unto the lector, but unto Him Who speaketh with all through him" [^813]. Concerning this imposition of silence mention is made also by St. Ambrose [^814] and Blessed Augustine [^815]. Of acclamations following the readings, even after the reading of the Gospels, monuments of the 4th and 5th centuries make no mention [^816].

units.slavonic_text: О том же благоговении говорит обстановка, в которой происходило чтение. Здесь прежде всего нужно отметить почти повсеместный обычай стояния за чтением Св. Писания (в противоположность синагогальному сидению), впервые отмечаемый памятниками IV–V вв. [234], но еще борющийся с обычаем сидения на этих чтениях. Борьба разрешилась тем, что стояние усвоено евангельскому чтению, а сидение прочим. Уже «Апостольские Постановления» предписывают: «Когда читается Евангелие, все пресвитеры, диаконы и весь народ да стоят в полной тишине» [235]. Но Св. Кассиан говорит, что египетские монахи во время чтений обыкновенно сидели на низеньких скамейках, причем он не отмечает какой-либо разницы в этом отношении для новозаветных чтений [236]. Созомен отмечает, как нечто странное (ξένον) в Александрийской церкви, чего он не знает и не слышал о других, — что епископ не встает на чтение Евангелия [237]. Филосторгий (IV–V вв.) рассказывает о Феофиле, епископе Арианском, что он, придя в Индию, «исправил многое, что там совершалось не по чину (οὐκ εὐαγῶς), ибо там сидя слушали и евангельское чтение и кое-что другое допускали, не дозволенное Божественным законом (ὧν μὴ θεῖος θεςμὸς ἐπεστάτει)» [238]. В жизни Св. Анастасия I, папы Римского (398–402 г.), рассказывается, что он установил, чтобы «каждый раз как читается Евангелие, священники не сидели, но стояли согбенно (curvi)» [239]. На упрек пресвитера Вигилянция, боровшегося против почитания мучеников, что Церковь допускает возжжение светильников при дневном свете у гробниц мучеников, блж. Иероним замечает: «и помимо мощей мучеников {с. 172} по всем церквам Востока, когда следует читать Евангелие, возжигаются светильники (luminaria), даже при свете солнечном, — чтобы под образом света вещественного представлялся тот свет, о котором в Псалтири читаем: «светильник ногама моима закон Твой и свет стезям моим» [240]. Следовательно, это обычай был еще не повсеместный, но едва ли новый: он сохранился от того времени, когда Евангелие всегда читалось вечером или ночью — на литургии, которая в древности совершалась вечером с агапой, а позднее (со II в.) глубоким утром, причем подготовительная часть ее сливалась с предрассветной
units.english_text: Unto the same reverence testifieth the setting wherein the reading took place. Here first of all one must note the almost universal custom of standing during the reading of Holy Scripture (in contrast unto the sitting of the synagogue), noted for the first time by monuments of the 4th and 5th centuries [^818], yet still contending with the custom of sitting during these readings. The contest was resolved by standing being assigned unto the Gospel reading, and sitting unto the rest. Already the *Apostolic Constitutions* prescribe: "When the Gospel is read, let all presbyters, deacons, and the entire people stand in complete silence" [^819]. But St. John Cassian saith that Egyptian monks during the readings customarily sat upon low benches, and he noteth no difference in this regard for New Testament readings [^820]. Sozomen noteth as something strange (*xenon*) in the Alexandrian Church—something he neither knoweth nor hath heard of in others—that the bishop does not rise during the reading of the Gospel [^821]. Philostorgius (4th–5th cc.) relateth concerning Theophilus, an Arian bishop, that upon arriving in India he "corrected many things that were performed there contrary unto the order (*ouk euagos*), for there they listened unto the Gospel reading sitting, and permitted certain other things not allowed by the Divine law (*hon me theios thesmos epestatei*)" [^822]. In the *Life of St. Anastasius I*, Pope of Rome (398–402), it is related that he established that "each time the Gospel is read, the priests should not sit, but stand bowed (*curvi*)" [^823].

units.english_text: Unto the reproach of the presbyter Vigilantius, who contended against the veneration of martyrs, that the Church permitteth the kindling of lamps in daylight at the tombs of martyrs, Blessed Jerome remarketh: "even apart from the relics of martyrs, *(Orig. p. 172)* throughout all the churches of the East, when the Gospel is about to be read, lights (*luminaria*) are kindled, even when the sun is shining—not, indeed, to banish darkness, but as a token of joy, so that under the figure of material light there may be represented that Light whereof we read in the Psalter: 'A lamp unto my feet is Thy law, and a light unto my paths'" [^824]. units.english_text: Alongside the canonical books of Holy Scripture, there were still read at divine worship in this period certain non-canonical sacred books. The distinction between the two consisted in this: that the canonical books were regarded as divinely inspired and therefore served as the rule of faith and piety, whereas the non-canonical books were regarded merely as pious compositions and were appointed for reading unto converts and catechumens [^826]. Blessed Jerome saith concerning the books of Judith, Tobit, Maccabees, the Wisdom of Solomon, and Sirach: "as the Church readeth the books of Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees, yet receiveth them not among the canonical scriptures [^827], so also these two volumes [^828] (Wisdom and Sirach) she readeth for the edification of the people (*ad aedificationem plebis*), yet not for establishing the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas" [^829]. Other writers of this period express themselves in similar fashion concerning these books, placing alongside them certain compositions of the Apostolic Fathers and ancient Christian writings as non-canonical books of the New Testament. St. Athanasius, having enumerated the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments, remarketh: "but for greater exactness, writing this also out of necessity, I subjoin that besides these there are others also, not included in the canon, which nevertheless have been appointed by the Fathers to be read unto those newly arriving (*anaginoskesthai tois arti proserchomenois*) and desiring to be instructed in the word of piety: such are the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the so-called Teaching (*Didache*) of the Apostles, and the Shepherd" [^830]. According unto *(Orig. p. 173)* Rufinus (presbyter of Aquileia, † 410), "there are also other books which by our ancestors were called not canonical, but ecclesiastical (*ecclesiastici*), such as the Wisdom of Solomon and the other Wisdom called of the Son of Sirach; of the same rank are the Book of Tobit and Judith and the Books of Maccabees; and in the New Testament the book called the Shepherd, or Hermas, and that called The Two Ways, or the Judgment of Peter (*Duae Viae sive Judicium Petri* = the 'Teaching of the Twelve Apostles', which beginneth with the words: 'Two ways...'); all these books they willed indeed to be read in the churches (*quae omnia legi quidem in ecclesiis voluerunt*), yet not to be brought forward for confirmation of faith therefrom" [^831]. Concerning the reading of the *Shepherd* in the churches Eusebius likewise makes mention: "it, as we know, hath been publicly read in the churches (*en ekklesiais ismen auto dedemosieumenon*)." In addition, he speaketh of the liturgical reading also of the Epistle of St. Clement, Bishop of Rome:

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: известно что оно было читано всенародно
units.slavonic_text: «известно, что оно было читано всенародно (ἐπὶ τοῦ κοινοῦ δεδημοσοιευμένην) и в древности и теперь у нас самих» [248]. Когда окончательно определился канон, чтение этих книг за богослужением должно было или прекратиться, или получить другой характер, чем чтение канонических книг. В некоторых церквах, по-видимому, имело место первое. Так св. Кирилл Иерусалимский увещевал: «ничего общего не должно иметь с апокрифами (так называет он все неканонические книги); то только нужно изучать, что в церкви открыто (μετὰ παῤῥησίας) мы читаем… а что в церкви не читается, то и у себя не читай» [249]. Тем не менее Созомен говорит (неодобрительно) о чтении именно в некоторых палестинских церквах апокрифического Апокалипсиса Петра (в Великую пятницу) [250]. В большинстве же церквей не только продолжалось, как показывают вышеприведенные свидетельства, чтение неканонических книг и после того, как они решительно были признаны неканоническими, но по примеру их стали читаться писания и позднейших учителей церкви, причем лишь полагалась резкая грань между чтениями боговдохновенных писаний и этих последних. Ограничивая богослужебное чтение каноническими писаниями, Собор Карфагенский воспрещает чтение других книг не безусловно, а «под именем божественных писаний» [251]. Блж. Иероним говорил о св. Ефреме Сирине: «Ефрем диакон Едесской церкви много написал на сирийском языке и достиг такой известности, что в некоторых церквах его сочинения читаются публично после чтения писаний» [252]. «Если пресвитер, — постановляет Вайсонский (в Галлии) Собор 529 г., — по какой-либо немощи не может сам проповедывать, пусть диаконами читаются гомилии св. отцев» [253]. Жизнеописатель вкладывает в уста Цезарию, еп. Арльскому (IV в.), такие слова: «если слова Господня пророков и апостолов читаются пресвитерами и диакона{с. 174}ми, почему не читать пресвитерам и диаконам слов Амвросия, Августина, или моей бедности, или каждого из святых?» [254]. Обычай чтения мученических актов за богослужением, начавшийся может быть еще во II–III вв. [255], получил теперь широкое распространение, хотя по местам вызывал законодательные ограничения и запрещения из-за неисправности этих актов. Евсевий (Кесарийский) ссылается на «записки о мучениках» и на составленную им же «книгу о мучениках» или «сборник мученичеств» (ἡ τῶς μαοτύρων συναγωγὴ) [256]. Блж. Августин неоднократно упоминает о чтениях этого рода за богослужением: «в страдании, которое сегодня нам читалось» [257]. Карфагенский Собор 397 г. постановляет: «пусть читаются и впредь (liceat etiam legi) страдания мучеников, когда совершаются ежегодные памяти (dies) их» [258]. Только в Римской Церкви декретом папы Геласия на Соборе 70 епископов в 494 г. было запрещено чтение мученических актов, которые «из особенной осторожности, по древнему обычаю, не читаются во св. Римской Церкви, потому что имена тех, которые
units.english_text: "it is known that it was publicly read (*epi tou koinou dedemosieumenen*) both in antiquity and now among ourselves" [^832]. When the canon was definitively established, the reading of these books at divine worship had either to cease or to take on a character distinct from the reading of canonical books. In certain churches, apparently, the former occurred. Thus St. Cyril of Jerusalem admonished: "one must have nothing in common with apocrypha (so he calleth all non-canonical books); that alone must one study which we read openly (*meta parresias*) in church... but that which is not read in church, read not even in private" [^833]. Nevertheless Sozomen speaketh (disapprovingly) of the reading in certain Palestinian churches of the apocryphal Apocalypse of Peter (on Great and Holy Friday) [^834]. In the majority of churches, however, not only did the reading of non-canonical books continue, as the above-cited testimonies demonstrate, even after they had been decisively recognized as non-canonical, but after their example there began to be read also the writings of later teachers of the Church, with only a sharp distinction drawn between the readings of divinely inspired scriptures and these latter. Restricting liturgical reading unto canonical scriptures, the Council of Carthage forbiddeth the reading of other books not unconditionally, but "under the name of divine scriptures" [^835]. Blessed Jerome said concerning St. Ephrem the Syrian: "Ephrem, deacon of the Church of Edessa, wrote much in the Syriac tongue and attained such renown that in certain churches his compositions are read publicly after the reading of the scriptures" [^836]. "If a presbyter," decreeth the Council of Vaison (in Gaul) of 529, "on account of any infirmity cannot preach himself, let the homilies of the holy fathers be read by the deacons" [^837]. The biographer placeth into the mouth of Caesarius, Bishop of Arles (6th c.), these words: "if the words of the Lord, of the prophets, and of the Apostles are read by presbyters and deacons, *(Orig. p. 174)* why should not presbyters and deacons read the words of Ambrose, of Augustine, or of my humble self, or of every one of the saints?" [^838]

units.english_text: The custom of reading the acts of the martyrs at divine worship, having begun perhaps already in the 2nd and 3rd centuries [^839], now attained widespread dissemination, although in certain localities it provoked legislative restrictions and prohibitions on account of the corruption of these acts. Eusebius of Caesarea referreth unto "memoirs concerning the martyrs" and unto the "book concerning the martyrs" or "collection of martyrdoms" (*he ton martyron synagoge*) composed by himself [^840]. Blessed Augustine repeatedly mentioneth readings of this kind at divine worship: "in the passion which was read unto us today" [^841]. The Council of Carthage of 397 decreeth: "it shall be lawful also hereafter (*liceat etiam legi*) for the passions of the martyrs to be read, when their annual commemorations (*dies*) are celebrated" [^842]. Only in the Roman Church by the decree of Pope Gelasius at the Council of seventy bishops in 494 was the reading of the acts of the martyrs forbidden, which "out of singular caution, according unto ancient custom, are not read in the holy Roman Church, because the names of those who wrote them are for the most part unknown, and in them, it is thought, much that is superfluous and incongruous with the matter hath been written by unfaithful simpletons (*idiotis*), such as, for instance, the passions of a certain Quiricus and Julitta, as also of Gregory and others, composed manifestly by heretics" [^843]. Nevertheless this same decree mentioneth the reading in many Roman churches, though not in the Lateran, of the acts of the holy Pope Sylvester.

units.slavonic_text: написали их большей частью не известны, (и в них), думают, написано неверными простецами (idiotis) много лишнего и несообразного с делом, каковы, например, страдания некоего Кирика и Иулитты, как и Григория и др., составленные явно еретиками» [259]. Тем не менее этот же декрет упоминает о чтении во многих римских церквах, только не в Латеранской, актов св. папы Сильвестра. Было в обычае читать в церкви и, конечно, за богослужением постановления Соборов. Блж. Августин говорит, что во многих африканских церквах принято было ежегодно во дни поста, т. е. в Четыредесятницу пред Пасхой, когда у строго постящегося народа есть более досуга, прочитывать деяния Карфагенского Собора (eadem gesta collationis) все с начала до конца по порядку [260]. Так как в чине литургии, даваемом Апостольскими Постановлениями [261], как и во всех так называемых апостольских литургиях, в основах своих восходящих к IV в. и ранее [262], указывается чтение только из канонических книг (закона, пророков, Евангелий, Деяний, посланий), то все другие чтения, должно быть, имели место за другими службами, как и ныне. Если так, то {с. 175} еще в IV в. получили начало так наз. уставные чтения за вечерней и утреней.

units.english_text: Since in the order of the Liturgy given by the *Apostolic Constitutions* [^845], as in all the so-called apostolic liturgies, which in their fundamentals ascend unto the 4th century and earlier [^846], reading is indicated only from the canonical books (the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, Acts, and the Epistles), all other readings must have taken place at other services, as is the case today. If so, then *(Orig. p. 175)* already in the 4th century did the so-called rubrical readings (*ordo*-mandated lections / *ustavnye chteniya*) at Vespers and Matins take their origin.

units.slavonic_text: Проповедь за богослужением IV–V вв. занимала не менее значительное место, чем в прежние века, благодаря живости богословских споров и повышению общего уровня образования в клире (многие церковные деятели IV–V вв. получили образование в лучших светских школах того времени). Едва ли какой период ставил более длинный ряд знаменитых проповедников и дал более материала для нынешних уставных чтений. На Востоке прославились: Евсевий Кесарийский. свв. Афанасий Великий, Василий Великий, Григорий Богослов, Кирилл Иерусалимский, Григорий Нисский, Макарий Великий, Ефрем Сирин, Иоанн Златоуст, Прокл патр. Константинопольский, Кирилл Александрийский, Епифаний Кипрский и блж. Феодорит; на Западе: св. Амвросий, блж. Августин, Петр Хрисолог, Лев Великий, Цезарий, еп. Арльский. Большинство сохранившихся от этого периода проповедей представляет из себя изъяснение Св. units.english_text: Preaching at divine worship in the 4th and 5th centuries occupied no less significant a place than in former centuries, owing unto the liveliness of theological controversies and the elevation of the general level of education among the clergy (many church figures of the 4th and 5th centuries had received an education in the finest secular schools of that epoch). Scarcely any period brought forth a longer series of illustrious preachers or furnished more material for our present rubrical readings. In the East there attained renown: Eusebius of Caesarea, Saints Athanasius the Great, Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nyssa, Macarius the Great, Ephrem the Syrian, John Chrysostom, Proclus Patriarch of Constantinople, Cyril of Alexandria, Epiphanius of Cyprus, and Blessed Theodoret; in the West: St. Ambrose, Blessed Augustine, Peter Chrysologus, Leo the Great, and Caesarius Bishop of Arles. The majority of the homilies preserved from this period represent expositions of Holy Scripture; a significant number are devoted unto dogmatic controversies; fewer are of a purely edifying character, and a comparatively small circle is constituted by festal panegyrics. Of sermons of the first kind there entered into our present divine worship in the widest measure the homilies of St. John Chrysostom, and in part of St. Basil the Great; the second kind of sermons of this period, having had a temporary character, entered not at all into our divine worship. Of the third kind there entered the discourses of St. Ephrem; of the fourth, the majority of the few works of this kind.

units.slavonic_text: пода. Проповедники этого периода нередко отмечают усердие, с которым посещались их поучения и иногда вынуждены бороться даже с преувеличенной оценкой места и значения проповеди в составе богослужения. «Проповедь», говорит св. Златоуст, «для вас все. Вы говорите, что делать в церкви, если нет проповеди? Это совершенно превратный взгляд. Что за нужда в проповеднике? Собственно из-за вас он стал необходимым. Зачем проповедь? Все ясно из Св. Писания» [263]. «Часто я искал в оный священный час (евхаристии) такого многочисленного собрания, какое теперь здесь составилось, и не находил нигде, и глубоко вздыхал я о том, что вы вашего сораба, говорящего с вами, слушаете с таким рвением, а когда Христос является на св. вечери, церковь пустеет» [264]. Но так было не везде и не всегда в этот период, может быть, только у таких витий, как Златоуст. Карфагенский Собор 399 г. постановляет: «кто выйдет из собрания (de auditorio), когда священник держит слово в церкви, да будет отлучен» [265]. Цезарий Арльский (нач. VI в.) после бесплодных убеждений не уходить с проповеди велел на время {с. 176} ее запирать церковные двери [266]. Вообще на Востоке проповедь за богослужением занимала гораздо более места, чем на Западе, как видно и из этих последних свидетельств, и из списка проповедников там и здесь, и наконец, из явно преувеличенного, но характерного свидетельства Созомена, что в Риме «ни епископ, ни другой кто не учит в церкви» [267].
units.english_text: Preachers of this period not infrequently note the zeal wherewith their instructions were attended, and at times were compelled to contend even with an exaggerated appraisal of the place and importance of preaching within the composition of divine worship. "Preaching," saith St. John Chrysostom, "is everything unto you. You say: what is there to do in church if there is no sermon? That is an entirely perverse view. What need is there of a preacher? It was properly on your account that he became necessary. Why a sermon? All is clear from Holy Scripture" [^847]. "Often have I sought at that sacred hour (of the Eucharist) for so numerous an assembly as is now gathered here, and found it nowhere; and deeply did I sigh that you listen unto your fellow-servant speaking unto you with such zeal, yet when Christ appeareth upon the mystical table, then the church is empty" [^848]. However, in that same hierarch there occur lamentations also concerning the inattention of the listeners, and concerning their departure from the church prior unto the conclusion of the instruction: "many of those standing and hearing me yawn, scratch their head, and grow weary... while others depart before I finish speaking" [^849]. Caesarius of Arles (early 6th c.), after fruitless exhortations not to leave the sermon, commanded for the duration *(Orig. p. 176)* thereof that the church doors be locked [^850]. In general, in the East preaching at divine worship occupied far more room than in the West, as is evident both from these latter testimonies, and from the catalogue of preachers here and there, and finally, from the manifestly exaggerated yet characteristic testimony of Sozomen, that in Rome "neither the bishop nor anyone else teacheth in church" [^851].

units.english_text: The principal moment for preaching remained as before the Liturgy, and specifically its preparatory portion, the Liturgy of the Catechumens, as is demonstrated by a whole series of homilies of St. John Chrysostom and others, who frequently remind their hearers of the liturgical acclamations and prayers they have just heard. But sometimes and in certain localities preaching took place also at other services. Thus the homilies on the Hexaemeron of St. Basil were delivered two in a day—at the morning office and at the evening office ("when you were present at the brief morning [*heothen*] discourse, we stumbled upon such concealed depth of thought that we despaired of that which followed, etc.") [^852]. According unto Socrates, "in Caesarea of Cappadocia and in Cyprus on Saturday and Sunday always in the evening at the lighting of the lamps (*meta tes lychnapsias*) the presbyters and bishops expound the Scriptures" [^853]. The homilies of St. John Chrysostom on Genesis were delivered in the evening ("we expound unto you the Scriptures, yet you, turning your eyes away from us, have directed your attention unto the lamps, unto him who was kindling the lamps") [^854]. "Turn your attention unto the continuation of the psalm whereof we spoke at Matins," Blessed Augustine inviteth his hearers [^855]. Since preaching was considered an indispensable constituent of the Liturgy [^856], it must, one must think, have taken place obligatorily on those days when the Liturgy was celebrated, and as frequently as the latter was celebrated in any locality. But during Great Lent (*Tessarakoste*) and Pentecost, especially during the former—in view of the catechumens—they preached for the most part daily. Thus in the homilies of St. John Chrysostom on Genesis and "On the Statues," as well as in the discourses of Blessed Augustine on the psalms, references unto "yesterday's" discourse constantly occur. In monastic communities, moreover, at least in certain ones, as we shall see, the abba daily instructed the brethren throughout the entire year.

units.slavonic_text: настолько часто, насколько где-либо совершалась последняя. Но в Четыредесятницу и Пятидесятницу, особенно в первую — в виду оглашенных, проповедовали большей частью ежедневно. Так в беседе св. Златоуста на Бытие и «о статуях», равно как в словах блж. Августина на псалмы постоянно встречаются ссылки на «вчерашнюю» беседу. В монашеских же общинах, по крайней мере некоторых, как увидим, авва и в течение целого года ежедневно поучал братию.
units.english_text: As regards the persons who preached, following the example of the Apostles and the practice of the 2nd and 3rd centuries [^857], the true minister of the word was considered to be the bishop. "The proper office (*proprium munus*) of a bishop is to teach the people" [^858]. According unto St. John *(Orig. p. 177)* Chrysostom, the ability to teach in a bishop "ought to be before all else" [^859]. Preaching talent in that era most of all advanced persons unto episcopal sees, as the examples of Eusebius of Caesarea, Saints Gregory the Theologian, John Chrysostom, and Blessed Augustine demonstrate. But in ecclesiastical teaching presbyters also took part far more than in former times. Already in the 3rd century so illustrious a preacher as Origen was merely a presbyter. The *Apostolic Constitutions* prescribe: after the readings, and in particular after the Gospel, "let the presbyters severally, and not all at once, exhort the people, and after them all the bishop, who is like unto a helmsman" [^860]. In conformity with this, in the Church of Jerusalem according unto the description of the *Pilgrimage* attributed unto Sylvia, on the Lord's Day "of all the sitting presbyters whosoe'er desireth preacheth, and after them all the bishop preacheth" [^861]. St. John Chrysostom preached in Antioch precisely in the rank of presbyter in the presence of his bishop Flavian, who sometimes added his own exhortation unto his sermon [^862]. Unto Blessed Augustine, when he was a presbyter, his aged bishop Valerius, who possessed poor command of the Latin tongue of his flock, committed preaching in church; and when the bishop was reproached for this, he appealed unto Eastern custom of this kind [^863]. Consequently, in the West prior unto that time preaching had been the prerogative of the bishop alone. But already Blessed Jerome saith concerning this: "it is a very bad custom that in certain churches the presbyters keep silence and speak not in the presence of the bishops, as though the latter envied them or disdained to listen unto them" [^864]. In cases of necessity or extraordinary circumstances, deacons also were admitted unto preaching. Already in the 3rd century, according unto the testimony of St. Cyprian, during persecutions which at times deprived the Church of presbyters, the right of preaching was granted also unto deacons [^865]. One of the most renowned preachers of the 4th century, St. Ephrem, possessed only the rank of deacon. St. Gregory the Great, Pope of Rome († 604), during illness commissioned deacons to read his homilies [^866]. Above we saw that deacons were commissioned with the reading at divine worship of the homilies of the holy fathers [^867]. Even laymen were admitted unto preaching, but only in the most exceptional cases. Thus it was already in the 3rd century according to the testimony of Eusebius, when Origen withdrew from Alexandria to Caesarea of Palestine, "here the local bishops (Alexander of Jerusalem and Theoctistus of Caesarea) requested him to discourse and expound the Holy Scriptures publicly in church, notwithstanding the fact that at that time he was not yet ordained unto the presbyterate"; and unto the reproach on the part of Demetrius, Bishop of Alexandria, "that it had never been heard of and was not now the custom *(Orig. p. 178)* for a layman to preach in the presence of a bishop," they appealed unto a whole series of former examples in diverse countries [^868]. But from the 4th and 5th centuries such examples are no longer known, if one discount the speech of Emperor Constantine the Great unto the First Ecumenical Council. On the contrary, when certain monks in the East began to arrogate unto themselves the right of church preaching, Pope Leo I the Great (440–461), unto whom, perhaps, even the preaching of a presbyter in church was unfamiliar, wrote against this unto Maximus, Bishop of Antioch, and Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, saying in his letter unto the former: "beside the priests of the Lord, let none dare to preach, whether he be monk or layman, under whatsoever name of learning (*cujuslibet scientiae nomine*) he may be renowned" [^869]. But the Council of Carthage of 399 decrees: "let not a layman (*laicus*) dare to teach in the presence of clerics, unless they themselves request him so to do" [^870].

units.slavonic_text: проповедованию, но только в самых исключительных случаях. Так было еще в III в. по свидетельству Евсевия, когда Ориген удалился из Александрии в Кесарию Палестинскую, «здесь местные епископы (Александр Иерусалимский и Феоктист Кесарийский) просили его беседовать и изъяснять Св. Писание всенародно в церкви, несмотря на то, что тогда он не был еще рукоположен в пресвитера» и на упрек со стороны Димитрия, еп. Александрийского, «что никогда не слыхано было и теперь не в обычае {с. 178} мирянину проповедовать в присутствии епископа», ссылались на целый ряд прежних примеров в разных странах [284]. Но от IV и V вв. неизвестно уже таких примеров, если не считать речи имп. Константина Великого к первому Вселенскому Собору. Напротив, когда некоторые монахи на Востоке стали присваивать себе право церковной проповеди, папа Лев I Великий (440–461), для которого, может быть, странна была и проповедь пресвитера в церкви, писал против этого Максиму, еп. Антиохийскому, и Феодориту, еп. Киррскому, говоря в письме первому: «кроме священников Господних никто не смеет проповедовать, монах ли то, или мирянин, какою бы ученостью (cujus libet scientiae nomine) ни славился он» [285]. Но Карфагенский Собор 399 г. постановляет: «мирянин (laicus) да не дерзает учить в присутствии клириков, если они сами не попросят его об этом» [286].
units.english_text: Only unto woman, as ever since apostolic times [^871], was preaching unconditionally forbidden. That same Council decrees: "A woman, however learned and holy, let her not presume (*non praesumat*) to teach men in the assembly" [^872]. In the Eastern Churches, however, deaconesses were permitted to engage in the catechization of women preparing for baptism, yet not publicly, but privately [^873]. In this regard certain heretical communities differed sharply from the Catholic Church, not only permitting the preaching of women, but possessing prophetesses, such as were Prisca and Maximilla among the Montanists, and elevating women unto the episcopal and presbyteral ranks, as among them Quintilla and Priscilla [^874]. The same was true among the Collyridians of the 4th century, among whom women celebrated sacred rites in honor of the Most Holy Virgin Mary, as also among the Cataphrygians [^875].

units.slavonic_text: Только женщине, как и всегда, с апостольских еще времен [287], безусловно воспрещалась проповедь, Тот же Собор постановляет: «Женщина, хотя бы ученая и святая, да не присваивает себе права (non praesumat) учить мужчин в собрании» [288]. В восточных Церквах, впрочем, диакониссам позволялось заниматься оглашением готовящихся ко крещению женщин, но не публично, а частно [289]. В этом отношении от Кафолической Церкви резко отличались некоторые еретические общины, не только допускавшие проповедь женщин, но имевшие пророчиц, какими у монтанистов были Приска и Максимилла, и возводившие женщин в степени епископскую и пресвитерскую, как у них же Квинтилла и Присцилла [290]. То же было у коллиридинан IV в., у которых женщины совершали священнодействия в честь Пресв. Девы Марии, как и у катафригов [291].
units.english_text: Inasmuch as preaching, serving as an exposition of Holy Scripture and wholly grounded upon it, was likewise regarded, in some measure, as the word of God, so also was preaching framed with rites and acclamations almost identical unto the reading of Holy Scripture. Thus before the sermon the deacon invited those present unto silence and attention [^876], perhaps with the acclamation **"Let us attend"** (*Proschomen*). Before the instruction the preacher offered a prayer, presumably secretly [^877]. Before the instruction it was customary for the preacher to greet the people in the name of God [^878]. *(Orig. p. 179)* This greeting was usually expressed by the acclamations: **"Peace be unto you"** [^879] or: **"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all,"** with the response **"And with thy spirit"** [^880]. The sermon began with diverse prayerful acclamations, for example, **"Blessed is God"** (*Eulogetos ho Theos*) [^881]. The conclusion of the sermon was ordinarily a doxology unto the Holy Trinity [^882].

units.english_text: As regards the bodily posture in which the sermon was delivered and heard, at least the bishop usually delivered the sermon seated upon his ambo [^883], which, perhaps, was a borrowing from the synagogue and was founded upon the example of the Savior [^884]. But in St. John Chrysostom indication is also made of the preacher standing [^885]. The hearers always stood. Blessed Augustine says: "that I may not detain you long, since I speak sitting, whereas it is difficult for you to stand..." units.slavonic_stem_tier2: монашеское богослужение
units.slavonic_text: Монашеское богослужение
units.english_text: Monasticism in the Church appeared much earlier than the 4th century. From her first days there was always within her something corresponding unto this institution. Not to speak of the great *(Orig. p. 180)* asceticism of John the Baptist, which properly opened the era of the New Testament, both the Savior and the Apostles presupposed and sanctioned ascetic dispositions in certain Christians [^889]. In the writers of the 2nd and 3rd centuries, indications increasingly occur concerning the existence in the Church of an entire class of persons who made continence the goal of their lives [^890]. In the 3rd century such ascetics already constitute entire communities. At least there is record of communities of virgins from this era; into one of such communities (*eis parthenona*) St. Anthony placed his only sister before withdrawing into the desert [^891]. The virgins also differed in their outward appearance and clothing from ordinary Christians [^892]. A series of 3rd-century writers occupy themselves with the question concerning them, writing epistles unto them and treatises concerning them, for the most part praising their continence [^893], yet at times also rebuking their shortcomings [^894]. From the 2nd century examples are likewise known of withdrawal for a more or less prolonged period into solitary places for ascetic purposes [^895], sometimes on account of external inducements, for example, owing to persecutions against Christians [^896], yet frequently solely for ascetic struggles of continence. The latter phenomenon is known at least in Egypt, where before St. Anthony hermits were not uncommon, yet they struggled near their own villages, so that "a monk did not yet know the great desert" [^897].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: отшельничество
units.slavonic_text: Отшельничество
units.english_text: All these anchorites and even their communities, both by reason of their small number and their little renown, and because they did not break definitively with the former way of life, exercised no influence upon the elaboration of divine worship. This influence on the part of asceticism began when, with the further development of the latter, certain of the anchorites attained universal *(Orig. p. 181)* ecclesiastical fame, when their way of life (*modus vivendi*) and prayerful labors began to evoke imitation among many.

units.slavonic_incipit: Все эти отшельники и даже общины
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: все эти отшельники и даже общины их и
units.slavonic_text: Все эти отшельники и даже общины их, и по немногочисленности своей, и по малоизвестности, и потому, что не порывали окончательно с прежним укладом жизни, не оказали влияния на выработку богослужения. Влияние это со стороны подвижничества началось тогда, когда, при дальнейшем развитии последнего, некоторые из отшельников достигли обще{с. 181}церковной славы, когда их образ жизни (modus vivendi) и молитвенные подвиги стали вызывать у многих подражание.
units.english_text: The first ascetic of this kind was St. Paul of Thebes, concerning whom it was revealed unto St. Anthony himself that the former was greater than he. An Egyptian by birth, having withdrawn into the desert [^898] at the age of 15 during one of the persecutions against Christians, fearing the betrayal of his brother-in-law, St. Paul lived there without ever leaving for about 100 years (he died at the age of 113 in the year 341, when St. Anthony was 90 years old), without seeing a human face; he lived in a cave near a spring beside which a date palm grew; its fruits served him for food, and from its fronds he made clothing for himself. St. Anthony discovered this ascetic only a few days before his death [^899]. Yet thereby everything was done that such a life should not pass without a profound influence upon the Church. Perhaps the significance of Anthony himself in the development of monasticism was merely broader and more noticeable. For the history of divine worship, it was important here that the ascetic completely renounced the consolation afforded by public divine worship and replaced it with his own prayer. Thereby was laid the foundation for the elaboration of a new type of divine worship.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: прп павел фивейский
units.slavonic_text: Прп. Павел Фивейский
units.english_text: St. Anthony the Great († 356) withdrew into the desert now exclusively from ascetic motives and spent therein his entire 105-year life from his twentieth year. He settled at first in a tomb-cave near his native village in Lower Egypt near the city of Heraclea and the Thebaid desert on the western bank of the Nile, then in an abandoned fortress of the eastern desert (between the Nile and the Red Sea), and finally in the depths of that same desert upon a mountain, in a cell hewn into the rock, of the length and breadth of a man's stature [^900]. St. Anthony nourished himself at first only with bread and salt, which was brought unto him some twice a year [^901]; in old age, partly in order to spare the labor of those who brought him bread, he began to cultivate a fertile plot in the desert, and at the request of his disciples began to eat olives and oil; St. Anthony took food once a day at sunset, remaining without food for 2 days and more, up to 4 or 5 [^902], frequently spending an entire night without sleep; he slept upon the bare ground, *(Orig. p. 182)* sometimes upon a rush mat [^903]. Everyone was especially astonished (which enhanced the attractive power of his ascetic feats) that under such a life "his body preserved its former appearance, not grown heavy from lack of movement, nor wasted away from fasts" [^904].

units.slavonic_incipit: Постоянным занятием прп. Антония были молитва
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: стоянным занятием прп антония были молитва и богомыслие
units.slavonic_text: Постоянным занятием прп. Антония были молитва и богомыслие, при чем на первых порах ему пришлось выдерживать тяжелую борьбу со смущавшими его помыслами и привидениями (φαντασίαι καὶ σχηματισμοί) [321]. С последними прп. Антоний, зная их последний источник (демонов), боролся благодатною силою Св. Писания, которое он, решительно отказавшись в детстве (не смотря на интеллигентное происхождение свое) от обучения грамоте, не мог читать, но помнил по чтениям в храме [322]; особенно пользовался он в этой борьбе некоторыми местами Псалмов, например Пс. 117, 7: «Господь мне помощник, и аз воззрю на враги моя», Пс. 26, 3: «Аще ополчится на мя полк, не убоится сердце мое», Пс. 67, 2: «Да воскреснет Бог и расточатся врази его и да бежат от лица Его ненавидящии Его». Это вообще свидетельствует о широком употреблении псалмов прп. Антонием за молитвою. Кроме того, это обстоятельство из жизни прп. Антония и др. подвижников, могло содействовать появления в богослужебном уставе прокимнов, versicula, capitula и т. п., которых IV–V в. еще не знали. Очень рано прп. Антоний сознал необходимость присоединить к молитве и ручной труд, мысль о чем, как очень важная и новая, по преданию, внушена преподобному особым видением (бывшим уже на втором месте его подвигов) — ангела в монашеской одежде, плетущего в промежутках между молитвою веревку из пальмовых листьев [323]. С этого времени до конца жизнь он молитву перемежал плетением корзин и рогож из пальмовых листьев. В рассказе Лавсаика об искусе, которым подверг прп. Антоний св. Павла Простого пред допущением его к себе в ученики, описывается отчасти молитвенно-подвижнический день самого прп. Антония. После работы прп. Павла (над плетением веревки) продолжавшейся до 9 часа, прп. Антоний хочет, по-видимому, предложить ему пищу; но в целях испытания откладывает это до захода солнца. Тогда
units.english_text: The constant occupation of Saint Anthony was prayer and the contemplation of God, wherein at the beginning he had to endure a grievous struggle against the thoughts and phantoms (*phantasiai kai schematismoi*) that troubled him [^905]. Against the latter St. Anthony, knowing their ultimate source (the demons), struggled through the gracious power of Holy Scripture, which he, having decisively refused in childhood (notwithstanding his cultured origin) to learn letters, could not read, but remembered from the readings in church [^906]; he especially made use in this struggle of certain passages of the Psalms, for example Ps. 117:7: "The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon mine enemies"; Ps. 26:3: "Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear"; Ps. 67:2: "Let God arise, and let His enemies be scattered, and let them that hate Him flee from before His face." This in general bears witness unto the extensive use of the psalms by St. Anthony in prayer. Moreover, this circumstance from the life of St. Anthony and other ascetics may have contributed unto the appearance in the liturgical typikon of prokeimena, *versicula*, *capitula*, and the like, whereof the 4th and 5th centuries knew nothing as yet. Very early St. Anthony recognized the necessity of joining manual labor unto prayer, a thought which, being very important and new, according to tradition was inspired unto the venerable father by a special vision (occurring already at the second place of his ascetic labors)—of an angel in monastic habit, weaving a rope from palm leaves in the intervals between prayer [^907]. From that time until the end of his life he alternated prayer with the weaving of baskets and mats from palm leaves. In the account of the *Lausiac History* concerning the testing unto which St. Anthony subjected St. Paul the Simple before admitting him unto himself as a disciple, the prayerful and ascetic daily routine of St. Anthony himself is partly described. units.slavonic_stem_tier2: антоний принес и положил на стол четыре сухих
units.slavonic_text: «Антоний принес и положил на стол четыре сухих хлебца, унций по 6 каждый, и размочил один для себя а для него три, потом начал петь псалом, какой знал он и пропев его двенадцать раз, столько же раз молился, чтобы и в этом {с. 183} испытать Павла (оттянуть время еды). После 12 молитв Антоний сказал ему: пойди ешь. Воспретив однако затем есть, преподобный «сказал ему: вставай, помолись и ложись спать. В полночь Антоний разбудил его на молитву», и продолжал молиться до девятого часа дня. После трапезы, бывшей поздно вечером, Антоний прочитал 12 молитв и пропел 12 псалмов. После молитвы они уснули немного первым сном; потом опять встали и пели псалмы от полуночи до самого дня» [324].
units.english_text: "Anthony brought and placed upon the table four dry loaves of bread, of some 6 ounces each, and moistened one for himself and three for him; then he began to chant a psalm that he knew, and having chanted it twelve times, he prayed as many times, in order in this also to *(Orig. p. 183)* test Paul (to prolong the time before eating). After 12 prayers Anthony said unto him: Go, eat. Forbidding him, however, thereafter to eat, the venerable father 'said unto him: Arise, pray, and lie down to sleep. At midnight Anthony awakened him unto prayer,' and continued to pray until the ninth hour of the day. After the meal, which took place late in the evening, Anthony read 12 prayers and chanted 12 psalms. After the prayer they slept a little during the first sleep; then they arose again and chanted psalms from midnight until the very day" [^908].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: дальнейшее отшельничество
units.slavonic_text: Дальнейшее отшельничество
units.english_text: Once having appeared, asceticism could not but develop and grow not only in extent, but also in degree and intensity. Indeed, the anchorites following Anthony the Great elaborate in detail and perfect unto the utmost limits the ascetic life and monasticism. If they do not surpass the first founders of monasticism, they evoke greater amazement by their ascetic feats, and consequently exercise an irresistible influence upon the entire structure of church life. These were living typika of fasting and prayer, whereof written typika were faint copies, and unto which in any event our Typikon owes more than unto all subsequent typika, ktetorial and otherwise. Of the incredible results which this younger generation of Egyptian ascetics achieved, an approximate idea may be given by certain traits from the life of St. Sisoes the Great († 429).

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: прп сисой великий
units.slavonic_text: Прп. Сисой Великий
units.english_text: "A brother asked Sisoes why he, having left Scete (a monastery founded by the younger contemporaries of St. Anthony in the Thebaid desert), had settled here (in the desert). The elder replied: When Scete began to become populous, and I heard that Abba Anthony had fallen asleep, I arose and came unto this mountain; and finding this place tranquil, I settled here for a little time.—And is it long, abba, that thou hast lived here?—the brother asked.—72 years,—the elder replied" [^909]. "The disciple of Abba Sisoes often used to say: Abba, arise, let us eat. The elder would say: Have we not eaten yet, my son? We have not eaten, father, the disciple replied. Then the elder would say: If we have not eaten, let us eat" [^910]; yet they ate no more than once a day—in the evening. "They recounted concerning Abba Sisoes: he did not eat bread (but only raw herbs). On the feast of Pascha the brethren entreated him to share the meal with them. The elder said unto them: I can do one of two things: I will eat either bread or the dishes prepared by you. They said unto him: Eat only bread. And so he did" [^911]. "One father related concerning Sisoes: once, desiring to overcome sleep, he suspended himself from a cliff in a cave. An angel came, took him down, and forbade him to repeat this, lest he set an example for others" [^912]. "They recounted concerning Abba Poemen: When certain elders visited him *(Orig. p. 184)* and, speaking of the elders, mentioned Abba Sisoes, Poemen would say: Cease speaking of Abba Sisoes; for his deeds are beyond narration" [^913].

units.slavonic_text: бывали у него {с. 184} какие-нибудь старцы и, разговаривая о старцах, упоминали об авве Сисое, Пимен говорил: перестаньте говорить об авве Сисое; ибо дела его выше повествования» [329].
units.english_text: In general, the life of the Egyptian ascetics of this era outlined an ideal for all aspects of the monastic order touched upon by written typika. Most of all, of course, was accomplished in regard to fasting. Spontaneously there became established certain norms, rules, minimal requirements—and very arduous ones—both as regards the kind of food for the ascetic, and concerning the time of its taking and the durations of fasting. Meat, of course, was unconditionally not used [^914], yet the tasting thereof in case of necessity was not accounted a transgression of the vow [^915]. Dairy products, it seems, were occasionally permitted [^916], fish— *(Orig. p. 185)* more frequently [^917]. Wine was in principle allowed [^918], but many did not drink it [^919] and in general nothing beside water [^920]. The ordinary food consisted, among the majority of the Egyptian anchorites, it seems, of bread alone with salt, with abstinence from all else [^921]; others for decades nourished *(Orig. p. 186)* themselves only with raw herbs, denying themselves even bread [^922]; but many permitted themselves in general any, provided it were the simplest, vegetable food, and even at times (for example, on feast days) oil [^923].

units.english_text: As regards the time of taking food, before the ninth hour (3 o'clock in the afternoon) they did not eat at all [^924]; but the most zealous ascetics could boast that *(Orig. p. 187)* "the sun had never seen them eating" [^925], and demanded of their disciples to take food not at the ninth hour, but in the evening [^926]. In regard to prolonged total abstinence from food, the norm for an accomplished ascetic was considered the taking of food every two days [^927]; this certain anchorites counseled also unto their disciples [^928]. Others tasted no food for 5 days [^929] or ate once a week [^930]. As exceptional cases, instances of total fasting for 40 days [^931] and more [^932] are recorded. Through long practice of such fasting certain anchorites attained, it seems, unto such a state that after two days of total abstinence they felt no hunger whatever [^933]. But with the passage of time asceticism nevertheless arrived at the conclusion that total abstinence for longer than one day, presumably as being not within the capacity of everyone, was dangerous, and they ceased to recommend it [^934].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: для каждого посильное опасно и его не стали
units.slavonic_text: для каждого посильное, опасно, и его не стали рекомендовать [350]. {с. 188} При таком посте, в который обращалась вся жизнь отшельника, тем не менее признавалось необходимым чтить общецерковные посты, выделять их из ряда подобных постов и, конечно, усилением воздержания, хотя у иных отшельников, по-видимому, некуда было здесь идти дальше. Это были таким образом посты из постов. Пред Четыредесятницей прп. Макарий Александрийский, «наломавши большое количество пальмовых ветвей (для рукоделия), стал в углу и в продолжении всей Четыредесятницы до самой Пасхи не принимал хлеба, не касался воды, не преклонял колен, не садился, не ложился и ничего не вкушал, кроме нескольких листьев сухой капусты; да их ел только по воскресеньям и то для того, чтобы видели, что он ест, и чтобы самому ему не впасть в самомнение; а ежели когда выходил из кельи для какой-либо нужды, то как можно скорее опять возвращался и принимался за дело; не открывая уст и не говоря ни слова, он стоял в безмолвии; все занятие его состояло в молитве сердечной и в плетении ветвей, которые были у него в руках» [351]. Прп. Павел Великий, галатянин, «провел всю Четыредесятницу в с малою мерою чечевицы и кружкою воды и был в затворе до самого праздника» [352]. Чтили подвижники и пост среды и пятницы. «Непозволительно, говорил прп. Аполлос Гермопольский (нач. V в.), нарушать без всякой нужды (nisi grandis aliqua necessitas fieret) всеобщие (καθολικὰς, legitima) посты (среды и пятницы), ибо в среду Спаситель предан, а в пяток распят; посему, кто нарушает это пост, тот вместе с врагами предает распинает Спасителя. Если в пост придет к тебе брат, имеющий нужду в успокоении (по Руфину: и ранее 9 часа захочет подкрепиться для дороги), предложи трапезу ему одному; если же ему не угодно, не принуждай; ибо все мы имеем общее предание о посте» [353].

units.english_text: With such a fast, into which the entire life of an anchorite was turned, it was nevertheless recognized as necessary to honor the general fasts of the Church, to distinguish them from the series of ordinary fasts, and, of course, by an intensification of abstinence, although among certain anchorites there was, it seems, nowhere further to go in this regard. These were thus fasts of fasts. Before the Great Fast (*Tessarakoste*), St. Macarius of Alexandria, "having broken off a great quantity of palm branches (for manual labor), stood in a corner and throughout the entire Great Fast until Pascha itself took no bread, touched no water, bowed not his knees, sat not down, lay not down, and tasted nothing save a few leaves of dry cabbage; and these he ate only on Sundays, and that so that they might see that he was eating, and that he himself might not fall into conceit; and if ever he went forth from the cell for any necessity, he returned as quickly as possible again and took up his work; not opening his lips and speaking not a word, he stood in silence; his entire occupation consisted in prayer of the heart and in weaving the branches which were in his hands" [^935]. St. Paul the Great, the Galatian, "spent the entire Great Fast with a small measure of lentils and a jar of water, and remained in seclusion until the feast itself" [^936]. The ascetics also honored the fast of Wednesday and Friday. "It is not permissible," said St. Apollos of Hermopolis (early 5th c.), "to violate without absolute necessity (*nisi grandis aliqua necessitas fieret*) the universal (*katholikas*, *legitima*) fasts (of Wednesday and Friday), for on Wednesday the Savior was betrayed, and on Friday crucified; therefore, whosoever violates this fast, together with His enemies betrays and crucifies the Savior. If in the fast a brother come unto thee, having need of refreshment (according to Rufinus: and before the 9th hour wishes to be strengthened for the journey), set a table for him alone; yet if it please him not, constrain him not; for we all have a common tradition concerning the fast" [^937].

units.english_text: The anchorites of the 4th and 5th centuries laid the foundations also for the elaboration of the monastic rule of prayer and psalmody. Our Typikon specifically inherited from them the extensive use of the Psalter. "The love of psalmody gave birth to monasteries," says Blessed Augustine [^940]. The narratives of the life of the anchorites are replete with mentions of the Psalter and citations of it in their sayings. Very early among the ascetics special rules were established also for the prayerful application of the Psalter. The most ancient rule of this kind was probably the reading at one time of the entire Psalter as a day or night prayer.

units.slavonic_incipit: Отшельники IV–V вв. положили основы и
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: отшельники вв положили основы и для выработки
units.slavonic_text: Отшельники IV–V вв. положили основы и для выработки монастырского правила молитвы и псалмопения. Наш устав именно от них унаследовал широкое употребление Псалтири. «Любовь к псалмопению родила монастыри», говорит блж. Августин [356]. Сказания о жизни отшельников пестрят упоминаниями о Псалтири и ссылками на нее в их изречениях. Очень рано у подвижников устанавливаются и особые правила для молитвенного применения Псалтири. Древнейшим правилом такого рода вероятно было прочитывание за раз всей Псалтири в качестве дневной или ночной молитвы.
units.english_text: "Once Abba Serapion († ca. 358) was passing through an Egyptian village, and seeing a harlot standing by her chamber, said unto her: Await me this evening; I will come unto thee and spend the night with thee.—Very well, abba, the harlot replied. And so she prepared herself and spread the couch. In the evening the elder locked the door and said unto her: Wait a little; I must only fulfill our customary rule (*epeide nomon echomen, heos hou poieso auton*). And the elder began his synaxis (*tes synaxeos*). Having begun the Psalter, he offered at (*kata*) each psalm a prayer (*euchen*) for her, entreating God to grant her repentance and salvation,—and God heard the monk. The harlot stood trembling and praying beside the elder. When the elder had finished the entire Psalter, she fell upon the earth. The elder took the Apostle, read much from it, and concluded his synaxis (*synaxin*)" [^942].

units.slavonic_text: характерен по проводимому в нем взгляду на благодатную силу молитвенного правила. Постепенно, должно быть, стали уменьшать такое очень уже большое «правило» (вся Псалтирь). Может быть правило исполнял и Эрон (вышеупоминавшийся), когда идя с автором Лавсаика и другими по пустыне, дорогою «прочитал 15 псалмов (1/10 часть Псалтири), потом великий псалом (118?), потом послание к евреям, потом Исаию и часть Иеремии пророка, затем Луку евангелиста и Притчи» [359]. Неоднократны указания на употребление у отшельников в качестве молитвенного правила 12 псалмов. Два отшельника, выбравшие себе в руководители прп. Макария Египетского, когда тот навестил их и переночевал у них, наутро предлагают ему:
units.english_text: "Wilt thou that we chant (*balomen*, *recitemus*) twelve psalms?—Very well, I replied,"—relates Macarius concerning this. "Then the younger chanted (*psallei*) 5 psalms, and after (*apo*) every 6 verses chanted one alleluia (literally: every, *apo*, 6 verses and 1 alleluia). And at each verse a ray of fire issued from his mouth and ascended unto heaven. In like manner, when the elder opened his mouth for singing, there issued from it as it were a cord of fire and reached unto heaven. And I also recited (*eipon*) a little from memory" [^944].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: хочеш ли мы споем двенадцат псалмов
units.slavonic_text: «Хочешь ли мы споем (βάλωμεν, recitemus) двенадцать псалмов? — Хорошо, отвечал я», — рассказывает об этом Макарий. «Тогда младший пропел (ψάλλει) 5 псалмов и после (ἀπὸ) каждых 6 стихов пел одно аллилуиа (букв.: по, ἀπὸ, 6 стихов и 1 аллилуиа). И на каждом стихе огненный луч выходил из уст его и восходил на небо. Подобным образом, когда и старший отверзал уста для пения, из них выходила как бы огненная вервь и достигала неба. И я также проговорил (εἶπον) немного наизусть» [360].
units.english_text: When a Roman ascetic in the monastery (Scete) was visited by a certain great Egyptian ascetic, at the onset of evening "they read (*ebalon*) 12 psalms and lay down. They did the same also at night," and again lay down [^945]. The same ascetic thus describes his prayer rule: "instead of music and singing I read through (*lego*) 12 psalms (by day or in the evening); in like manner also at night, for the sins which I have committed, immediately after taking rest (*arti met' anapauseos*—after a short sleep?) I perform my little office (*poio ten mikran mou leitourgian*)" [^946]. Besides the psalms and Holy Scripture, brief prayers were employed, recited hundreds of times. Paul of Ferme (4th c.) performed 300 prayers in a day, of which he kept count by drawing pebbles from his bosom (the germ of prayer ropes); when, however, he heard that a certain virgin performed 700 prayers, his rule began to seem small unto him, and he turned for the resolution of his perplexity unto St. Macarius of Egypt; the latter replied: "Behold, for sixty years now I perform only the 100 prescribed prayers (*tetagmenas euchas*)" [^947]. An example of such a brief prayer is given in the instruction of St. Macarius unto those who asked him: "How ought one to pray?"

provenance.verbatim_source: When a Roman ascetic in the monastery (Scete) was visited by a certain great Egyptian ascetic, at the onset of evening "they read (*ebalon*) 12 psalms and lay down. They did the same also at night," and again lay down [^945]. The same ascetic thus describes his prayer rule: "instead of music and singing I read through (*lego*) 12 psalms (by day or in the evening); in like manner also at night, for the sins which I have committed, immediately after taking rest (*arti met' anapauseos*—after a short sleep?) I perform my little office (*poio ten mikran mou leitourgian*)" [^946]. Besides the psalms and Holy Scripture, brief prayers were employed, recited hundreds of times. Paul of Ferme (4th c.) performed 300 prayers in a day, of which he kept count by drawing pebbles from his bosom (the germ of prayer ropes); when, however, he heard that a certain virgin performed 700 prayers, his rule began to seem small unto him, and he turned for the resolution of his perplexity unto St. Macarius of Egypt; the latter replied: "Behold, for sixty years now I perform only the 100 prescribed prayers (*tetagmenas euchas*)" [^947]. An example of such a brief prayer is given in the instruction of St. Macar

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: когда подвижника римлянина в монастыре скиту посетил какой то великий
units.slavonic_text: Когда подвижника-римлянина в монастыре (Скиту) посетил какой-то великий египетский подвижник, они с наступлением вечера «прочитали (ἔβαλον) 12 псалмов и легли. То же сделали и ночью», и опять легли [361]. Тот же подвижник так описывает свое молитвенное правило: «вместо музыки и пения я прочитываю (λέγω) 12 псалмов (днем или вечером); равным образом и ночью, за грехи, которые содеял, тотчас с упокоением (ἄρти μετ᾽ ἀναπαύσεως — после короткого сна?) совершаю малую мою службу (ποιῶ τὴν μικρὰν μου λειτουργίαν)» [362]. Кроме псалмов и Св. Писания употреблялись краткие молитвы, произносившиеся сотнями раз. Павел Фермейский (IV в.) совершал 300 молитв в сутки, которым вел счет, вынимая из пазухи камешки (зародыш четок); когда же он услышал, что одна девственница совершает по 700 молитв, ему его правило стало казаться малым, и он обратился за разрешением недоумения к прп. Макарию Египетскому; тот ответил: «я вот уже шестидесятый год совершаю только по 100 положенных молитв (τεтаγμένας εὐχὰς)» [363]. Образец подобной краткой молитвы дан в наставлении прп. Макария вопросившим его: «как должно молиться?»

units.slavonic_text: [364]. Воспоминанием об этих кратких отшельнических молитвах служит у нас молитва «Господи Иисусе {с. 191} Христе», которую положено сотни раз произносить неграмотным за опускаемые церковные службы. Как всегдашний пост у пустынножителей усиливался в период церковных постов, так и обычное молитвенное правило увеличивалось для праздников.
units.english_text: [^948] As a memorial of these brief anchoritic prayers there serveth among us the prayer **"Lord Jesus *(Orig. p. 191)* Christ"** (*Gospodi Iisuse Khriste*), which is appointed to be recited hundreds of times by the illiterate in place of omitted church services. As the perpetual fast among the desert-dwellers was intensified during periods of church fasts, so likewise was their customary prayer rule increased for feast days.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: в воскресные дни также и в субботу отшельники
units.slavonic_text: В воскресные дни, также и в субботу, отшельники обычно причащались. «Монахов, живущих в пустыне, жжет яд злых демонов, и они с нетерпением ждут субботы и воскресения, чтобы идти на источники водные, т. е. приступить к телу и крови Господней, дабы очиститься от скверн лукавого» [366]. Для этого отшельники ходили большей частью в соседние храмы, не смотря на отдаленность их [367]. «Рассказывали, что авва Сисой Фивейский имел обычай бегом бежать в свою келью по окончании церковного служения, и говорили: в нем бес» [368]. О приобщении отшельников запасными Дарами говорит Василий Великий: «все отшельники (μονάζοντες), живущие в пустыне, где нет священника, храня причастие в доме, сами себя причащают» [369]. Есть указания на совершение литургии специально для отшельника в его келии пресвитером. «Рассказывали об авве Марке Египетском: он 30 лет прожил, ни разу не выходя из своей кельи; к нему обыкновенно приходил пресвитер совершать для него св. приношение (ποιεῖν αὐτῷ τὴν ἁγίαν προσφορὰν)» [370]. «К некоему отшельнику ходил одни пресвитер, совершая для него приношение св. Таин (τῶν ἁγίων μυστηρίων τὴν προσφορὰν)» [371].
units.english_text: On Sundays, as likewise on Saturday, the anchorites customarily communicated. "The monks dwelling in the desert are burned by the venom of evil demons, and they wait with impatience for Saturday and Sunday to go unto the fountains of water, that is, to draw near unto the Body and Blood of the Lord, in order to cleanse themselves from the defilements of the wicked one" [^950]. For this purpose the anchorites went for the most part unto neighboring churches, notwithstanding their remoteness [^951]. "They recounted that Abba Sisoes of Thebes was accustomed to run in haste unto his cell at the conclusion of the church service, and they said: a demon is in him" [^952]. Concerning the communion of anchorites with reserved Gifts, St. Basil the Great saith: "all the hermits (*monazontes*) dwelling in the desert where there is no priest, keeping the communion in their dwelling, communicate themselves" [^953]. There are indications of the celebration of the Liturgy specifically for an anchorite in his cell by a presbyter. "They recounted concerning Abba Mark of Egypt: he lived for 30 years without ever going forth from his cell; unto him there customarily came a presbyter to celebrate for him the holy oblation (*poiein autōi tēn hagian prosphoran*)" [^954]. "Unto a certain anchorite there went a presbyter, celebrating for him the oblation of the Holy Mysteries (*tōn hagiōn mystēriōn tēn prosphoran*)" [^955].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: отшельнический устав
units.slavonic_text: Отшельнический устав
units.english_text: Thus in regard both unto fasting and prayer or divine worship there gradually became established among the holy anchorites a more or less uniform practice, common rules, a single typikon. This will not appear surprising if one take into consideration that intimate and constant intercourse wherein the desert-dwellers stood with one another, not only within the bounds of Egypt, but also the Sinaitic and Palestinian ascetics with the Egyptian; they frequently visited one another for mutual edification, while those nearest lovingly cared for one another; among them here and there luminaries of asceticism arose, becoming centers of spiritual instruction for a wide surrounding region. The anchorites constituted a single corporation, as it were a single monastery with a gradually evolving typikon and a certain organization. Beginners and the young *(Orig. p. 192)* had directors, yet the authority of the latter was wholly grounded upon immeasurable moral superiority [^956]. This was the most extensive and excellent monastery that the earth had ever beheld.

units.slavonic_text: общение, в котором находились между собою пустынножители не только в пределах Египта, но синайские и палестинские с египетскими; они часто посещали друг друга для взаимного назидания, ближайшие же любовно заботились друг о друге; среди них то там, то здесь являлись светила подвижничества, делавшиеся центром духовного назидания для обширной окрестности. Отшельники составляли одну корпорацию, как бы один монастырь с постепенно вырабатываемым уставом и некоторой организацией. Начинающие и молодые {с. 192} имели руководителей, но власть последних всецело основывалась на неизмеримом нравственном превосходстве [372]. Это был обширнейший и лучший монастырь, какой когда-либо видела земля.
units.english_text: St. Anthony relinquished his seclusion after thirty-five years, at the second place of his ascetic labors. "Acquaintances coming unto him, seeing that he did not permit them to enter within the fortification (the abandoned one wherein he struggled), not infrequently spent days and nights in the courtyard. But since many strove and desired to imitate his ascetic life, while certain of his acquaintances came and broke down and opened the door by force, Anthony came forth as an initiate of sacred mysteries and a God-bearer from a certain sanctuary." Following the healings performed on the spot and words of edification, the venerable father "persuaded many to choose the monastic life; thus in the mountains monasteries appeared; the desert was populated by monks who had forsaken their possessions... By the power of his marvelous word numerous monasteries arose" [^957]. By the term "monastery" (*monastērion*, from *monazō*, to dwell alone; *monastēs*, one dwelling solitary) there is designated here (in Athanasius' *Life of St. Anthony*) a cell-cottage [^958] or cave [^959], as is evident from the fact that the abandoned fortification wherein St. Anthony dwelt is likewise termed his "monastery" [^960], as is further evident from the remark that before St. Anthony "monasteries were few in Egypt" [^961], and from the comparison of a monastery with a tent [^962]. When St. Anthony withdrew unto the final site of his ascetic labors, there soon arose there likewise an entire colony of monastic cells; the neighboring mountains were covered with them, but these too soon became cramped for the imitators of St. Anthony, and the monks began to settle upon the other side of the Nile near the city of Arsinoë [^963]. "These monasteries in the mountains were like taberna-*(Orig. p. 193)*cles filled with divine choirs of psalmists, lovers of learning, fasters, men of prayer, who were gladdened by the hope of future blessings and engaged in handiwork to distribute alms" [^964]. In this description are indicated also the occupations of the monks in the "monasteries" of St. Anthony. In the monastery-cell the entire day of the monk was to pass. In it he was to remain as far as possible without going forth: "As a fish," said St. Anthony, "taken out of the water dieth, so likewise perisheth the fear of God in the heart of a monk if he vainly goeth forth from his cell"

units.slavonic_text: [381]. В этом уединении или затворничестве инока в его келии прп. Антоний различает разные степени. К полному затвору, в котором он сам жил (который, впрочем, тоже не был безусловным), он считал способным и допускал только немногих. Прп. Павлу (Простому) он говорит: «если тебе хочется быть монахом, то пойди в общежительный монастырь (κοινόβιον), где много братий, которые могут снисходить к немощам твоим; а я здесь живу один»; только когда Павел выдержал тяжелый искус, прп. Антоний устроил ему келью поприща за 3 или 4 от своей [382]. Большинство же учеников прп. Антония, живя уединенно по своим келиям, однако имели некоторое общение друг с другом: «к научению достаточно и писания», говорил Антоний своим ученикам, «однако же нам прилично утешать друг друга верою и умащать словом» [383]. В чем ближайшим образом и конкретно выражалась общая жизнь в «монастырях», руководимых непосредственно прп. Антонием, не позволяют сказать сохранившиеся известия. Не упоминается в них о молитвах монахов общих или частных [384], о пище их и мере воздержания. Есть указания только на общую трапезу [385]. Но довольно отчетливо выступает в известиях система духовного руководительства, управления общинами. По-видимому, молодые иноки находились под неослабным наблюдением старших, опытных. «Монах», говорил прп. Антоний, «должен откровенно сказывать старцам, сколько он делает шагов, или сколько пьет капель в своей келии, чтобы как-нибудь не погрешить в этом» [386]. Высшим руководителем духовной жизни в возникших подле места подвигов прп. Антония монастырях являлся, конечно, он сам. В ближайших от его местожительства «монастырях» он «часто беседует» [387] с иноками. Одна из таких бесед должно быть примерная, объединяющая {с. 194} в себе разновременные наставления преподобного (о борьбе с демонами), передается и описывается св. Афанасием: «в один день он выходит, собираются к нему все монахи и желают слышать от него слово. Антоний же египетским языком говорит им» [388]. Иногда преподобный принимает участие и в общей трапезе иноков. «Нередко со многими другими иноками приступая ко вкушению пищи и вспомнив о пище духовной, отказывался от вкушения и уходил от них далеко, почитая для себя за стыд, если увидят другие, что он ест. По необходимому же требованию тела, вкушал пищу, но особо, а нередко и вместе с братиею, сколько стыдясь их, столько уповая предложить им слово на пользу» [389]. Влияние и авторитет св. Антония в его монастырях всецело основывались на нравственной высоте его. Обычным наименованием его у иноков было «Великий»: «Великий сказал», «Великий сделал» [390]. «И лицо его имело важную и необычайную приятность.
