units.slavonic_text: ### Воскресное бдение на Синае и в Палестине (посещение Нила Мосхом и Софронием)
units.english_text: The Life of St. Sabas, like all accounts concerning Palestinian monasticism—in contrast unto reports concerning, for example, Egyptian monasticism—containeth absolutely no data concerning the divine services there. This can apparently be explained solely by the fact that the latter in Palestinian monasteries, as is directly known concerning the Syro-Mesopotamian monasteries [^1504], followed the customary rite, the order of secular parish churches. And this latter rite, as we have seen, even in the V century was already quite close unto the present one. For example, at Vespers there was already Ps. 140, the Great Litany and the Litany of Supplication, **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Phos Hilaron / Svete Tikhiy*), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Kataxioson, Kyrie / Spodobi Gospodi*), **"Now lettest Thou"** (*Nyn apolyeis / Nyně otpushchayeshi*); at Matins, Ps. 62 and Ps. 50, certain Old Testament and New Testament canticles, the Lauds (*Ainoi / Khvalitny*) psalms, **"Glory to God in the highest"** (*Doxa en hypsistois Theo / Slava v vyshnikh Bogu*), and the same litanies. Unto these invariable portions was conjoined a series of hymns, sometimes termed troparia, corresponding unto the given day, as well as corresponding readings from the Old and New Testaments [^1505]. Such, at least, was the order of the divine office in the churches of Syria and Palestine—that is, precisely those in whose bosom arose that branch of monasticism which is regarded as the progenitor of the present Typikon. Into this already established order of divine worship, monasticism needed only to insert the Psalter, inasmuch as the Psalter from antiquity was regarded as the handbook for the monk. This insertion could be effected either in such manner that the hitherto existing psalm element in divine worship might be stretched and expanded, or, without disturbing that element, the Psalter could be externally inserted into divine worship, fashioning from it as it were a distinct monastic office upon the ordinary secular service. The former was accomplished in the liturgical rite of the Western Church; the latter, in the Eastern Typika by the system of kathismata and the kanon (understanding by the latter the Biblical canticles). As unto how this addition was originally effected in the VI century, a precious report concerning this hath been preserved in the narrative of the visit unto the Sinaitic Abba Nilus [^1506] by the Palestinian monks John Moschus, author of the *Spiritual Meadow* (*Pratum Spirituale*), and Sophronius, subsequently Patriarch of Jerusalem—a visit which took place ca. 606 AD. This narrative hath been preserved in certain ancient Paterika (in manuscripts of the Vatican Library) [^1507] and in Nikon of the Black Mountain [^1508]. We cite the narrative in the first recension, with variants from Nikon in parentheses (*italics denote that which is absent in Nikon*):

units.slavonic_incipit: Житие прп. Саввы, как и все
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: житие прп саввы как и все известия о
units.slavonic_text: Житие прп. Саввы, как и все известия о палестинском монашестве, в противоположность известиям например об египетском монашестве, совершенно не заключает в себе каких-либо данных о тамошнем богослужении. Объяснить это, по-видимому, можно только тем, что это последнее в палестинских монастырях, как то прямо известно о сирско-месопотамских монастырях [15], следовало обычному чину, чину мирских церквей. А этот последний, как мы видели, и в V в. был уже довольно близок к нынешнему. Например, на вечерни был уже пс. 140, ектении великая и просительная, Свете Тихий, Сподоби Господи, Ныне отпущаеши, на утрени пс. 62 и 50-й, некоторые ветхозаветные и новозаветные песни, хвалитные псалмы, Слава в вышних Богу, те же ектении. К этим неизменяемым частям присоединялся ряд песней, называвшихся иногда тропарями, соответствующих известному дню, и такие же чтения из Ветхого и Нового Завета. [16]. Такой, по крайней мере, порядок имело богослужение в церквах Сирии и Палестины, т. е. тех именно, в недрах которых возникла отрасль монашества, считающаяся родоначальником нынешнего устава. В этот, уже сложившийся чин богослужения, монашеству нужно было вставить только Псалтирь, так как она издревле считалась настольною книгою для инока. Вставка эта могла быть произведена или так, что бывший доселе псалтирный элемент в богослужении мог быть раздвинут и расширен, или же, не касаясь этого элемента, псалтирь можно было внешним образом вставить в богослужение, сделав из нее как бы особую иноческую службу на обычном мирском богослужении. Первое было сделано в богослужебном уставе Западной Церкви, второе — в восточных уставах системою кафизм и канона (разумея под последними библейские песни). Как делалась эта прибавка первоначально, в VI в., драгоценное известие об этом сохранилось в рассказе о посещении синайского аввы Нила [17] палестинскими иноками Иоанном Мосхом, автором «Луга Духовного» и Софронием, впоследствии патриархом Иерусалимским, посещении, имевшем место ок. 606 г. Рассказ этот сохранился в некоторых древних патериках (в рукописях Ватиканской библиотеки) [18] и у Никона Черногорца [19]. Приводим рассказ в первой редакции с вариантами из Никона в скобках (курсивом то, чего нет у Никона):
units.english_text: "Abba John and Abba Sophronius related unto us: before the holy Sunday (*at the dawning of the Lord’s *(Orig. p. 295)* Day*), we went unto Abba Nilus upon Mount Sinai. The elder was up upon the summit of the mountain with two disciples. Inasmuch as we arrived for Vespers, the elder began: **"Glory to the Father"** (*Slava Ottsu*), and the rest; and after they had said: **"Blessed is the man"** (*Blazhen muzh*) and **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Kyrie ekekraxa / Gospodi vozzvakh*) without troparia, and **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Phos Hilaron / Svete Tikhiy*), and **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Kataxioson, Kyrie / Spodobi Gospodi*), they began **"Now lettest Thou"** (*Nyn apolyeis / Nyně otpushchayeshi*) and the rest. Upon the conclusion of Vespers he set before us a refection. After the refection we began the kanon (rule); and after the Six Psalms (*Hexapsalmos*), having said **"Our Father Who art in the heavens"** (*Otche nash, Izhe yesi na nebesech*), they began the psalms chanted melodiously. And when they had said the first stasis of 50 psalms, the elder began **"Our Father Who art in the heavens"** (*+ the elder began to recite the Epistle*), fifty times **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Gospodi pomiluy*); and when they had sat down, one of his disciples read the Catholic Epistle of James. Rising up, we again began the second stasis of 50 psalms; and upon the completion of the 50 psalms he gave [the book] unto another brother, and that one read from the same book the Catholic Epistle of Peter. And rising up, they began the 3rd stasis; and upon the completion of the 150 psalms, and after they had said **"Our Father"** and **"Lord, have mercy"**, they sat down, and the elder gave me the book, and I read the Catholic Epistle of John. And rising up, they began the Canticles (*ōdas*) of Moses (softly) chanted melodiously without troparia; and neither at the third nor at the sixth did they make an intercalary hymn (*mesōdion*), but **"Our Father"** and **"Lord, have mercy"**; and having said the Lauds (*Ainoi / Khvalitny*) psalms without troparia, they began **"Glory to God in the highest"** with the **"I believe"** (*+ in one God*) and **"Our Father"** and **"Lord, have mercy"**. The elder then added: 'O Son and Word of God (*+ Lord*), Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy upon us, and help, and save our souls!' And when we said 'Amen', we sat down. And I say unto the elder: 'Why, Abba, dost thou not preserve the order of the Catholic and Apostolic Church?' And the elder saith unto me: 'He that preserveth not the order of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, let him be anathema both in this age and in that which is to come!' And I say unto him: 'How then dost thou not recite (*+ from the night*) at the Vespers of the holy Sunday troparia at **"Lord, I have cried"**, nor a troparion at **"O Gladsome Light"** (*+ at **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"***), nor at the kanon **"God is the Lord"**, nor at the psalmody of the Sunday kathisma psalms, nor troparia at the Song of the Three Holy Children, nor at the Magnificat (*at the Gospel*) **"Let every breath"**, nor at the Doxology **"The Resurrection of the Savior"** (*+ which we praise*)?' Unto the inquiries of the visitors the elder replied that the reason for such departures from the general ecclesiastical Typikon in his prayer rule was his lack of any sacred orders. 'All that thou hast spoken is the office of reader and chanter, subdeacon and presbyter, and in general of those possessing ordination; whereas those not possessing the latter ought not to dare to perform this. For this very reason the ecclesiastical order appointeth the reader and the chanter, the subdeacons and the presbyters: the chanter, in order to sing and to lead off with singing and voice and chant, and "to guide the people in the **'Holy God'**, and the prokeimena, and the precenting, and the sanctuary hymns, and at the entrance of the Mysteries the Cherubic Hymn, and the Communion verses"; the reader, for the paroemias (proverbial), prophetic, and apostolic books; the subdeacons and deacons, to minister at the altar; and the presbyters, to celebrate the sacred mysteries, to accomplish the rites, and to baptize. I too will ask of you an 'ecclesiastical head' [capital question]: tell me, in the divine offices, evening supplications, night vigils, and morning services, who ought to precent and lead off the alleluia, the introits, the sessional hymns, the readings, and the antiphons?" We said unto him: "The readers, chanters, and subdeacons." The elder said: "Rightly have ye spoken. And on solemn feasts *(Orig. p. 296)* and on holy Sundays, who ought to begin **'God is the Lord'**, both at the beginning of the kanon, and in the intercalary canticles of the Three Children, and **'Let every breath'**, and in the doxologies **'The Resurrection of the Savior which we praise'**, and at the end of the kanon?" We said unto him: "This is the office of presbyters; in the ecclesiastical tradition we have received that this be proclaimed by the priests." Adding then that he in this manner doth not cast aside the ecclesiastical order, but on the contrary by his manner of action expresseth a singular reverence toward it, looking upon it as something analogous unto the heavenly hierarchy, the elder noteth in passing also (like the aforementioned Egyptian fathers) that "unto hesychasts and those weeping for their own sins, troparia are not fitting"; yet he repeateth that he singeth them not principally because, in his judgment, they usurp the priesthood, like King Uzziah and Uzzah (who upheld the falling Ark), who, lacking ordination, "proclaim the psalms with song and utterance, and the people at the ends of the verses respond with voice and melody, usurping the prokeimena and sanctuary precentings, and appointing themselves chanters, readers, and subdeacons."

units.slavonic_incipit: того-то и церковный чин поставляет чтеца
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: того то и церковный чин поставляет чтеца и певца
units.slavonic_text: того-то и церковный чин поставляет чтеца и певца, иподиаконов и пресвитеров; певца, — чтобы петь и начинать с пением и гласом и песнью и «преднаставляти люди в Святый Боже и предлежащая и предпевания и алтарная и во происхождение тайнам Иже херувим и причастная»; чтеца же на паремии (приточные), пророческие и апостольские книги; иподиаконов и диаконов — чтобы служить жертвеннику; пресвитеров же, чтобы священнодействовать и совершать и крещать. Спрошу и я вас «главизну церковную», — скажите мне: в божественных службах и вечерних молениях и ночных бдениях и утренних служениях кто должен предвоспевать и предначинать аллилуиа, предпевания, седальны, чтения, антифоны? Мы сказали ему: чтецы, певцы, иподиаконы. Старец сказал: верно вы сказали. А в нарочитые праздники {с. 296} и в св. недели кто должен начинать «Бог Господь (и) в начале канона и в междопеснех триех отрок и Всяко дыхание и во славословия Воскресения Спасова еже хвалим и на концы канону»? Мы сказали ему: это дело пресвитеров; в церковном предании мы так приняли, чтобы это предвозглашалось иереями». Прибавив затем, что он таким образом не отметает церковного чина, а напротив своим образом действий выражает особенное благоговение к нему, взирая на него как на нечто аналогичное небесной иерархии, старец замечает мимоходом еще (как вышеупоминавшиеся египетские отцы), что «молчальником и иже своя грехи плачущим не подобни суть тропаре»; но повторяем, что не поет их главным образом потому, что, по его мнению, восхищают священство подобно царю Озии и Озе (поддержавшему падавший ковчег) те, которые, не имея «управления псалмы с песнию и глаголом предвозглашающе(й) и людие на концы стиховом отпевающе со главом и пением, от прокимен же и предпетий олтарных тии восзищающе и себе певца и чтеца и иподиаконы поставляюще».
units.english_text: This narrative affordeth us a conception simultaneously of three types of divine worship of that period: the Sinaitic eremitic—and monastic Sinai was the spiritual offspring of Egypt; the Palestinian monastic; and the cathedral-parish type. The first is described in all completeness of detail. Concerning the composition of the second, one may deduce from that which arouseth perplexity in the first on the part of the visitors: unto them it seemeth strange that there should be an absence of "troparia" at **"Lord, I have cried"** (stichera), at **"O Gladsome Light"** (the prokeimenon), at **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (the aposticha), as well as the absence of **"God is the Lord"** "at the beginning of the kanon" (of Matins), of Sunday sessional hymns, of intercalary hymns (*mesōdia*) at the 3rd and 6th canticles (sessional hymns or something similar), and furthermore the absence of troparia at the Biblical canticles—especially at the Song of the Three Children and the Magnificat (presently the 8th and 9th odes of the kanon), of **"Let every breath"**, and of the Sunday hymn (**"The Resurrection of the Savior which we praise"**) at the Doxology. In Palestinian and other monasteries, consequently, all this was already in existence. But the most valuable indications are afforded us by the narrative concerning the cathedral-parish, secular divine service—valuable in view of the fact that no other information concerning it hath survived from this era. According unto the narrative, this divine service was reduced principally unto singing: there were sung—and evidently unto artful and intricate melodies—a) psalms, b) prokeimena and verses corresponding unto them: alleluia, antiphons, **"God is the Lord"**, **"Let every breath"**, c) stichera, sessional hymns, and troparia. The chanting of all this was initiated before the altar by the chanter, who was followed by the people singing along on appointed verses. Festal divine service differed from weekday service both in composition (for example, by the fact that instead of **"God is the Lord"**, alleluia was sung) and in the celebrants: whereas on weekdays the chanting of the most important portions was initiated by the chanters, readers, and subdeacons, on feasts it was begun by the priests. The subdeacons appear chiefly in the role of chanters. Reading was almost analogous in performance unto chanting. All these are characteristics of the so-called Chanted Office (*asmatike akolouthia*), detailed orders of which have been preserved from the IX and subsequent centuries, whose essence consisted precisely in the solemn singing *(Orig. p. 297)* of psalms, antiphons, prokeimena, and similar short verses, in frequent prayers (broad participation of the presbyter in the divine service), and in the congregational execution of diverse refrains unto the psalms. This office, especially in the form in which it is presented by the present narrative, hath much in common with the Western liturgical worship of that era. One of the common features of both, as we shall see, was the paucity of hymns of Christian composition (the dominance of biblical material): throughout the entire divine service there would occur only one or two such hymns (troparia), or canticles. Yet the divine worship in the homeland of the actual narrators already stands upon the transition unto the later type (the present one): in it are found many hymns of the latter kind—stichera, sessional hymns, and troparia for the kanon.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: сетителей им кажется странным отсутствие тропарей на господи
units.slavonic_text: посетителей: им кажется странным отсутствие «тропарей» на Господи воззвах (стихир), на Свете тихий (прокимна), на Сподоби Господи (стиховных стихир), затем отсутствие Бог Господь «в начале канона» (утрени), воскресных седальнов, междопесния на 3 и 6 песнях (седальнов или чего-либо подобного), затем отсутствие тропарей на библейских песнях, особенно на песни 3 отроков и Величит (ныне 8 и 9 песни канона), Всякого дыхания и воскресной песни (Воскресение Спасово (еже) хвалим») на славословии. В Палестинских и других монастырях, следовательно, все это уже было. Но наиболее ценные указания дает нам рассказ о соборно-приходском, мирском богослужении, ценные в виду того, что других сведений о нем из этой эпохи не сохранилось. По рассказу это богослужение сводилось главным образом к пению: пелись, и очевидно искусственными и сложными напевами а) псалмы, б) прокимны и соответствующие им стихи: аллилуиа, антифоны, Бог Господь, Всякое дыхание, в) стихиры, седальны, тропари. Пение всего этого начиналось пред алтарем певцом, за которым следовал народ, подпевавший известные стихи. Праздничное богослужение отличалось от будничного как составом (например тем, что вместо Бог Господь пелось аллилуиа), так и исполнителями: тогда как на будничном пение важнейших частей начиналось певцами, чтецами и иподиаконами, на праздничном — священниками. Иподиаконы выступают главным образом в роли певцов. Чтение почти аналогично по исполнению с пением. Все это признаки так называемого песненного последования, подробные чины которого сохранились от IX и последующих веков, сущность которого и состояла именно в торжественном пении {с. 297} псалмов, антифонов, прокимнов и т. п. небольших стихов, в частых молитвах (широкое участие пресвитера в богослужении) и в народном исполнении разных припевов к псалмам. Это последование, особенно в том виде, как оно представляется настоящим рассказом, имеет много общего с тогдашним западным богослужением. Одною из общих особенностей того и другого, как увидим, являлось немногочисленность песен христианского составления (господство библейского материала): на всем богослужении бывала одна, две таких песни (тропари), гимна. Но богослужение на родине настоящих рассказчиков стоит уже на переходе к позднейшему типу (нынешнему): в нем много последнего рода песен: стихиры, седальны, тропари к канону.
units.english_text: As a transitional stage from the earlier chanted type of divine worship (with the predominance of psalms and their verses in the form of antiphons, etc.) unto the new type with the predominance of stichera, one must suppose the existence of the kontakarian system of divine worship. Unto the most ancient and solitary hymn at divine worship—the troparion, which expressed in brief the essence of the liturgical celebration and was sung as a refrain unto the verses of certain psalms (for example, Ps. 50, Ps. 117 [LXX], etc.)—they began to annex a similarly concise hymn, but executed already independently of the psalm and having following upon it a series of similar songs: the kontakion with a series of ikoi. The first creator of kontakia was a reader or chanter of St. Sophia in Constantinople, St. Romanus the Melodist (*ho Melodos*, † first half of the VI century). He composed kontakia and ikoi, in all probability, for all the most important feasts of his era (with great certainty one may ascribe unto him this composition for at least 15 feasts and commemorations of the year) [^1509]. The number of ikoi in St. Romanus for each feast vacillateth between 24 and 14. Consequently, this was a long series of hymns, which in the services of that time occupied the place of stichera and the kanon: in liturgical books containing stichera and the kanon, only a single kontakion and ikos are ever indicated, rather than such a long series thereof. Stichera and especially the kanon appeared already to replace the kontakarian services, and as one of the first creators of kanons one may recognize St. Andrew of Crete († ca. 712 AD).

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: богослужении тропарю кратко выражавшему собою сут богослужения
units.slavonic_text: богослужении — тропарю, кратко выражавшему собою суть богослужения и припевавшемуся к стихам некоторых псалмов (например 50, 117 и т. п.), стали присоединять такое же краткое песнопение, но исполнявшееся уже независимо от псалма и имевшее за собою ряд подобных же песен — кондак с рядом икосов. Первым творцом кондаков был чтец или певец св. Софии Константинопольской св. Роман Сладкопевец († перв. пол. VI в.). Он составил кондаки и икосы должно быть, на все важнейшие праздники своего времени (с большою достоверностью ему можно приписать это составление по крайней мере для 15 праздников и памятей года [20]. Число икосов у прп. Романа для каждого праздника колеблется между 24 и 14. Следовательно, это был длинный ряд песней, который на тогдашних службах заступал место стихир и канона: в богослужебных книгах, имеющих стихиры и канон, всегда указывается по одному кондаку и икосу, а не такой длинный ряд их. Стихиры и особенно канон явились уже на смену кондакарным службам и одним из первых творцов канонов можно признать св. Андрея Критского († ок. 712 г.).
units.english_text: More detailed information concerning the aforementioned third type of divine worship—cathedral-parish worship—from the era of the VI–VIII centuries doth not exist. Only from the IX century and subsequent centuries have offices come down unto us, yet already in conjunction with later accretions—for example, stichera and kanons—which cannot be isolated with scholarly certainty, and therefore a reliable conception of this type of divine worship for the present period cannot be formed. Nevertheless, the exposition of the Chanted Office (*asmatike akolouthia*) of the IX–XVI centuries will simultaneously *(Orig. p. 298)* afford us subsequently certain conjectural suppositions concerning the form which it possessed at this time.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: часослов в
units.slavonic_text: ### Часослов VIII в.
units.english_text: Meanwhile, concerning Palestinian-monastic divine worship of the era under examination, information hath been preserved for its further course as well—from the VIII century. This is the Greek "Horologion according unto the Typikon of the Lavra of Our Holy Father Sabas" (*Hōrologion kata kanona tēs lauras...*) in a manuscript of the VIII–IX century [^1510]. The Horologion was intended for cell use; for which reason it doth not contain not only all parts of the service (for example, litanies, priestly exclamations), but even certain services, such as Matins. Apparently, in lieu of Matins there stands at the beginning of the Horologion the first kathisma. Then follow the services for the 1st hour of the day, the 3rd, 6th, and 9th, the service for Communion of the Presanctified Gifts (corresponding unto the Typika / *Izobrazitel'ny*), Vespers, and the service for the 1st hour of the night (corresponding unto Compline), upon which the Horologion breaketh off. The services are very close unto the present ones. Thus Vespers (*ta hesperina*) consisteth of Ps. 103, the 18th kathisma with 3 *Glorias*, Ps. 140 with **"Glory... Now and ever..."** at the end, **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Phos Hilaron / Svete Tikhiy*), the Alleluia with diverse verses for different days (at first verses from the present prokeimenon **"The Lord reigneth"** [*Kyrios ebasileusen / Gospod' votsarisia*]), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Kataxioson, Kyrie / Spodobi Gospodi*), **"Now lettest Thou"** (*Nyn apolyeis / Nyně otpushchayeshi*), and the Trisagion (*Sviatoe Trishchastie*). The service of each hour consisteth of psalms, the number of which is distinct for different hours: for the First—8; for the Third—7; for the Sixth—6; for the Ninth—4; the Alleluia with verses; the troparion (such as exists at present for each hour, excluding the 1st), before which and after which is written its conclusion, which must have served as its refrain; then the verse of the hour, such as exists at present (that is, for the 1st hour [the printed Russian edition has '10-го часа', an obvious misprint for the 1st hour]: **"Order my steps"** [*Stopy moia*], etc.) with the tripling of its first half (as at present at the 1st Hour in Great Lent); and finally—the Trisagion; consequently, that part of the hour following upon the Trisagion did not yet exist. The service for Communion (= the Typika / *Izobrazitel'ny*) consisteth of the Beatitudes with the refrain **"Remember us, O Lord, when Thou comest"** (*Pomiani nas, Gospodi, egda priideshi*), the **"Heavenly Choir"** (*Lik nebesnyi*), the Symbol of Faith (**"I believe"** [*Veruiu*]), **"Our Father"** (*Otche nash*), **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Gospodi pomiluy*) thrice, **"One is Holy"** (*Heis Hagios / Yedin sviat*), **"O taste and see"** (*Geusasthe kai idete / Vkusite i vidite*), Ps. 33—**"I will bless the Lord"** (*Blagoslovliu Gospoda*), prayers after Communion with the intermediate verse: **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** (*Eiē to onoma Kyriou / Budi imia Gospodne*). The extant portion of Compline hath the following composition: **"Come, let us worship"** (*Priidite poklonimsia*), **"Having traversed the day, I glorify Thee"** (*Tēn hēmeran dielthōn / Den' preshed blagodariu Tia*), Pss. 4, 12, 26, **"Glory..."**, Pss. 30, 90, 6, **"Glory..."**, **"God is with us"** (*Meth' hēmōn ho Theos / S nami Bog*), the Alleluia with verses (for example, **"Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God"** [*Prizri, uslyshi mia Gospodi Bozhe*]) and troparia changing according unto the days, **"Lord, have mercy"** thrice, and **"Deliver not unto the beasts the soul that doth praise Thee"** (*Ne predazhd' zverem dushu ispovedaiushchuiusia Tebe*).

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: разных дней сначала стихи из нынешнего прокимна господ
units.slavonic_text: разных дней (сначала стихи из нынешнего прокимна Господь воцарися), Сподоби Господи, Ныне отпущаеши и Трисвятое. Служба каждого часа состоит из псалмов, число которых различно для разных часов, для первого — 8, для третьего — 7, для шестого — 6, для девятого — 4, аллилуиа со стихами, тропари (такого, как ныне для каждого часа, исключая 1-й), пред которым и после которого написан конец его, должно быть служивший ему припевом; затем стих часа, такой как ныне (т. е. для 10-го часа «Стопы моя» и т. п.) с утроением его первой половины (как ныне на 1 часе в Великий пост), и наконец — Трисвятое; следовательно части часа, следующей за Трисвятым, еще не существовало. Служба на причащение (= изобразительные) состоит из блаженств с припевом Помяни нас Господь, егда приидеши, Лик небесный, Верую, Отче наш, Господи помилуй 3. Един свят, Вкусите и видите, пс. 33 — Благословлю Господа, молитвы по причащении с промежуточным стихом: Буди имя Господне. Сохранившаяся часть повечерия имеет такой состав: Приидите поклонимся, День прешед благодарю Тя, Пс. 4, 12, 26, Слава 30, 90, 6, Слава, С нами Бог, аллилуиа со стихами (например Призри, услыши мя Господи Боже) и тропарями, меняющимися по дням, Господи помилуй, 3, Не предаждь зверем душу исповедающуюся тебе.
units.english_text: During the period of the VI–VIII centuries, the daily office assumed its present form not only in the Orthodox Church, but also in the heretical communities that separated from Her during this time—the Nestorians, Monophysites, and Monothelites, as well as throughout the entire western half of the Christian world. Acquaintance with the liturgical rites of all these churches sheddeth much light upon the history of our divine worship, all the more so since in the period under consideration the latter *(Orig. p. 299)* possessed much that was similar across diverse churches, and in the less cultured lands of the East could be preserved more invariantly than our own.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: инославное богослужение
units.slavonic_text: ## Инославное богослужение
units.english_text: The Nestorian divine service possesseth almost no invariable elements. Vespers and Matins begin with **"Glory to God in the highest"** (*thrice*) **"and on earth peace, good will among men"**, and **"Our Father"**; then follow the appointed kathismata (the Psalter is divided into 20 kathismata, while the 21st is constituted by the 2 Canticles of Moses) and the so-called "Tone of Matins", that is, according unto the appointed tone (of which there are only two) one of the 2 kathismata—the 12th (with Ps. 67) or the 21st, with hymns assigned unto it on feasts, and on weekdays with litanies and dismissal prayers—all according unto the tone. Besides this, every Matins hath also Ps. 50, while Sunday Matins hath a Six Psalms (*Hexapsalmos*) composed of Pss. 99, 90, 103 (vv. 1–16), 62, 149, and 150. At every service the Nicene Creed is recited [^1511]. Concerning the composition of the Hours we possess no information.

units.slavonic_text: этого каждая утреня имеет еще пс. 50, а воскресная шестопсалмие из пс. 99, 90, 103 (ст. 1–16), 62, 149 и 150. На каждой службе читается Никейский символ [22]. О составе часов не имеем сведений.
units.english_text: The Armenians (Monophysites) possess the following daily offices: the Midnight Office (*Gisherayin Zham*), Dawn (*Aravotyan Zham* = Matins), Sunrise (*Arevagal*, 1st Hour), the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours (*Jashu Zham*), Vespers (*Erekoyan Zham*), Peace (*Khaghaghakan Zham* = Compline), and the Service before Sleep (*Hangstyan Zham* / Rest). The services begin and end with **"Our Father"**. The Midnight Office: **"O Lord, open Thou my lips"** (*Kyrie ta cheilē mou anoixeis / Gospodi ustne moi otverzeshi*) thrice; "Blessed is the consubstantial, undivided, and holy Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages". Psalms: **"Lord, how are they increased"** (Ps. 3), **"O Lord God of my salvation"** (Ps. 87), **"Bless the Lord, O my soul"** (Ps. 102), **"Hear my prayer, O Lord, give ear unto my supplication"** (Ps. 142). At the end of the psalms, **"Glory..."**. A prayer beginning: "Having arisen from the rest of sleep, which God Who loveth mankind hath granted unto us..." Then an exhortation or instruction is read. After it, **"Lord, have mercy"** on weekdays 50 times, in Lent 100 times, on feasts 3 times. Prayer: "We give thanks unto Thee, O Lord our God..." Hymns (of Christian composition). The Gospel—on Sundays. A special prayer: "By the intercession of the Holy Mother of God, of St. John the Baptist, and of the saint whose day it is, grant unto us, O Almighty God..." (corresponding unto our prayer before the kanon: **"Save, O God, Thy people"** [*Spasi Bozhe liudi Tvoia*]). Two divisions or "kanons" of the Psalter (the Armenians divide the Psalter into 8 portions, corresponding unto our kathismata and termed *kanons* [Ganonk']). Four instructions corresponding unto the day, and after each the singing of a similar prayer in diverse tones. Hymn: "King of the Ages", and another according unto the day. A special supplication, reading of the Menology (*Chet'yi-Minei*). The 3rd, 4th, and 5th divisions of the Psalter. — The service of "Dawn": **"We were filled in the morning with Thy mercy"** (Ps. 89:14). Song of the Three Children. A hymn in honor of the saints. Prayer unto the Blessed Virgin. **"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** (*Velichit dusha moia*). Hymn unto the Blessed Virgin. The Canticle *(Orig. p. 300)* of Zacharias. Then followeth on Sundays only: a prayer in the nature of a litany composed of priestly exclamations "Let us pray unto the Lord for such-and-such or for such a person", with the congregational response "Unto the Lord let us pray". Prayer: "Thou art the King of the ages". Three verses from the psalms according unto the day. **"Blessed be the name of the Lord from henceforth and for evermore"** (*Budi imia Gospodne blagoslovenno ot nyne i do veka*). The Resurrection Gospel. A homily or instruction beginning: "Rejoicing with great joy over the tidings of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ..." and a brief prayer. On other days, after the Canticle of Zacharias, Ps. 50, an exhortation unto prayer through the intercession of the saints of the day, a laudatory hymn unto the saints, and a prayer with kneeling. After this variable portion, again the invariable: Psalm: **"Praise the Lord from the heavens"** (Ps. 148) with the 2 following (Pss. 149–150). Three verses in honor of God and the saints of the day. **"Glory to God in the highest"**. Two verses from the psalms according unto the day. A prayer chanted by three monks or clerics. Another prayer. The Trisagion. Psalm: **"Praise, O ye servants, the Lord"** (Ps. 112). On Sundays—the Gospel of the day. A canticle or hymn. Psalms: **"Give ear unto my words, O Lord"** (Ps. 5), **"I loved, because the Lord hath heard"** (Ps. 114), **"Out of the depths"** (Ps. 129), **"Save me, O God, by Thy name"** (Ps. 53). The two final verses of Ps. 85 (**"Shew me a token for good..."**). Supplications for diverse classes of people (= the Augmented Litany / *ekteneia*). Hymn. Instruction. Prayer. — Sunrise (the 1st Hour): **"Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever: His name endureth before the sun..."** and so forth unto the end of Ps. 71. **"Glory..."**. Prayer. Psalm—**"It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord"** (Ps. 91). Prayer. Psalms: **"O God, my God, unto Thee do I rise early"** (Ps. 62), **"A psalm is due unto Thee"** (Ps. 64). Prayer. In fasts—a special hymn. Psalms: **"O God, my God, look upon me"** (Ps. 21); Ps. 142 from the verse: **"Cause me to hear Thy lovingkindness in the morning"**; **"My heart is ready"** (Ps. 107); **"O God, attend unto my help"** (Ps. 69). The two final verses of Ps. 85. Instruction. Prayer. — The 3rd Hour: Prayer unto the Holy Spirit. Ps. 50. A Canticle (Biblical) and instruction. The 6th division of the Psalter. Prayer unto the Holy Spirit. Pss. 21 and 142:8 ff. (**"Cause me to hear Thy lovingkindness in the morning"**). **"Glory..."**. Instruction. Prayer. — The 6th Hour: Prayer unto God the Father. Ps. 50. Instruction, prayer. The 8th division of the Psalter. Ps. 40:1–4 (**"Blessed is he that considereth the poor and needy"**). **"Lord, who shall abide"** (Ps. 14). Instruction. Prayer. — The 9th Hour: Prayer unto the Son of God. Ps. 50. Instruction, prayer; psalms: **"I loved"** (Ps. 114), **"I believed"** (Ps. 115), **"Praise the Lord, all ye nations"** (Ps. 116). Canticle, instruction. — After the 9th Hour the Liturgy is celebrated. units.slavonic_text: ### Богослужение коптов и абиссин
units.english_text: The daily office of the Copts (Monophysites) consisteth of Matins, the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours, Compline, Vespers, and the Midnight Office. The services begin: "In the name of the Father...", **"Glory to the Father..."**, **"Our Father"**, and the verse "We give thanks unto the Beneficent, the Merciful One", and each consisteth of an initial series of psalms, the Gospel, troparia, and prayers, with certain additions unto this composition for the more important services. Matins hath 19 psalms: 1–6, 8, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 24, 26, 62, 66, 69, 112, 142; the Gospel of John 1:1–16; a hymn similar unto our Doxology; the Symbol of Faith; a series of short prayer exclamations; and 2 prayers. Vespers hath 10 psalms: 129, 130, 131, 136, 137, 140, 141, 145, 146, 147; the Gospel of Luke 2:25–30 (concerning the Meeting of the Lord with the Canticle of Symeon the God-Receiver); the Trisagion; the Creed; **"Our Father"**; and 2 prayers. The Midnight Office—7 psalms: 3, 6, 69, 85, 116, 117, 118; the Gospel of Matthew 25—the parable of the 10 virgins; troparia: **"Behold, the Bridegroom cometh"** (*Se Zhenikh griadet*), **"That day"** (*Den' on*), **"An invincible bulwark"** (*Tebe neoborimuiu stenu*); the Trisagion; the Gospel of Luke 7:36 ff. concerning the woman who was a sinner; 3 troparia which are met with among us as penitential sessional hymns; the Gospel of Luke 12:35 ff. concerning the expectation of the Second Coming; penitential troparia; laudatory verses unto the Most Holy Theotokos **"Rejoice"**, resembling our Akathist; and a lengthy prayer. Conversely, Compline (celebrated prior unto Vespers) consisteth solely of psalms and the Gospel. At the Hours are almost all of our troparia and, for the most part, as at Compline, 12 psalms (at the 9th Hour—11) [^1513]. Consequently, for the majority of the services the system of 12 psalms is adopted—as we have seen, the distinctive characteristic of ancient Egyptian monastic worship. — In doctrine and ecclesiastical structure, *(Orig. p. 302)* the Abyssinian Christians, likewise Monophysites, are very close unto the Copts. The divine worship of the two differeth somewhat. Yet the divine worship of the Abyssinians, both contemporary and especially ancient, possessed several types, a complete conception of which is not yet accessible unto European scholarship—owing unto the fact that in Abyssinia liturgical books are in manuscript and only certain of them have been published in recent times. Among others, there hath been published also the Horologion of the Abyssinian Church [^1514], yet in the form which it received by the XIV century under Coptic and Greek influence [^1515]. The services in it are very close unto the Coptic, but more extensive than they, and in places approach our own more closely than the Coptic. The most important differences from the Coptic Horologion are that in lieu of Matins there are two services: the "prayer (service) at the 3rd hour of the night" and the "prayer at cockcrow"; the 1st Hour significantly differeth from the others and is close unto the concluding portion of our Matins; Compline followeth after Vespers, as with us. Besides this Horologion, in Abyssinia even at the present day horologia of other types are in use, in all probability more ancient. One of these horologia, presently in use in only a single Abyssinian monastery, presenteth services consisting entirely of metrical hymns in honor of the Holy Trinity, the Mother of God, and diverse choirs of saints (at Vespers venerable monastics are praised; at the 1st Hour, the Apostles, etc.) and a multitude of biblical and edifying readings, yet possessing no psalms whatever; in another, in use in certain monasteries, the services consist of psalms, priestly prayers, and biblical readings. It must be noted that the Abyssinians in general take a rather free approach toward the order of divine service, and, while observing its general structure (scheme), fill it with hymns from their diverse collections and with improvisations; for this reason hymnography at their services occupieth an overwhelming position. There exist immense collections of these hymns: the *Deggwa*, the *Psalter of Christ*, the *Psalter of the Virgin*; the hymns are for the most part in verse, some of them resembling our Akathists—presenting a series of praises (*malk'e*), sometimes addressed unto diverse parts of the saint's body and beginning with the word "peace" ("Peace unto thy head, which...", "Peace unto thy hands...") or "rejoice". These are the so-called "likenesses" (*effigies / portraits*); furthermore there are distinguished also antiphons—refrains unto psalms and biblical canticles, and the *wazema*—akin unto our stichera. The greatest stamp of antiquity among Abyssinian liturgical orders is borne by the All-Night Vigil set forth in the book *Me'eraf* ("chapters", that is, Typikon) and the *Deggwa*. Its composition is: Ps. 23 [LXX Ps. 23 / Masoretic Ps. 24] **"The earth is the Lord's"**, titled among the Abyssinians, like Ps. 103, "the beauty of creation"; Ps. 92 **"The Lord reigneth"**, and Ps. 140 with *wazema* (stichera). The psalms are separated by litanies; then follow the appointed section of the Psalter (it is divided into 10 decades), the evening prayer of the priest, paroemias from the Apostolic Epistles, the prokeimenon, and the Gospel. The morning prayers of the priest; (p. 337) the prayer **"Save, O God, Thy people"** (*Spasi Bozhe liudi Tvoia*); the morning Litiya (litany petitions); the Four Psalms: Pss. 62, 91, 5, 64; the appointed section of the Psalter: Ps. 50; the Biblical canticles with refrains from the *Wazema*—namely: the Prayer of Manasseh, the Canticles of the holy Habakkuk, of the Three *(Orig. p. 303)* Children, and of Zacharias; the Lauds (*Ainoi*) psalms with refrains; the Synaxarion (*Senkessar*); Theotokia; the Gospel; the reading of the "Miracles of Mary" (*Ta'amra Maryam*); the Song of Songs (in Lent); improvised or collected refrains (*mawwaddes*) for Sunday (the Great Doxology at the 1st Hour) [^1516].

units.slavonic_text: отличается от других и близок к последней части нашей утрени; повечерие после вечерни, как и у нас. Кроме этого часослова в Абиссинии и ныне употребляются часословы других типов, должно быть более древние. Один из этих часословов, ныне употребляемый в одном только абиссинском монастыре, дает службы, состоящие всецело из стихотворных песен в честь Св. Троицы, Богородицы и различных ликов святых (на вечерне восхваляются преподобные, на 1-м часе апостолы и т. п.) и множества библейских и назидательных чтений, но совершенно не имеющие псалмов; в другом, употребляющемся в некоторых монастырях, службы состоят из псалмов, молитв священника и библейских чтений. Надо заметить, что абиссинцы вообще довольно свободно относятся к чину богослужения, и, соблюдая общий строй (схему) его, наполняют его песнями из разных сборников их и импровизированными; поэтому песнопения на их службах занимают подавляющее положение. Существуют громаднейшие сборники этих песней: Дегва, Псалтирь Христа, Псалтирь прп. Девы; песни большей частью в стихах, одни из них похожи на наши акафисты — представляют ряд величаний, иногда обращенных к разным частям тела святого и начинающихся словом «мир» («Мир главе твоей, которая…» «Мир рукам твоим…») или «радуйся». Это так наз. «подобия» (портреты); кроме того различаются еще антифоны — припевы к псалмам и библ. песням, «вазема» — вроде наших стихир. Наибольшую печать древности из абиссинских богослужебных чинов носит всенощное бдение, изложенное в книге «Меераф» «главы» (т. е. устав) и «Дегва». Состав его: Пс. 22 «Гоподня земля», озаглавленный у абиссин, как и 103 пс., «красота творения», Пс. 92 «Господь воцарися» и 140 с «вазема» (стихирами). Псалмы разделяются ектениями; а затем очередной отдел Псалтири (она делится на 10 декад), вечерняя молитва священника, паремии из апост. Посланий, прокимен и Евангелие. Утренние молитвы священника, (стр. 337) молитва «Спаси Боже люди Твоя»; утренняя лития (ектенийные прошения); четырепсалмие: Пс. 62, 91, 5, 64; рядовой отдел Псалтири: Пс. 50; библейские песни с припевами из Ваземы — именно: молитва Манассии, песни прп. Аввакума, 3 от{с. 303}роков и Захария; хвалитные псалмы с припевами; сенкесарь (синаксарь); Богородичны; Евангелие; чтение «знамений Марии» (чудес Ее); Песнь песней (в посту); импровизованные или из сборника припевы (маввадес) на воскр. день (славосл. великое на 1-м часе [27].
units.english_text: The Maronites (Monothelites) possess 7 daily services: the Midnight Office, Matins, the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours, Vespers, and Compline. They do not chant the entire Psalter (as neither do the Copts) either in a day or in a week, but only certain psalms; at the Midnight Office—Pss. 62, 14, 50, and 116; at the 3rd and 9th Hours—Ps. 50; at Vespers—Pss. 50, 140, 141, and from Ps. 118 vv. 105–112 (**"Thy law is a lamp unto my feet..."** [*Lucerna pedibus meis lex tua* / *"Svetil'nik nogama moima zakon Tvoi..."*]); at Compline—Pss. 50, 14, and 116. At the beginning and conclusion of each office: the Trisagion, **"Our Father"**, **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** (*Bogoroditse Devo, raduisia*), the Symbol of Faith (**"I believe"**), and one prayer: following the customary opening, a hymn is performed alternately with a psalm or a biblical canticle or some prayerful invocation, so that after a part of a hymn there follows a part of a psalm or canticle, and so forth, with the entire hymn in conclusion; thereafter prayers, biblical canticles, psalms, and hymns alternate with one another, so that after a prayer there follows a canticle, after it a hymn or psalm, and the like. The Midnight Office contains 16 prayers, 11 canticles, 6 hymns, 2 psalms, 1 responsory, and other prayerful exclamations. Matins has 11 prayers, 7 hymns, 7 canticles, 4 psalms, and 1 responsory; the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours—5 prayers, 3 or 2 canticles, and 1 psalm (the 6th Hour has no psalm). Vespers has 7 prayers, 2 hymns, 4 canticles, 4 psalms, and 1 responsory. Compline—5 prayers, 3 psalms, 2 hymns, and 2 canticles [^1517].

units.slavonic_text: псалмы; на полунощнице — пс. 62, 14, 50 и 116; на 3 и 9 часе — 50 пс.; на вечерне 50, 140, 141 и из пс. 118 ст. 105–112 («светильник ногама моима закон Твой…»); на повечерии — пс. 50, 14 и 116. В начале и конце каждой службы: Трисвятое, Отче наш, (Богородице Дево) радуйся, Верую и одна молитва: по обычном начале исполняются попеременно гимн с псалмом или библ. песнью или каким либо молитвенным призыванием, так что за частью гимна следует часть псалма или песни и т. д., в заключение весь гимн; а далее чередуются друг с другом молитвы, библ. песни, псалмы и гимны, так что за молитвою следует песнь, за нею гимн или псалом и т. п. Полунощница заключает 16 молитв, 11 песен, 6 гимнов, 2 псалма, 1 респонсорий и другие молитвенные возгласы. Утреня имеет 11 молитв, 7 гимнов, 7 песен, 4 псалма и 1 респонсорий; 3, 6 и 9 часы — 5 молитв, 3 или 2 песни и 1 псалом (его не имеет 6 час). Вечерня имеет 7 молитв, 2 гимна, 4 песни, 4 псалма и 1 респонсорий. Повечерие — 5 молитв, 3 псалма, 2 гимна и 2 песни [28].
units.english_text: The development of Western divine worship took a different course, although at times it exhibited significant convergence with the Eastern. In the daily offices here, the fixed psalms adapted to the time of day soon disappeared, leaving only brief excerpts from them in the form of antiphons and responsories, which, thanks to the solemn manner of their performance (complex melodies and the special alternation of officiants during their chanting), occupied the most prominent position in the service; antiphons accompanied the chanting of the psalms, and responsories accompanied the readings. The psalms themselves, as also the liturgical readings, were selected not to suit the specific moment (the hour of the office or the commemorated event), but were recited in continuous cursus: the entire Psalter was chanted through in regular order at the services, just as the books read in divine worship were read consecutively; consequently, the whole essence of divine worship lay in the quantity of psalms and antiphons, readings and responsories; by this quantity the solemnity of the office was measured. Only for certain offices, namely for the final portion of Matins, the 1st Hour, and Compline, were there fixed psalms adapted to them; and the connection of an office to the celebrated event was expressed only by a single reading (for example, on Sunday one of *(Orig. p. 304)* the readings was the Gospel of the Resurrection). Thus, only the antiphons and responsories bore a relation to the specific liturgical moment. Yet almost the principal difference between Western and Eastern worship, both in this epoch and in the subsequent one (as partly also in the preceding), was the extremely restricted use of hymns of Christian composition. In some places there was even a movement in favor of entirely excluding hymns from the body of divine service. The Second Council of Braga (*Bracarensis*, in Spain) of 563 requires "that, apart from the psalms and canonical scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, no poetic composition (*nihil poetice compositum*) be sung in church, as the holy canons also command" (canon 12). units.slavonic_stem_tier2: богослужения собор в испании 2 й 563 г
units.slavonic_text: богослужения. Собор Bracarensis (в Испании) 2-й 563 г. требует «чтобы кроме псалмов и канонических писаний Ветхого и Нового Завета никакое поэтическое произведение (nihil poetice compositum) не пелось в церкви, как и повелевают св. каноны» (пр. 12). Но Турский 2 Собор (в Италии) 567 г. постановляет: «хотя в каноне мы имеет только Амвросиевы гимны, однако так как некоторые из остальных по форме достойны пения, то мы охотно соглашаемся и на принятие кроме них тех, имена авторов которых означены на полях» (пр. 23). 1-й Толедский Собор 633 г. (прав. 13) обстоятельно и настойчиво доказывает законность гимнов в богослужении против отрицающих это. В Лионской церкви гимны поются только на повечерии; тоже и в Вьенской только на повечерии поются гимны разные в различные праздники [29].
units.english_text: "Although in the canon we possess only the Ambrosian hymns, nevertheless, since certain of the remaining ones are worthy of being sung in form, we willingly agree to accept, in addition to them, those whose authors' names are indicated in the margins" (canon 23).

units.slavonic_text: Как и на Востоке, все дело разработки богослужения взяло на себя монашество; поэтому о соборно-приходском богослужении очень скудные сведения. Суточные службы были те же, что на Востоке; но полунощница и утреня составляли одну службу, называвшуюся часто, за начало ее в глубокую ночь, vigilia (бдение); соответственно частям ночи она делилась на несколько, большей частью на три, nocturni, за которыми следовала утреня в собственном смысле, называвшаяся matutinum или ad Laudes. Часы не везде совершались, так что со стороны Цезария, еп. Арльского (в Галлии † 542 г.) потребовалось особое распоряжение, чтобы клирики, кроме утрени и вечерни, совершали в Арльском Соборе св. Стефана и 3, 6, 9 часы с их гимнами [30]. О порядке и чине приходских служб сохранились следующие известия. Ночную службы или утреню, по крайней мере, по местам, постепенно стали начинать все позже. units.english_text:
As in the East, the entire task of developing divine worship was assumed by monasticism; therefore, information regarding cathedral-parochial worship is very sparse. The daily offices were the same as in the East; but the Midnight Office and Matins formed a single service, frequently termed *vigilia* (vigil) from its commencement in the deep of night; according to the divisions of the night, it was divided into several, for the most part three, *nocturni* (nocturns), followed by Matins in the strict sense, designated *matutinum* or *ad Laudes*. The Hours were not celebrated everywhere, so that on the part of Caesarius, Bishop of Arles (in Gaul, † 542), a special ordinance was required so that the clerics, besides Matins and Vespers, would celebrate in the Cathedral of St. Stephen in Arles the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours with their hymns [^1519]. Regarding the order and rite of parochial services, the following testimonies have been preserved. The night service or Matins, at least in certain localities, gradually began to be started later and later. Whereas Gregory of Tours in the VI century says of his contemporaries that they "arise at midnight to render thanksgiving unto the Lord" [^1520], in the VIII century Chrodegang (*Grodegangus*), Bishop of Metz, in his rules for canons permits them "in wintertime, that is, from the Kalends of November until Pascha, to arise at the 8th hour (= 2 o'clock) of the night, in order to sleep a little even after midnight and be more alert for the vigil" [^1521]; and Amalarius in the IX century, explaining the psalm verses at the night vigils that precede the readings, says: "The second verse: **"At midnight I arose"** (*"Polunoshchi vostakh"* / *Media nocte surgebam*); it indicates at what hour of the night one must arise; but since *(Orig. p. 305)* we neglect the time at which our fathers were accustomed to arise, we dare not lie, and we replace this verse with another: **"For Thou wilt light my lamp"** (*"Yako Ty esi prosveshchiaiai svetil'nik moi"* / *Quoniam tu illuminas lucernam meam*)" [^1522]. There is an indication regarding the structure of the night service in the acts of the Gallic Council of 499 against the Arians in the presence of Gundobad, King of the Burgundians. When the bishops celebrated a vigil at the tomb of St. Justus on his feast day,
"it came to pass that when the reader at night according to custom began the reading of Moses, he came upon the words: **"And I will harden his heart"**; then, when after the singing of the psalms he read from the Prophets, there occurred the words of the Lord to Isaiah: **"Go, and say unto this people: Hearing ye shall hear..."** When the psalms were sung again, and he (the reader) read from the Gospel, he came upon the words with which the Savior rebukes the unbelief of the Jews: **"Woe unto thee, Chorazin..."** When at last there was a reading from the Apostle, the following words were pronounced: **"Or despisest thou the riches of His goodness..."** This was noticed by all the bishops, and all recognized that these readings fell out by the will of God, so that it might be known that the king's heart was hardened" [^1523].

Юста совершали вигилию на его гробе, «случилось, что когда чтец ночью по обыкновению начал чтение Моисея, он попал на слова «Аз же ожесточу сердце его»; затем когда после пения псалмов он читал из пророков, встретились слова Господни к Исаии: «иди и рцы людем сим: слухом услышите…» Когда опять были пропеты псалмы, и он (чтец) читал из Евангелия, то попал на слова, которыми Спаситель обличает неверие иудеев: «горе тебе Хоразине…» Когда же наконец было чтение из апостола, были произнесены следующие слова: «или о богатстве благости Его…» Это было замечено всеми епископами, и все признали, что эти чтения пришлись по воле Божией, чтобы известно было, что сердце царя ожесточено» [34]. units.english_text: "At Matins on feast days let 6 antiphons be expanded (*explicentur*), each with two psalms; throughout the whole of August let there be accelerated Matins (*manicationes*, from *mane*), because at that time there are feasts and masses of saints; in September, 7 antiphons with two psalms each; in October, 8 with 3 psalms; in November, 9 with 3; in December, 10 with 3; in January and February the same until Pascha (consequently, the greatest number of psalms at Matins was 30, and the smallest 12); but whoever recites fewer than 12 psalms, let him fast until evening, eating bread with water, and let him have no other nourishment on that day; and whoever neglects to do this latter, let him eat bread with water all week and fast every day until evening" (canon 18).

units.english_text: At the night service, a special independent position was occupied by its concluding portion, which fell at dawn (*ad Laudes*); it was celebrated with particular solemnity. Gregory of Tours recounts of Gallus of Arverna (Clermont) that, although in other places at dawn they sang only the Benediction (*Benedictio*—the Canticles of the Three Holy Children and of Zacharias, which begin with the verb "to bless" and are appointed now in the final part of Catholic Matins [^1524]), he concluded Matins having chanted Ps. 50, the Benediction, and performed the Alleluiaticum with a little chapter (*alleluiatico cum capitello*—a brief excerpt from the Old or New Testament)" (all this is appointed even today at *ad Laudes*). — Regarding the office of the 1st Hour in the Western Church of this epoch, it is known that confession of sins took place at it: "Before Ps. 50," says Chrodegang (*Grodegangus*), Bishop of Metz in the VIII century concerning the 1st Hour, "let them make confession one to another, saying: **"I confess unto the Lord and unto thee, brother, that I have sinned in thought, word, and deed; therefore I beseech thee, pray for me"**; and the other brother answers: **"May Almighty God have mercy upon thee, and forgive thee all thy sins, deliver *(Orig. p. 306)* thee from every evil, preserve thee in all good, and bring thee unto life everlasting"**" [^1525] (a similar confession exists in a different formula even today at the Roman Catholic 1st Hour; cf. among us the mutual forgiveness at the end of Compline and the Midnight Office). Following the 1st Hour in certain churches there was a distinct office—the *officium capituli* (chapter office), consisting of the reading of some canonical or pastoral rule (cf. among us the Catechesis of St. Theodore the Studite at the 2nd Hour) and the martyrology, followed by the verse: **"Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints"** (*"Chestna pred Gospodem smert' prepodobnykh Ego"* / Ps. 115:6; cf. our prokeimenon); on Sundays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and feast days of saints, the first reading was replaced by a homily [^1526]. Among the other offices there is mention of the 6th Hour and Vespers. The aforementioned Council of Tours states: "The patristic ordinances command that at the 6th hour 6 psalms with Alleluia be said, and at the 12th hour 12 psalms likewise with Alleluia" (canon 18). By the 12th hour must be understood, presumably, Vespers, since Compline could only have appeared after Vespers. The Council of Mérida (*Emeritensis*) in Spain of 606 requires that "as in other churches on feast days in the evening, after the bringing in of the light (*post lumen oblatum*), the *vespertinum* (evening psalm) is said before the *sonus* (sound), so let this be observed also by us in our churches" (canon 2). The obscure terms encountered here are well explained by the order of Vespers in the Mozarabic (Spanish) Breviary: "Whether on a feast day or an ordinary day, the hours (the reckoning of liturgical time) always begin with Vespers on the eve [^1527], and the beginning is made through the invocation of Jesus Christ with the preceding Lord's Prayer—through pronouncing in a low voice: **"Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison. Our Father"**. And in a loud voice: **"In the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ, light be with you"** [^1528], that is, light hath been brought in. Those present respond: **"Thanks be to God"** (*Deo gratias*). And the presbyter says: **"The Lord be always with you"**. Response: **"And with thy spirit"**. And the order of Vespers, whether a feast or not, proceeds as follows: first the psalm is said, that is, the *Vespertinum* (evening psalm) [^1529]; upon its conclusion the presbyter says: **"The Lord be with you"**. Response: **"And with thy spirit"**. Immediately the *sonus* is said, if it be a feast, seeing that a weekday hath no *sonus*, with the exception of Sunday, when it is said for the sake of solemnity. Such is the rule. And this *sonus* is: **"O come,** **let us rejoice unto the Lord..."** (*"Priidite, vozraduemsia Gospodevi..."* / *Venite, exsultemus Domino* [Ps. 94:1 / MT 95:1]) [^1530].

units.english_text: On Sundays the office was more solemn: according to the ancient rite of the churches of Cambrai (*Cameracensis*) and Arras (*Atrebatensis*), the Sunday vigil was to begin before midnight, the ringing for it with all the bells (*signa*), the church was to be illuminated abundantly, the readings and responsories were to be performed protractedly (*tractim*), the ninth reading was evangelical from patristic homilies and was read by the deacon, presbyter, or bishop in its entirety, unless dawn intervened; at the beginning of each of the three nocturns there was censing with 2 censers, which at the *(Orig. p. 307)* first nocturn were brought to the altar, at the second into the choir, and at the third to the people; the morning portion of the vigil was chanted still more slowly and in a higher pitch than the nocturns [^1531].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: антифоны респонсории и коллекты
units.slavonic_text: ### Антифоны, респонсории и коллекты
units.english_text: For a complete conception of Western cathedral-parochial divine worship in the VI–VIII centuries, a few additional remarks must be made regarding the manner of performing antiphons and responsories, which occupied such an important place in it, as also concerning the rite of concluding the service, since even greater significance was attached to this conclusion of worship here than in the East. In the epoch under consideration, the term *antiphon* had already fully acquired that meaning which it bears in contemporary Roman Catholic worship, that is, the meaning of a brief verse before a psalm or series of psalms or after it—a verse taken for the most part from that very psalm, expressing its central theme or adapting the psalm to the feast. Today, however, the antiphon is chanted only once before or after the psalm, whereas in the period under consideration antiphons were sometimes chanted with every verse of the psalm. Thus the canons of the Church of St. Martin of Tours, according to the testimony of John the Monk in the Life of St. Odo (Abbot of Cluny, † 943), wishing to prolong the service until dawn, chanted the antiphons twice at every verse of the psalm. The same is evident from the fact that on the greatest feast days at Matins (*in Laudibus*) at the end of the Canticle of Zacharias, and at Vespers at the end of the Canticle of the Theotokos (Magnificat), the antiphon was repeated thrice: once before **"Glory to the Father..."**, a second time at **"Both now and ever..."** (*Sicut erat*), and a third time at the entire concluding verse (such chanting of the antiphon was termed *triumphare—ter fari*, to 'triple') [^1532]. In a manuscript antiphonary of the XI century, to every verse of the Canticle of the Theotokos there is assigned as an antiphon a verse from the Gospel of Matthew concerning the Resurrection of Christ. The chanting of the antiphon was begun (*impositio*), at a sign from the archdeacon, by particularly skilled cantors holding the rank of subdeacon, of whom there were 7 in the Roman Church: the first antiphon being intoned by the foremost of these subdeacons (*primicerius*), the second by the second-ranking (*secundicerius*), and so forth; only at Pascha did a deacon intone the antiphon to the Gospel [^1533]. (Cf. below the Asmatic Cursus / Sung Office and above the assessment of Abba Nilus of Sinai regarding cathedral divine worship). By *responsory* was meant, for the most part, a verse sung in connection with a reading (cf. our prokeimenon), specifically following the reading. This is a verse taken mostly from a psalm, expressing the fundamental thought of the lesson; today by responsory is properly understood the second half of such a verse, constituting the choir's response to its first half sung by the cantor or priest, which is termed the verse—*versus*, *versiculum*. Amalarius (IX century) notes the difference in the singing of the responsory between the Roman and Gallican churches: the Romans, upon finishing the verse, 'begin the responsory from the beginning,' that is, they answer the singing of the verse by repeating that same entire verse *(Orig. p. 308)* (as among us in chanting the prokeimenon the second time), whereas in Gaul 'from the final verse they make a responsory by means of its two parts, joining them into a single body' (as among us in chanting the prokeimenon the 3rd time); for this reason, for a responsory it was necessary to select a verse both parts of which would possess their own meaning, while their union would yield a new thought [^1534]. The responsory was chanted in a special place of the temple or in the midst of the choir, but not upon the ambo. The verse preceding the responsory was always chanted more softly than the latter (cf. among us the chanting of the verse unto the prokeimenon), out of apprehension that the voice might not suffice for the responsory: 'while at the repetition of the responsory they raise the voice with confidence, no longer fearing the verse' [^1535]. According to canon 17 of the Fourth Council of Toledo of 633, 'some at the end of the responsory do not say **"Glory to the Father..."** on the ground that it sometimes sounds unsuitable; but let there be such a distinction, that on joyful responsories **"Glory..."** should follow, while on mournful ones the beginning should be repeated' (cf. among us the Alleluia of Lenten Vespers without the **"Glory..."**). In the Arabic recension of the canons of the Council of Nicaea it is required to chant the responsories from memory, and not from a book [^1536] (cf. our canonarch). — A very important part of Matins and Vespers was constituted by their conclusion, the final, dismissive prayer, termed the *collecta*. It was pronounced by the highest-ranking cleric present at the service. The Council of Barcelona (*Barcinonensis*) of 540 prohibits 'presbyters in the presence of the bishop to conclude (*non colligant*) the prayers' (canon 5). This conclusion was always identical for different offices, and Agrestius accused Abbot Columbanus at the Council of Mâcon (*Matisconensis*, in Gaul) in 585 of having introduced different collects for different offices. In the Lateran Basilica the Lord's Prayer served as the collect (cf. among us at the end of Vespers and at the end of the Hours according to the Horologia of the VIII–IX centuries), but this was a peculiarity and, as it were, a privilege of this single church, in which an indication was seen of the primacy and dignity of the Roman Church. In the words of the Spanish Abbot Beatus of the VII century, 'upon the conclusion of the office one must not depart from the church before they say: **"In the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us go in peace"**' [^1537].

units.slavonic_incipit: богослужении) Респонсорием назывался большей частью стих
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: богослужении респонсорием назывался большей частью стих к чтению
units.slavonic_text: богослужении) Респонсорием назывался большей частью стих к чтению (ср. прокимен) и именно после чтения. Это стих большей частью из псалма, выражающий основную мысль чтения; ныне респонсорием называется собственно вторая половина такого стиха, составляющая ответ хора на поемую певцом или священником его первую половину, называемую стихом — versus, versiculum. Amalarius (IX в.) отмечает ту разницу в пении респонсория между римской и галльской церквами, что римляне по окончании стиха «начинают респонсорий с начала», т. е. на пение стиха отвечают повторением этого же целого стиха {с. 308} (как у нас пение прокимна во второй раз), в Галлии же «из конечного стиха делают респонсорий посредством двух частей его, составляя из них одно тело» (как у нас пение прокимна в 3-й раз), почему для респонсория приходится выбирать такой стих, обе части которого имели бы своей смысл, а соединение их давало бы новую мысль [45]. Пелся респонсорий на особом месте храма или среди хора, но не на амвоне. Стих, предшествующий респонсорию, пелся всегда тише последнего (ср. у нас чтение стиха к прокимну) из опасения, что не достанет голоса для респонсория: «повторении же респонсория поднимают голос уверенно, уже не боясь стиха» [46]. По 17 правилу 4 Толедского Собора 633 г. «некоторые в конце респонсория не говорят Слава (Отцу…) на том основании, что это иногда звучит неподходяще; но пусть будет такая разница, что на радостных респонсориях следовала бы Слава, а на печальных повторялось бы начало» (ср. у нас аллилуиа вечерни «и во веки веков» без Славы). В арабской редакции постановлений Никейского Собора требуется петь респонсории на память, а не по книге [47] (ср. у нас канонарх). — Весьма важную часть утрени и вечерни составляло их заключение, последняя, отпустительная молитва, называемая collecta. Она произносилась высшим из присутствовавших за богослужением священнослужителей. Собор Барцелонский (Barcinonensis) 540 г. запрещает «пресвитерам в присутствии епископа заключать (non colligant) молитвы» (пр. 5). Это заключение было всегда одинаково для разных служб, и Агрестий обвинял аббата Колумбана на Соборе Matisconensi (в Галлии) 585 г. за то, что тот завел разные коллекты для различных служб. В Латеранском Соборе коллектой служила молитва Господня (ср. у нас в конце вечерни и в конце часов по часословам VIII–IX в.), но это было особенностью и как бы привилегией одной этой церкви, в чем видели указание на первенство и достоинство Римской Церкви. По словам испанского аббата Беата VII в. «по окончании службы нельзя выходить из церкви прежде чем скажут: «Во имя Господа нашего Иисуса Христа пойдем с миром» [48].
units.english_text: We possess far more information concerning monastic divine worship in the West during the period under consideration. It differed in different monasteries (just as even now many Roman Catholic monasteries possess special liturgical Typika / rules). Several renowned abbots and bishops of this period left behind their rules for divine worship, which, albeit in varying degrees, influenced the development of the present Roman liturgical rite and exhibit in places interesting correspondences with our own Typikon. To these monastic rules, it would appear, Roman worship is primarily indebted for the elimination from the offices of the fixed psalms (for example, the morning psalms, *(Orig. p. 309)* the evening psalm) and their replacement by continuous divisions of the Psalter. The most important of these monastic rules is: 1) that of St. Benedict of Nursia († 543), founder of the famous monastery of Monte Cassino in southern Italy and of the order bearing his name, and generally the principal organizer of Western monasticism. In his *Rule* (*Regula*) he refers unto the rules of Basil the Great, the *Collationes* of St. Cassian, and at times reveals dependence upon the Pachomian rules [^1538]. 2) Benedict's rival in influence upon Western monasticism was Columbanus († 615), an Irishman [lit. *Scot*], founder of a series of monasteries first in Gaul, then in Italy; his monastic rules are entirely distinctive, rather severe (bearing the imprint of his northern origin), contain no references unto older rules, including that of Benedict, and were adopted in many monasteries prior unto the introduction of the Benedictine Rule. Further noted for their monastic rules were: 3) Caesarius, Bishop of Arles (*Arelatensis*, in Gaul, † 542), and his second successor in the see, 4) Aurelian; unto the former, besides the *Regula ad monachos*, is also attributed the *Regula ad virgines* (intended for the sister of Caesarius and the nuns living with her) with a more complex and detailed liturgical order than in the first *Rule*, which excites doubt concerning their authenticity; Aurelian's rules coincide in places with those of Columbanus; 5) Isidore, Bishop of Seville, † ca. 666; 6) Donatus, Bishop of Besançon (*Vesontionensis*) in northern Gaul [or *Vesontio*], † ca. 624 (*Regula ad virgines*); 7) Fructuosus, Bishop of Braga (*Bracarensis*) in Spain, † after 675; 8) an anonymous author, surnamed *Magister* of the VII century (*Regula Magistri*); and 9) two unknown abbots: the rule of one of them was published with the works of Blessed Augustine, that of the other with the rules of St. Benedict [^1539].

units.slavonic_incipit: на Западе за рассматриваемый период. Оно
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: на западе за рассматриваемый период оно было разное
units.slavonic_text: на Западе за рассматриваемый период. Оно было разное в разных монастырях (как и теперь многие римско-католические монастыри имеют особые богослужебные уставы). Несколько знаменитых аббатов и епископов этого периода оставили после себя свои правила для богослужения, которые, хотя в разной степени, повлияли на выработку нынешнего римского чина богослужения и представляют по местам интересные совпадения с нашим уставом. В первые этим монашеском уставам, по-видимому, обязано римское богослужение устранением из служб постоянных псалмов (например утренних, {с. 309} вечернего) и заменою их чередными отделами псалтири. Важнейший из этих монашеских уставов — 1) прп. Венедикта Нурсийского († 543 г.), основателя известного Монтекасинского монастыря в южной Италии и ордена своего имени и вообще главного организатора западного монашества. В своих «Правилах» (Regula) он ссылается на правила Василия Великого, Collationes прп. Кассиана и иногда обнаруживает зависимость от Пахомиевых правил [49]. 2) Соперником Венедикта по влиянию на западное монашество был Колумбан (Columbanus) † 615 г., шотландец, основатель ряда монастырей сначала в Галлии, затем в Италии; его монашеские правила совершенно своеобразны, довольно суровы (носят отпечаток его северного происхождения), «не заключают ссылок на древнейшие уставы, и в том числе на Венедикта и были приняты во многих монастырях до введения Венедиктова устава. Известны затем своими монашескими уставами. 3) Цезарий, еп. Арльский (Arelatensis в Галлии † 542 г.) и его второй преемник по кафедре. 4) Аврелиан, причем первому приписываются кроме Regula ad monachos еще Regula ad virgines (предназначенные для сестры Цезария и живших в нею монахинь) с более сложным и подробным чином богослужения, чем в первых «Правилах», что возбуждает сомнение в подлинности их; правила Аврелиана по местам совпадают с Колумбановыми; 5) Исидор, еп. Севильский, † ок. 666 г.; 6) Донат, еп. Vesonrionensis в сев. Италии † ок. 624 г. (Regula da virgines); 7) Фруктуоз (Fructuosus), еп. Bracarensis в Испании, † после 675 г.; 8) аноним, по прозванию Magister VII в. (Regula da virginsi); и 9) два неизвестных аббата; правила одного из них издавались с творениями блж. Августина, другого с правилами прп. Венедикта [50].

units.slavonic_incipit: Ветхого Завета и одно из Нового
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: ветхого завета и одно из нового на каждом
units.slavonic_text: Ветхого Завета и одно из Нового на каждом из ночных собраний; на собраниях же с субботу и воскресенье служба должна совершаться до пения петухов» (пр. 30). Для ночной службы близок к этому правилу по простоте чин наблюдавшийся Колумбаном во многих (до 1000) современных ему монастырях: «есть некоторые кафолики, у которых одно и тоже каноническое число псалмов 12 и для коротких и для длинных ночей, и из этого правила они для каждой {с. 310} ночной смены берут по 4 псалма: для начала ночи, для полуночи или пения петухов и для утрени…: в особо же священные (reverentissimis) ночи субботы и воскресенья это число (псалмов) утрояется, т. е. их бывает 36» (гл. 7). Замечательно, как в обоих этих чинах выдерживается 12-псалмие, перенесенное из Египта на Запад еще прп. Кассианом. Несколько сложнее, но ближе других в этим чинам ночная служба у прп. Венедикта: в ней также проводится система 12-псалмия, но 12 псалмов резко делятся на два отдела по 6 псалмов (ср. у нас шестопсалмие и хвалитные псалмы на утрени); кроме того служба получает у прп. Венедикта все аксессуары церковно-приходской: антифоны, респонсории и др. стихи; большое значение придается также чтениям. Ночное богослужение (vigiliae) по уставу прп. Венедикта начинается стихами «Боже в помощь мою вонми» и (dicitur) «Господи устне мои отверзеши» трижды (ныне в обратном порядке и 2-й стих однажды; ср. у нас); далее пс. 3-й (ср. у нас) со Слава и 94 «Придите возрадуемся Господеви» (как ныне), поемый с антифонными припевами (следовательно мелодически, — как ныне) или просто (certe decantandus), — должно быть в зависимости от торжественности службы), гимн Амвросия (как ныне; не Te Deum); все это вступительная часть службы, как и ныне. Далее следуют 6 псалмов с антифонами; после произнесения (dictis) их и благословения аббата бывают три чтения из Ветхого и Нового Завета или из толкований на них с респонсориями между ними, на которых братия сидят; встают на Слава последнего респонсория, который один имеет ее (Славу; ср. у нас на кафизмах). units.english_text: 'There are certain catholics who have one and the same canonical number of 12 psalms for both short and long nights, and from this rule they take for each *(Orig. p. 310)* night watch 4 psalms: for the beginning of the night, for midnight or cockcrow, and for Matins...; but on the especially sacred (*reverentissimis*) nights of Saturday and Sunday this number (of psalms) is tripled, that is, there are 36 of them' (ch. 7).
