Its kernel, as we have seen, could have been the 4th of the 'fasts of the four seasons' [Ember fasts]. Yet from the 5th century there are reports for the West regarding a fast specifically preparatory unto the Nativity of Christ. units.slavonic_text: предписывает пост по понедельникам, средам и субботам с 11 ноября до Рождества Христова и совершение во все это время Таин (sacrificia) по чину Четыредесятницы (пр. 9). Позднее пост был принят в Риме и Италии. Августин и Лев I не говорят о нем, но ряд гомилий Григория Великого начинается с бесед на вторую неделю адвента (так назван рождественский пост, как подготовление к пришествию, adventus, Спасителя). Сакраментарий папы Геласия, относимый к VI в., дает 5 мисс (т. е. для 5 недель) адвента; древне-испанский Силосский лекционарий — столько же, а медиоланский и мозарабский чины имеют 6 недель адвента (42 дня, как у нас 40). Но лекционарии Luxoviensis VII в. и так наз. Gotico-Gallicanum начинаются с рождественской вигилии, следовательно не имеют адвента. Папа Григорий VII в XI в. сократил число недель адвента до 4 (должно быть, в соответствие 4000 лет по римскому счислению до Рождества Христова). На Востоке первое указание на Рождественский пост (с 15 ноября) в Коптском календаре VIII в. [76]. В IX в., как увидим, здесь еще спорят об обязательности и продолжительности этого поста.
units.english_text: prescribes fasting on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays from November 11 until the Nativity of Christ, and the offering throughout all this time of the Sacrifices (*sacrificia*) according unto the order of the Forty Days [canon 9]. Later the fast was adopted in Rome and Italy. Augustine and Leo I make no mention of it, yet the series of homilies of Gregory the Great begins with discourses for the second Sunday of Advent (such being the name given unto the Nativity Fast, as a preparation for the coming, *adventus*, of the Savior). The Sacramentary of Pope Gelasius, assigned unto the 6th century, provides 5 masses (that is, for 5 weeks) of Advent; the ancient Spanish Silos Lectionary has the same number, whereas the Milanese and Mozarabic rites possess 6 weeks of Advent (42 days, corresponding unto our 40). However, the 7th-century Lectionary of Luxeuil (*Lectionarium Luxoviense*) and the so-called *Missale Gothicum* (*Gotico-Gallicanum*) begin with the vigil of the Nativity, and consequently have no Advent. Pope Gregory VII in the 11th century reduced the number of weeks of Advent unto 4 (in all likelihood, corresponding unto the 4,000 years according unto Roman chronology prior unto the Nativity of Christ). In the East the first indication of the Nativity Fast (from November 15) occurs in a Coptic calendar of the 8th century [^1565]. In the 9th century, as we shall see, the obligatoriness and duration of this fast were still disputed here.

units.slavonic_text: ### Церковная песнь
units.english_text: With the development of the church year in the 6th–8th centuries is closely linked the activity of the Eastern hymnographers of that era. On the one hand, it was evoked and expanded by this development; on the other hand, it contributed unto it, elevating ecclesiastical commemorations by hymns extolling them. Therefore this activity, no less than the history of menologia, may serve as an index of the growth and enrichment of the church year during this period.

units.slavonic_incipit: С развитием церковного года в VI–VIII
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: с развитием церковного года в вв стоит
units.slavonic_text: С развитием церковного года в VI–VIII вв. стоит в тесной связи деятельность тогдашних восточных песнописцев. Она, с одной стороны, вызывалась и расширялась этим развитием, с другой, содействовала ему, возвышая церковные памяти восхвалявшими их песнями. Посему эта деятельность не менее, чем история месяцесловов, может служить показателем роста и обогащения церковного года в этот период.
units.english_text: Properly speaking, only from the 6th century did hymnographic creation in the East achieve immortality, since not a single hymn prior unto this time hath come down unto us, at least under its author's name. Evident it is that only now did such creative labor enter upon the true path. Remarkable it is that precisely in this era hymnography completely languished in the West, and local councils there, as we have seen, attempted definitively to bar its access unto church services. If we compare the Eastern hymns of that era with the Western, the cause of this difference will become manifest: Western compositions continued to content themselves with general, indefinite themes; Eastern hymns responded vividly unto the rapid development of the church year, striving to exhaust each ecclesiastical commemoration. Therefore Eastern hymnography could not cease so long as this development continued. A special invigoration of it is observable precisely toward the beginning of the 6th century in Constantinople, and for this invigoration it was indebted unto the above-mentioned *(Orig. p. 329)* St. Auxentius. units.slavonic_stem_tier2: вифинский подвижник 470 г по словам его
units.slavonic_text: вифинский подвижник († 470 г.), по словам его жизнеописателя, для сходившегося к его пещере народа «составлял тропари из 2–3 речений, весьма приятные и полезные, хотя и простые, и заставлял петь их голосом самым простым и безыскусственным. Когда несколько раз повторялся попеременным пением один стих, то начинали по приказанию блаженного петь другой, потом третий и прочие по порядку». Жизнеописатель приводит и образцы этих тропарей Авксентия; один из этих образцов имеет темой ангельское славословие Господа, другой — миротворение Божие, 3 — искупление, 4 и 5 — покаянного характера, 6 — прославление святых («Радуйтеся праведные о Господе и молите за нас. Слава Тебе Христе Боже святых»). Замечает также жизнеописатель, что иные присутствовали при этом общем пении до 3 ч. (с утра), иные до 6 ч. (9 и 12 ч. дня), и что с особою торжественностью сам лично преподобный произносил песнь 3 отроков с припевом народа: «Хвалите и превозносите Его во веки», заключая эту песнь своим поучением [77]. В этом рассказе находится указание на первоначальный способ пения тропарей: каждую строфу их пели по дважды на оба лика; отголосок этой практики в нынешнем пении целого тропаря дважды или трижды, а в великие праздники в таком же исполнении и большинства стихир, ирмосов и тропарей. Так пелись и псалмы в IV–V вв.
units.english_text: Bithynian ascetic († 470), according unto the words of his biographer, for the people gathering at his cave 'composed troparia of two or three clauses, exceedingly pleasant and profitable, though simple, and caused them to chant them in a voice most simple and artless. When one verse had been repeated several times in alternating chant, they began at the command of the blessed one to chant the second, then the third, and the others in order.' The biographer cites specimens of these troparia of Auxentius: one of these specimens hath as its theme the angelic doxology of the Lord; another, God's creation of the world; the third, redemption; the fourth and fifth are of a penitential character; the sixth is a glorification of the saints (**"Rejoice in the Lord, O ye righteous, and pray for us. Glory to Thee, O Christ, God of the saints!"**). The biographer likewise observes that some remained at this common singing until the 3rd hour (of the morning), others until the 6th hour (9:00 a.m. and 12:00 noon), and that with special solemnity the venerable father himself pronounced the Canticle of the Three Holy Children with the refrain of the people: **"Praise and exalt Him supremely unto all ages"**, concluding this canticle with his own homily [^1566]. In this narrative is found an indication of the original manner of chanting troparia: each strophe was chanted twice by both choirs; an echo of this practice remains in our present chanting of the entire troparion twice or thrice, and on great feasts in the identical execution of the majority of stichera, irmoses, and troparia. In this same manner psalms were chanted in the 4th–5th centuries.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: кондак
units.slavonic_text: ### Кондак
units.english_text: Yet very soon such singing was abandoned both for psalms and for the troparion. If for psalms it was abandoned under the influence of the desire to chant as great a number of them as possible (ascetics chanted the entire Psalter within twenty-four hours), for troparia it was abandoned owing unto the multiplication of these hymns. Then the thought arose, in place of the solemn congregational chanting of each verse in a troparion, to chant in this manner only its final verse as a refrain unto an entire series of troparia. With the change in the manner of chanting the troparion (*τρέπω* = I turn; *τρόπος* = among other things, melody, tune), the designation likewise had to change: such hymns came to be called *kontakion* (*κοντάκιον*), a corruption of *κονδάκιον* (a scroll [^1567], from *κόνταξ*—a rod or stick), in all likelihood because they drew after themselves an entire series of other hymns; these latter, supplementary unto the kontakion and of longer length, were called *oikos* (*οἶκος*—house, temple, household, or the 12th part of the zodiac [^1568]).

units.slavonic_incipit: Но очень скоро такое пение было
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: но очен скоро такое пение было оставлено как
units.slavonic_text: Но очень скоро такое пение было оставлено как для псалмов, так и для тропаря. Если для псалмов оно было оставлено под влиянием мысли о необходимости петь их возможно большее число (подвижники пели в сутки целую Псалтирь), то для тропарей оно было оставлено с умножением этих песнопений. Тогда пришли к мысли взамен торжественного всенародного пения каждого стиха в тропаре, петь таким образом только последний его стих в качестве припева к целому ряду тропарей. С изменением способа пения тропаря (τρέπω обращаю, — τρόπος — между прочим, и мелодия, напев) должно было измениться и название; такие песни стали называться κοντάκιον, испорченное κονδάκιον (свиток [78] от κόνταξ — палка), должно быть, потому что вели за собою целый ряд других песней; эти последние, прибавочные к кондаку и более длинные песни называли οἶκος (дом, храм, семейство, 12-я часть зодиака [79]).
units.english_text: The founder of this genre of ecclesiastical song is considered to be St. Romanos the Melodist (6th century), a Syrian and chanter of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople; and his first kontakion *(Orig. p. 330)*, according unto tradition chanted by a special heavenly inspiration, was the kontakion for the Nativity of Christ, **"Today the Virgin giveth birth unto the Transcendent One"** (*"Deva dnes' Prekushchestvennago rozhdaet"* / *Ἡ Παρθένος σήμερον τὸν ὑπερούσιον τίκτει*): in a Greek Kondakarion of the 12th–13th centuries according unto MS No. 437 of the Moscow Synodal Library, unto this kontakion are appended 24 ikoi with the same conclusion as in the kontakion: **"A little child, God before the ages"** (*"Otrocha mlado prevechnyi Bog"*), bearing the acrostic: *τοῦ ταπεινοῦ Ῥωμανοῦ ὕμνος* ('A hymn of humble Romanos'); the number 24 corresponds unto the quantity of letters in the Greek alphabet and hath a parallel in Ps. 118 [LXX 118 / MT 119], which consists of 22 sections beginning in order with all the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Even more closely corresponds unto the structure of this psalm the kontakion and ikoi of the Annunciation, constituting the so-called Akathist, arranged alphabetically and attributed by diverse scholars either unto St. Romanos, or unto Sergius I, Patriarch of Constantinople (610–638), or unto his referendary and deacon of Hagia Sophia, George of Pisidia [^1569]. In addition unto the kontakion and ikoi for the Nativity of Christ, such hymns bearing the name of Romanos in the acrostic have survived for other feasts as well. Thus in that same Kondakarion the name of Romanos is borne by the kontakia and ikoi for Pascha (**"Though Thou didst descend into the grave"** / *"Ashche i vo grob snizshel esi"* / *Εἰ καὶ ἐν τάφῳ κατῆλθες*), for Meatfare Sunday (**"When Thou comest, O God, upon earth with glory"** / *"Egda priideshi Bozhe"*), and for Meatfare Saturday (the 1st kontakion not being the present one)—comprising 1 kontakion and 24 ikoi each; for January 6, December 17 (the Prophet Daniel), June 29, the Sunday of the Veneration of the Cross, Great Friday, the Ascension, and Pentecost—comprising a kontakion and 18 ikoi each, including those lost (as indicated by the missing letters of the acrostic); for February 2 and Palm Sunday—a kontakion and 16 ikoi; for All Saints—a kontakion and 13 ikoi; and for November 1—a kontakion and 4 ikoi. In other Kondakaria there occur, bearing the name of St. Romanos in title or acrostic, kontakia and ikoi for the following feasts and in the following numbers: September 1—28; January 6—13; Great Monday—20; Great Tuesday—23; Great Wednesday—20; Great Thursday—25; on the Denial of Peter (at the Passions)—24; Great Friday (another set)—24; the Sunday of Antipascha [Thomas Sunday]—21; August 29—20; September 8—12; December 6—26; November 1—14. The number of ikoi in the first collection corresponds more or less unto the importance of the feast. As regards the ikoi in the other collections, the attribution of certain of them unto St. Romanos may be questioned, even if his name appears in the acrostic [^1570]; yet their very quantity demonstrates that they arose in that era when kontakia and ikoi occupied the same position in divine worship as in the days of St. Romanos, that is, during the predominance of the kontakion-based structure of liturgical services. Furthermore, the Akathist on the occasion of the deliverance of Constantinople from the invasion of the Avars under Emperor Heraclius, which constituted *(Orig. p. 331)* an entire all-night service, was not an extraordinary office, but an ordinary one for that period; unusual in it was only that it was heard entirely standing upright.—St. Romanos naturally found imitators, new creators of kontakia and ikoi, and these imitations could continue throughout the entire period of the kontakion-based liturgical system, until such time as the 'kanon', a new genre of hymnography, supplanted this system, just as the kontakion in its turn had once supplanted the troparion (while the troparion had perhaps arisen to replace the antiphon). In that same Kondakarion there occur in like quantity ikoi bearing the names of other authors, notably in an acrostic bearing the name of Cosmas (for the Dormition, the kontakion **"The Mother of God, vigilant in prayers"** / *"V molitvakh neusypaiushchuiu Bogoroditsu"* and 21 ikoi), the renowned creator of kanons, for whom it was natural to begin his hymnographic activity by imitating older models. In similar quantity (around 20) kontakia and ikoi were composed occasionally by other later hymnographers, such as George (9th century), author of kanons for the Entry into the Temple (23 ikoi); and especially numerous ones by a certain Studite. Yet the majority of ikoi in the most ancient Kondakarion are without the names of authors, the number of ikoi for each feast conforming unto its solemnity, as partly with Romanos: thus for the Transfiguration an unknown author provides the kontakion (the present one) and 22 ikoi; on the Sundays of Antipascha and All Saints the present kontakia and 11 ikoi each; for the Exaltation and November 8 the present kontakia and 10 ikoi each; on September 26, October 26, and January 7, besides the kontakion, 5 ikoi; on September 8 and July 20—4 ikoi; on September 1, July 1 and 27, August 2 and 29, and on the 1st Saturday of Lent—3 ikoi; there are also sets of 2 and 1.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: творцы канонов
units.slavonic_text: ### Творцы канонов
units.english_text: The first creator of kanons was, in all likelihood, St. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem († 644), a native of Damascus. He composed triodia [three-ode kanons] of a penitential character for all the days of the Forty Days [Great Lent] and for the Resurrection of Christ, which are no longer in use today (having been supplanted, in all probability, by Studite compositions); thus the original form of the kanon was the triodion, perhaps even the diodion [two-ode kanon], just as at Matins originally not all biblical canticles were chanted, but only several (as hath survived unto this day in Armenian and Roman Catholic worship). Apart from triodia, St. Sophronius wrote Anacreontic verses and epigrams for many feasts (evidently not intended for liturgical use). Under his name are inscribed in the most ancient manuscripts the Royal Hours of Great Friday, the Eve of the Nativity of Christ, and the Order of the Great Blessing of Water at Theophany. St. Andrew († c. 712) of the Lavra of St. Sabbas, subsequently Archbishop of Crete, was in all likelihood the first to write complete kanons [nine-ode kanons], yet he began with triodia, which he composed for all the days of Holy Week (now chanted at its Complines, having been supplanted at Matins by the triodia of Cosmas), with the exception of Holy Saturday; for the more solemn feasts he wrote complete kanons—those presently in use being: the Great Kanon, that for the Raising of Lazarus, the Sunday of the Myrrh-bearers, Mid-Pentecost, the Nativity of the Theotokos, *(Orig. p. 332)* the Conception of Anna, June 24 [Nativity of the Forerunner], and December 20 unto St. Ignatius the God-Bearer; those not presently in use: for the Exaltation, the Meeting of the Lord, June 29, July 23 (unto the Martyr Trophimus and his companions), and August 1 (unto the Maccabees). St. Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, who died in exile for the veneration of the holy icons (the son of an executed senator, previously Bishop of Cyzicus), composed kanons presently in use: for the Forefeast of the Exaltation, May 30 unto St. Isaacius, and June 17 unto the Martyr Hermias. St. Cosmas, Bishop of Maiuma, the elder foster-brother and fellow ascetic in the monastery of St. Sabbas of St. John of Damascus, who died shortly after him, wrote kanons or triodia or tetraodia [four-ode kanons]

units.slavonic_text: (последние в субботу ваий и Великую другими превращены в полные каноны) на все дни Страстной седмицы от Лазаревой субботы и на двунадесятые праздники кроме Пасхи, Вознесения, Рождества Пресв. Богородицы, Введения и Благовещения, сверх того каноны на 26 дек. богоотцам, 23 апр. вмч. Георгию. Св. Иоанн Дамаскин († ок. 780 г.), сначала министр Дамасского халифа, потом инок обители Св. Саввы и иерусалимский проповедник, исповедник за иконы, написал воскресные каноны октоиха на 8 гласов и каноны на двунадесятые праздники кроме Воздвижения, Введения, Сретения и Ваий (на Благовещение — четверопеснец или двупеснец), сверх того каноны в неделю Фомину, 1 сент. началу индикта, 13 сент. Обновлению, 7 мая Явлению Креста, 23 сент. зачатию Иоанна Предтечи, 24 июня Рождеству, 29 авг. Усекновению и 24 февраля Обретению главы его, 29 июня апп. Петру и Павлу, 8 мая еванг. Иоанну, 30 ноября ап. Андрею, 27 декабря архид. Стефану, 1 окт. ап. Анании; затем святым (по ликам) прав. Иову 6 мая; пророкам: Илии 20 июля, Елисею 14 июня, Исаии 9 мая; святителям: прав. Лазарю (не употребляется), Ипполиту 30 янв., Павлу Константинопольскому 6 ноября, Василию Великому 1 янв., Григорию Нисскому 10 янв., Иоанну Златоусту два 27 янв., Епифанию Кипрскому 12 мая; мученикам: Вавиле 4 сентября, Автоному 14 сентября, Евфимии 16 сентября, Фекле 24 сентября, Сергию и Вакху 8 октября, Епимаху 31 октября, Косме и Дамиану два 1 ноября, Акепсиму 3 ноября, Мине 11 ноября, Евстратию 13 декабря, Киру и Иоанну 31 янв., Феодору Тирону 17 февраля, Протерию 28 февраля (не употр.), 40 мчч. 9 марта, Георгию 23 апр., Леонтию 18 июня, Иулиану Килик. 21 июня; преподобным: Павлу Фивейскому 15 янв., Арсению 8 мая, Иоанну Колову 9 ноября, Онуфрию 8 сентября, Симеону Дивногорцу 24 мая, Максиму исповеднику 21 янв. Св. Стефан Савваит т. е. инок монастыря Саввы († ок 807 г.), написал каноны Обрезанию, Кириаку Отшельнику 29 сентября, прп. отцам, избиенным в обители св. Саввы 20 марта, св. Варваре и Иоанну Дамаскину 4 дек. — Все эти авторы канонов писали и стихиры на некоторые памяти. От этого же периода известны и другие песнописцы, например Феодор Сикеот еп. Анастасиопольский VIII в., Георгий, еп. Сира{с. 333}кузский († ок. 669 г.), и др., оставившие после себя по несколько стихир и канонов.
units.english_text: (the latter on Lazarus Saturday and Great Saturday having been transformed by others into complete kanons) for all the days of Holy Week from Lazarus Saturday and for the Twelve Great Feasts, except Pascha, the Ascension, the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos, the Entry into the Temple, and the Annunciation; in addition, kanons for December 26 unto the Ancestors of God, and April 23 unto the Great-Martyr George. St. John of Damascus († c. 780), at first a minister of the Caliph of Damascus, later a monk of the Monastery of St. Sabbas, a Jerusalem preacher, and a confessor for the holy icons, composed the Sunday kanons of the Octoechos for the 8 tones and kanons for the Twelve Great Feasts, except the Exaltation, the Entry into the Temple, the Meeting of the Lord, and Palm Sunday (for the Annunciation—a tetraodion or diodion); furthermore, kanons for Thomas Sunday; September 1 for the Beginning of the Indiction; September 13 for the Dedication; May 7 for the Apparition of the Cross; September 23 for the Conception of John the Forerunner; June 24 for his Nativity; August 29 for his Beheading; February 24 for the Finding of his Head; June 29 for the Apostles Peter and Paul; May 8 for John the Evangelist; November 30 for the Apostle Andrew; December 27 for the Archdeacon Stephen; October 1 for the Apostle Ananias; then unto saints (by choir): unto Righteous Job on May 6; unto prophets: Elias on July 20, Elisha on June 14, Isaiah on May 9; unto hierarchs: Righteous Lazarus (not in use), Hippolytus on January 30, Paul of Constantinople on November 6, Basil the Great on January 1, Gregory of Nyssa on January 10, John Chrysostom (two kanons) on January 27, Epiphanius of Cyprus on May 12; unto martyrs: Babylas on September 4, Autonomus on September 14, Euphemia on September 16, Thecla on September 24, Sergius and Bacchus on October 8, Epimachus on October 31, Cosmas and Damian (two kanons) on November 1, Akepsimas on November 3, Menas on November 11, Eustratius on December 13, Cyrus and John on January 31, Theodore the Recruit [Tyro] on February 17, Proterius on February 28 (not in use), the Forty Martyrs on March 9, George on April 23, Leontius on June 18, Julian of Cilicia on June 21; unto venerable fathers: Paul of Thebes on January 15, Arsenius on May 8, John the Dwarf [Colobos] on November 9, Onuphrius on September 8, Symeon of the Admirable Mountain on May 24, Maximus the Confessor on January 21. St. Stephen the Sabaite, that is, a monk of the Monastery of St. Sabbas († c. 807), wrote kanons for the Circumcision; Cyriacus the Hermit on September 29; the Venerable Fathers Slain at the Monastery of St. Sabbas on March 20; and St. Barbara and John of Damascus on December 4.—All these authors of kanons composed stichera likewise for certain commemorations. From this same period other hymnographers are known, such as Theodore of Sykeon, Bishop of Anastasiopolis (8th century), George, Bishop of Syra*(Orig. p. 333)*cuse († c. 669), and others, who left behind them several stichera and kanons.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: размер церковной песни
units.slavonic_text: ### Размер церковной песни
units.english_text: Greek ecclesiastical chant in all the indicated genres (troparion, kontakion, kanon, sticheron) of this era, as of subsequent periods, is constructed according unto a special poetic system: not the ancient metric system based upon the quantity (length and brevity) of syllables, but upon the so-called rhythmic system, based upon the number of syllables in a verse and the placement of accents upon them; this because the distinction between letters according unto their length and brevity had by that time already vanished from spoken speech. units.slavonic_stem_tier2: феодосий александрийский говорит что желающий составит канон должен
units.slavonic_text: (Феодосий Александрийский) говорит, что желающий составить канон, должен написать тропари, которые имели бы одинаковое число слогов и одинаковое ударение с ирмосом. Таким образом ударение играет главную роль в построении греческих песнопений. Например в кондаке Рождества Христова: Ἡ παρθένος σήμερον Τὸν ὑπερούσιον τίκτει Καὶ ἡ γῆ τὸ σπήλαιον Τῷ ἀπροσίτῳ προσάγει… в 1 и 3 стихах по 7 слогов, во 2 и 4 по 8; в 1 и 3 стихе ударения на 3 и 5 слоге, во 2 и 4 на 4 и 7-м слоге. (В переводе на славянский язык, понятно, ритм не сохраняется). В целях этого ритма допускаются и грамматические вольности: так в двухсложных частицах, предлогах, местоимениях (ἀλλὰ, παρὰ, ἐγώ) допускается перенос ударения на первый слог; трехсложные слова с ударениями на первом или последнем слоге в случае надобности признаются имеющими два ударения и на первом, и на последнем слоге (как делается и в русском стихосложении): πόлемос, τάπεινος. Стихотворный размер греческих церковных песен подтверждается и тем, что многие из них имеют акростих (слав. «краегранесие») и рифму; например у св. Романа в кондаке на Рождество Христово σήμερον рифмует со σπήλαιον, δοξολογοῦσι с ὁδοιποροῦσι (днесь — вертеп, славословят — путешествуют) [82]. Но надо заметить, что каноны св. Иоанна Дамаскина на Рождество Христово («Спасе люди»), Богоявление («Шествует морскую») и Пятидесятницу («Божественным покровен») написаны древне-классичес{с. 334}ким метром, именно ямбом, а акростихи к ним гекзаметром (последнее было особенно трудно).

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: западная гимнография
units.slavonic_text: ### Западная гимнография
units.english_text:
Ἡ παρθένος σήμερον
Τὸν ὑπερούσιον τίκτει
Καὶ ἡ γῆ τὸ σπήλαιον
Τῷ ἀπροσίτῳ προσάγει in the 1st and 3rd lines there are 7 syllables each, in the 2nd and 4th lines 8 each; in the 1st and 3rd lines accents fall upon the 3rd and 5th syllables, in the 2nd and 4th upon the 4th and 7th syllables. (In the translation into Church Slavonic, understandably, the rhythm is not preserved). For the purposes of this rhythm grammatical liberties are likewise permitted: thus in disyllabic particles, prepositions, and pronouns (*ἀλλά*, *παρά*, *ἐγώ*) the shifting of the accent unto the first syllable is allowed; trisyllabic words with accents upon the first or last syllable are in case of necessity recognized as possessing two accents, both upon the first and upon the last syllable (as is done likewise in Russian versification): *πόлемос*, *τάπεινος*. The poetic meter of Greek ecclesiastical hymns is confirmed likewise by the fact that many of them possess an acrostic (Slavonic: *krayegranesiye*) and rhyme; for example, in St. Romanos in the kontakion for the Nativity of Christ *σήμερον* rhymes with *σπήλαιον*, and *δοξολογοῦσι* with *ὁδοιποροῦσι* ("today" — "the cave", "they give glory" — "they travel") [^1571]. Yet it must be observed that the canons of St. John of Damascus for the Nativity of Christ (**"He saved the people"** [*Spase liudi* / *Ἔσωσε λαόν*]), Theophany (**"He traverses the sea"** [*Shestvuyet morskuyu* / *Στείβει θαλάσσης*]), and Pentecost (**"Covered by divine protection"** [*Bozhestvennym pokroven* / *Θείῳ καλυφθείς*]) are written in ancient classical *(Orig. p. 334)* meter, namely iambic trimeter, and their acrostics in dactylic hexameter (the latter being exceedingly difficult).

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: осмогласие
units.slavonic_text: ### Осмогласие
units.english_text: With regard unto ecclesiastical chant, the present era accomplished especially much likewise in that only now was the cycle of liturgical chants definitively established both in the West and in the East. In the West this achievement is attributed unto Pope St. Gregory the Great; in the East, unto St. John of Damascus. According unto the words of his biographer, the Deacon John (9th century), St. Gregory assembled the melodies that had arisen across centuries in the Church, removed the less valuable, corrected the remainder, and supplied what was lacking; from the material thus obtained he compiled a new Antiphonary [^1572]. On the basis of this testimony the present Antiphonary of the Roman Church and the system of tones adopted therein are denominated Gregorian. A still later tradition attributes the ordering of ecclesiastical melodies in the East unto St. John of Damascus: unto his name and that of his teacher Cosmas is inscribed a musical treatise bearing the title 'The Hagiopolite' (*Sviatogradets*) [^1573]. As we have seen (see above, pp. 160–161), the ordering of church melodies must have begun far earlier than both Gregory the Great and John of Damascus; and tradition links the beginning of this ordering in the West with the name of St. Ambrose, whereas unto Gregory the Great is attributed solely the addition unto the 4 Ambrosian tones existing prior unto him—at the foundation of which lay the Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian modes (see *ibid.*)—of four new melodies kindred unto them, the 'plagal tones' (*toni plagales*), namely: the Hypodorian, beginning upon A and having its dominant upon the 6th degree; the Hypophrygian, beginning upon B with its dominant upon the 7th degree; the Hypolydian, upon F with its dominant upon the 6th degree; and the Hypomixolydian, upon D with its dominant upon the 7th degree. Thus were obtained 8 tones (subsequently a 9th was added, representing a mixture of the 2nd and 8th—*tonus peregrinus sive irregularis*). An identical number of tones and with an identical musical character was established, according unto tradition, by John of Damascus in the Eastern Church, only the reckoning of tones here is different: first come all the authentic tones, and *(Orig. p. 335)* then their plagal (*πλάγιοι*) counterparts, whereas in the West each authentic tone is followed immediately by its plagal:

units.slavonic_incipit: ценные, а остальные исправил и восполнил
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: ценные а остальные исправил и восполнил недостающие из
units.slavonic_text: ценные, а остальные исправил и восполнил недостающие; из полученного таким образом материала он составил новый Антифонарий [83]. На основании этого известия нынешний Антифонарий Римской Церкви и принятая там система гласов называются Григорианскими. Еще более позднее предание приписывает упорядочение церковных напевов на Востоке св. Иоанну Дамаскину: именем его и учителя его Космы надписывается музыкальный трактат с заглавием «Святоградец» [84]. Как мы видели (см. выше, стр. 160–161), упорядочение церковных напевов должно было начаться гораздо ранее и Григория Великого и Иоанна Дамаскина; и предание связывает начало этого упорядочения на Западе с именем св. Амвросия, Григорию же Великому приписывается только прибавление к существовавшим до него 4 амвросианским гласам, в основу коих легли напевы дорийский, фригийский, лидийский и миксолидийский (см. там же), новые четыре напева, сродные с теми, «побочные гласы» (toni plagales), именно: иподорийский, начинающийся с ля и имеющий доминанту на 6 ступени, ипофригийский, начинающийся с си с доминантой на 7 ступени, иполидийский с фа с доминантой на 6 ступени, ипомиксолидийский с ре с доминантой на 7 ступени. Так получилось 8 гласов (впоследствии прибавлен 9-й, представляющий смесь 2-го и 8-го — tonus peregrinus sive irregularis). Столько же гласов и с таким же музыкальным характером установил, по преданию, и Иоанн Дамаскин в Восточной Церкви, только счет гласов здесь другой: сначала идут все прямые гласы, а {с. 335} потом их побочные (πλάγιοι), тогда как на Западе за каждым прямым следует его побочный:

units.english_text: Now it remained for the liturgical typikon to define itself only in the minutest details and particulars, and its history from this era onward must assume the character of an explanatory (*tolkovy*) Typikon. By the 9th century our Typikon had already essentially formed in its fundamental conception. Now complete manuscript copies thereof could make their appearance, which, by virtue of the preceding foundational labor, might diverge from one another only in non-essential particulars. Soon, moreover, even such divergence between them disappeared, and a single liturgical typikon arose for virtually the entire Eastern Church.

units.slavonic_text: ### С IX века.
units.english_text: Nevertheless, even now such unification was long hindered by the existence within the sphere of influence of this increasingly unified typikon—the persistence of an entirely distinct liturgical rite competing with, if not surpassing it in antiquity: an order long maintained in the principal temple of the imperial capital, Hagia Sophia of Constantinople, and in the cathedrals of other major cities. We have in mind the so-called Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople and the order of the Sung Office (*ᾀσματικὴ ἀκολουθία* / *Asmatike Akolouthia*), which is closely related unto it, if not identical with it.

units.slavonic_text: Теперь богослужебному уставу нужно было определиться только в самых мелких частностях и подробностях и история его с этого времени должна принять характер толкового Типикона. Наш Типикон к IX в. идейно уже сложился. Теперь могли появиться полные списки его, которые, благодаря основной прежней работе, могли разниться друг от друга в несущественном. Но скоро и такая разница между ними исчезла, и появился единый богослужебный устав почти для всей Восточной Церкви.
units.english_text: The daily cycle of divine worship at Hagia Sophia of Constantinople hath remained unto this day an enigma, notwithstanding the fact that there hath come down unto us—and that in more than one redaction—a complete Typikon of this church from the 9th century [^1575], alongside several other monuments of this rite. In this Typikon there are indicated only the proper characteristics *(Orig. p. 337)* of divine worship for each day, and those mostly ceremonial; nowhere is a complete order of service provided, and exceedingly few hints are given regarding its constituent elements.

units.slavonic_text: ### Устав Великой Константинопольской церкви и песненное последование
units.english_text: In order to comprehend these sparse intimations, one must bear in mind that the Typikon of the Great Church—that is, of Hagia Sophia of Constantinople—presupposes the services subsequently denominated the 'Sung Office' (*ᾀσματικὴ ἀκολουθία*). Its order is set forth in detail by St. Symeon, Archbishop of Thessalonica († 1430), who terms it the 'Office of the Typikon of the Great Church', adopted in all cathedral churches, yet adds that since the capture of Constantinople by the Latins (from 1204) this order had ceased to be observed even in the 'imperial city' itself, much less in other churches, and that in his day this order was preserved solely in the Cathedral of Thessalonica.

units.slavonic_text: Соборе. Название «песненный» св. Симеон объясняет тем, что в этом последовании «не произносили ничего без пения (χωρίς μέλους) кроме молитв священника и прошений (ектений) диакона» [3]. Такой чин богослужения естественно мог образоваться в великолепном храме св. Софии, построенном в 532–538 г. имп. Юстинианом, бывшем главным дворцовым храмом и снабженным многочисленным штатом священнослужителей и певцов. Богослужение здесь не могло не отличаться особою торжественностью и не получить некоторых особенностей по сравнению не только с монастырями, но и приходскими церквами. Присутствие императора за богослужением требовало не только торжественных встреч его, но и некоторого приспособления к нему богослужения, в котором он иногда принимал и деятельное участие (совершал каждение, участвовал во входах). В таком богослужении одни части могли получить особое развитие и разработку, другие ставиться на второй план и даже исчезнуть. Нелегко богослужение в такой обстановке могло получать (так как не допускало особой продолжительности) и какие-либо добавления, особенно монашеского (подвижнического) характера, вроде обязательного выпевания всей Псалтири в течение известного пери{с. 338}ода (кафисмы и библейские песни, т. е. канон) [4]. Все это мы и наблюдаем в уставе св. Софии и песненном последовании, изложенном у св. Симеона Солунского. Но надо помнить, что чин песненного последования, даваемый у св. Симеона, отстоит от дошедших до нас Типиконов Великой церкви на 5 веков, в течение которых Константинополь и св. София пережили такие потрясения, как разрушение крестоносцами. По удалении последних св. София перестала быть дворцовым храмом, так как императоры поселились в другом дворце и за богослужением присутствовали во Влахернском храме, а в св. Софию выезжали только в торжественных случаях. Это не могло не отразиться на уставе ее в сторону уменьшения торжественности и приближения к обычному монастырско-приходскому богослужению. Во всяком случае, песненный чин служб, даваемый Симеоном Солунским, нельзя во всем объеме переносить в практику св. Софии IX–X в. и договаривать по нему частые недомолвки ее тогдашнего Типикона. То же нужно сказать и о других дошедших до нас памятниках песненного последования и чинах Великой церкви, которые большей частью не старее XV в., каковы, например: «Чин (τάξις), бываемый на вечерни, утрени, Божественной литургии и хиротонии епископа» в каноническом рукописном сборнике XV в. русского Андреевского скита на Афоне [5], имеющий в виду св. Софию, но позднейшего, чем сохранившиеся полные Типиконы, времени (он, впрочем описывает исключительно патриаршие и царские выходы и почти не заключает литургических указаний; «последование песненной вечерни» в Типик. Иерус. библ. XVI в. [6] и т. п. (Эти памятники важны только тем, что могут восполнять Симеона Солунского). Нельзя того же
units.english_text: The designation 'Sung' St. Symeon explains by the circumstance that in this office 'nothing was uttered without chant (*χωρὶς μέλους*) except the prayers of the priest and the petitions (litanies) of the deacon' [^1576]. Such an order of worship could naturally develop in the magnificent cathedral of Hagia Sophia, erected in 532–538 by Emperor Justinian, which was the principal palatine church and was endowed with an extensive staff of clergy and cantors. Divine worship here could not fail to be distinguished by extraordinary solemnity and to acquire certain peculiarities in comparison not only with monasteries, but likewise with parish churches. The presence of the Emperor at divine services demanded not only solemn receptions for him, but likewise a certain adaptation of the liturgy unto him, in which he at times took an active part (performing censing, participating in entrances). In such divine worship certain elements could receive special development and elaboration, while others were relegated unto the background or even disappeared. Under such conditions divine worship could not easily admit (as it did not permit of excessive length) any additions, particularly of a monastic (ascetic) character, such as the mandatory chanting of the entire Psalter within a fixed *(Orig. p. 338)* period (kathismata and biblical canticles, that is, the canon) [^1577]. All of this we observe in the Typikon of Hagia Sophia and in the Sung Office as set forth by St. Symeon of Thessalonica. Yet it must be remembered that the order of the Sung Office given by St. Symeon is separated from the surviving Typika of the Great Church by five centuries, during which Constantinople and Hagia Sophia experienced such convulsions as devastation by the Crusaders. Following the expulsion of the latter, Hagia Sophia ceased to be a palatine church, since the emperors took up residence in another palace and attended divine worship in the Church of Blachernae, traveling unto Hagia Sophia only on solemn occasions. This could not fail to affect its typikon in the direction of diminishing solemnity and approaching the ordinary monastic-parochial order of services. In any event, the chanted order of services provided by Symeon of Thessalonica cannot be transferred in its entirety unto the practice of Hagia Sophia of the 9th–10th centuries, nor may one fill in from it the frequent silences of its contemporary Typikon. The same must be said concerning other surviving monuments of the Sung Office and rites of the Great Church, which for the most part are no older than the 15th century, such as, for example: the 'Order (*τάξις* / *taxis*) observed at Vespers, Matins, the Divine Liturgy, and the Consecration of a Bishop' in a 15th-century canonical manuscript collection of the Russian Skete of St. Andrew on Mount Athos [^1578], which hath Hagia Sophia in view, yet dates from an era later than the surviving complete Typika (it, moreover, describes exclusively patriarchal and imperial processions and contains virtually no liturgical directions); the 'Order of Sung Vespers' in a 16th-century Typikon of the Jerusalem Library [^1579], and others. (These monuments are important solely in that they may supplement Symeon of Thessalonica). Nor can the same be said of the treatise *De Officiis Aulae Byzantinae* [*De Ceremoniis*], attributed unto Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (912–959), yet definitively redacted, in all likelihood, in the 11th century [^1580]: the liturgical directions occasionally provided therein are close in date unto the practice of the surviving complete Typika of the Great Church and may be adduced for their elucidation and supplementation. Nonetheless, a portion of the fragmentary indications of these Typika finds explanation in Symeon of Thessalonica and in the monuments mentioned; and, in any event, these Typika confirm the testimony *(Orig. p. 339)* of St. Symeon that the Great Church possessed a distinctive liturgical order, justly denominated 'Sung', distinct from the contemporary practice of monasteries and perhaps of other churches, and partially coinciding with the 'Sung Office' of the era of the Hierarch of Thessalonica.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: сказат и о соч
units.slavonic_text: сказать и о соч. «De officiis aulae Byzantinae», приписываемом имп. Константину VII Багрянородному (912–959 г.), но окончательно редактированном должно быть, в XI в. [7]: даваемые ими иногда литургические указания близки по времени к практике сохранившихся полных Типиконов Великой церкви и могут быть привлекаемы для объяснения и дополнения их. Все же часть отрывочных указаний этих Типиконов у Симеона Солунского и в указанных памятниках находит себе объяснение и, во всяком случае, эти типиконы подтверждают сообще{с. 339}ние св. Симеона, что Великая церковь имела своеобразный чин службы, справедливо называемый «песненным», отличный от тогдашней практики монастырей, а может быть и других церквей, и отчасти совпадавший с «песненным последованием» эпохи Солунского святителя.
units.english_text: Apart from the Liturgy, the Great Church of the 9th–11th centuries possessed, apparently, among its services only Vespers and Matins, occasionally (on the eves of feasts) after Vespers a *pannychis* (*παννυχίς*, an all-night vigil distinct from Matins), and during Great Lent the office of *trithekte* (*тритекти*). The Hours are not mentioned. Of the constituent elements of Vespers there is indicated, at least at times, as its beginning: **"Incline Thine ear, O Lord"** (*"Prikloni Gospodi ukho Tvoye"*), that is, Ps. 85, with which the Vespers of the Sung Office began according unto Symeon of Thessalonica; after it a certain *τὸ τελευταῖον* (in all likelihood, the final antiphon of the opening antiphons of Vespers: see below) and **"Lord, I have cried"** (invariably); after **"Lord, I have cried"** there is indicated a troparion or '3 small antiphons' (at times these occur after the prokeimenon) or immediately the *synapte* prayer with petition (*εὐχὴ συναπτὴ μετὰ αἰτήсеως*), that is, litanies, in all probability the Great Synapte or Augmented Litany with the Litany of Supplication (at times this occurs after the prokeimenon and antiphons), then the Entrance (at times), the prokeimenon, and readings (paremias); in conclusion invariably—a troparion, at times thrice with the verses of the psalm and the *perisse* (*καὶ τὴν περισσήν*, that is, the troparion in conclusion; thus on the eve of Pentecost, followed by the deacon's exclamation: **"Wisdom!"**, whereupon the reading of the Apostle begins until the pannychis) [^1581]. Still fewer are the indications regarding the composition of Matins. At it there is customarily named the *amomos* (*ἄμωμος*, the "Blameless"), that is, indubitably, Ps. 118 [the 17th Kathisma], indicated in the 1st part of Matins of the Sung Office likewise by Symeon of Thessalonica; the Blameless [Amomos] was divided into 3 antiphons, and at the third a troparion was at times appointed and an entrance took place [^1582]. Apparently on more solemn Sundays (Cheesefare Sunday, Palm Sunday, Thomas Sunday [Antipascha], Myrrhbearers Sunday) and kindred days (Lazarus Saturday, Great Saturday, from Pascha through Wednesday inclusive, the Saturday of the 2nd Week after Pascha for the commemoration of James the Brother of the Lord, at Ascension, and at Pentecost) [^1583], after the Amomos there was appointed a certain *Eulogetos* (*Εὐλογητός*, "Blessed", perhaps the verse of Ps. 118: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord"**, in an especially solemn execution or with certain refrains after the manner of our present troparia unto it [the Evlogitaria]). On immovable Great Feasts there is no mention at Matins either of the Amomos or of the *Eulogetos*; yet in place of both at the Nativity of Christ there stand 18 antiphons *σὺν τοῦ μεγάλου* ("with the Great"—in all likelihood the beginning of a certain hymn), one of two troparia, then another troparion at **"God is the Lord"**; consequently on all immovable feasts (and perhaps on certain Sundays as well, since the Matins of some of them likewise begins with the indication of a troparion at the 50th Psalm) the Amomos was not chanted and, in all probability, *(Orig. p. 340)* was replaced by another psalm. In a manuscript typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library, No. 333–391, of the 14th century (fol. 150v) there is an article under the heading: 'And these are the kathismata for feasts according to the typikon of the cathedral church', appointing one kathisma for each of the major feasts and ranks of saints (such kathismata are known likewise unto the most ancient Studite typika): for the Nativity of Christ—the 10th Kathisma; Theophany—the 16th; Transfiguration—the 12th; Exaltation—the 13th; Ascension—the 7th; Descent of the Holy Spirit—the 19th; Dormition—the 17th; Entry into the Temple—the 6th; for hierarchs and unmercenaries—the 5th; for martyrs—the 9th. It may be that these kathismata replaced the Amomos on feast days. All of this may be designated the first part of Matins according unto the ancient Sophia Typikon. From this type of Matins, provided by the Patmos manuscript of the Typikon (the earliest of the surviving copies), the first part of Matins in the Dresden manuscript (the latest, yet no later than the 10th–11th century) diverges considerably: for the Exaltation it is stated here concerning Matins: 'there is chanted *τὸ πρῶτον* (the first, the 1st antiphon?) of the day and 12 antiphons with the canon (*μετὰ καὶ τοῦ κανόνος*), and there is chanted likewise the Polyeleos and the *Benedicite* [*Благословите*]'. What is meant here by the canon, the polyeleos, and the *Benedicite* (the Canticle of the Three Holy Children?), it is difficult to say, yet scarcely do the first two terms bear their present significance. The subsequent constant, if not the most central, portion of Sophia Matins was constituted by Psalm 50; for all festal and many Sunday Matins there is invariably indicated a troparion *εἰς τὸν Ν* (that is, at Psalm 50), at times two troparia; the troparion was chanted, if not with every verse of the psalm, then at least with several; in the Dresden manuscript at the above-mentioned Matins a proper troparion is appointed for each of the first five verses of Psalm 50 and for the Doxology (*Glory...*) [^1584]. In addition unto Psalm 50, there is mentioned in this part of Matins **"Glory to God in the highest"** [^1585] (the Great Doxology). From these fragmentary and incomplete indications, naturally, it is impossible to construct an exhaustive conception of the order of Vespers and Matins at Hagia Sophia in the 9th century; nevertheless, scarcely is it accidental that no mention is made of such prayers as **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** and **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** at Vespers, nor of the opening morning psalms (the Six Psalms), the biblical canticles, and the Gospel at Matins, the more so as several of these elements are not mentioned by Symeon of Thessalonica either. Their absence is all the more remarkable given that they entered into the composition of the services, at least in certain localities, as early as the 4th century, and some not only in the East but in the West as well. If silence concerning them is not accidental, is this not an abbreviation of the service for a palatine cathedral? Nevertheless, the rite in general bears the imprint of the most profound antiquity: a limitation of hymns (troparia) similar unto Western liturgical orders, and a predominant position of antiphons and prokeimena (= responsories).

provenance.verbatim_source: Apart from the Liturgy, the Great Church of the 9th–11th centuries possessed, apparently, among its services only Vespers and Matins, occasionally (on the eves of feasts) after Vespers a *pannychis* (*παννυχίς*, an all-night vigil distinct from Matins), and during Great Lent the office of *trithekte* (*тритекти*). The Hours are not mentioned. Of the constituent elements of Vespers there is indicated, at least at times, as its beginning: **"Incline Thine ear, O Lord"** (*"Prikloni Gospodi ukho Tvoye"*), that is, Ps. 85, with which the Vespers of the Sung Office began according unto Symeon of Thessalonica; after it a certain *τὸ τελευταῖον* (in all likelihood, the final antiphon of the opening antiphons of Vespers: see below) and **"Lord, I have cried"** (invariably); after **"Lord, I have cried"** there is indicated a troparion or '3 small antiphons' (at times these occur after the prokeimenon) or immediately the *synapte* prayer with petition (*εὐχὴ συναπτὴ μετὰ αἰτήсеως*), that is, litanies, in all probability the Great Synapte or Augmented Litany with the Litany of Supplication (at times this occurs after the prokeimenon and antiphons), then the Entrance (at times), the prokeimen

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: службы для дворцовой церкви тем не менее чин
units.slavonic_text: службы для дворцовой церкви? Тем не менее чин вообще носит печать самой глубокой древности: подобная западным уставам ограниченность гимнов (тропарей) и преобладающее положение антифонов и прокимнов (= респонсориев).
units.english_text: The order of Vespers and Matins provided by St. Symeon already contains a series of accretions from other typika (monastic and, in all likelihood, parochial churches). We shall set it forth, supplementing and elucidating St. Symeon by the data of the two above-mentioned monuments (the 'Order' according unto the Athos manuscript and the Sung *(Orig. p. 341)* Vespers according unto the Jerusalem manuscript). Prior unto the beginning of Vespers the temple was filled with sweet fragrance (not by censing, but in all probability as is done among us at present before Paschal Matins). 'The priest, having taken his stand before the holy table', exclaimed: **"Blessed is the Kingdom…"**; not **"Blessed is our God…"**, observes St. Symeon, 'for this is not customary in the Sung Office, since such (the latter exclamation) hath reference solely unto Old Testament Scripture… thus the order of the Liturgy alone hath remained (with regard unto the opening exclamation) faithful unto the ancient rite'. Yet in the order of the 15th-century Athos manuscript the exclamation is: **"Blessed is our God"** or **"Blessed is the Kingdom"**. Following the petitions of the Great Synapte—which in the 'Order of Sung Vespers' of the Jerusalem manuscript possesses entirely our present composition—the chanting of 3 antiphons begins: specifically, after **"Help us, save us"** before **"Remembering our all-holy, immaculate…"** in the Great Synapte, according unto Symeon of Thessalonica the cantors (*οἱ ψάλται*) chant: **"Hear me. Glory to Thee, O God!"**, while according unto the Jerusalem manuscript the domestikos exclaims: **"And hear me"**; this is the second half of the 1st verse of Psalm 85, which constitutes the 1st Antiphon of Vespers; it was proclaimed prior unto the chanting of the entire psalm either as its theme or as a model for chanting the whole psalm according unto it [^1586]; characteristic is the introduction of this refrain into the interior of the litany before its conclusion, in all likelihood as a token of the close bond between psalm-praise and Christian prayer; in Symeon of Thessalonica unto this refrain are added several others: **"Incline Thine ear, O Lord, and hear me"**, **"Glory to God in the highest"**, **"Heaven and earth are full of Thy glory"**, **"Blessed is the glory of the Lord"** (all angelic hymns). Following the exclamation of the Great Synapte the entire 85th Psalm, **"Incline Thine ear, O Lord"**, is chanted by verses between both choirs with the refrain unto each verse: **"Glory to Thee, O God!"** According unto the Jerusalem manuscript, the domestikos chants the 1st verse of the psalm and for the final time the refrain unto it after *Glory... Now and ever...* After Psalm 85, according unto Symeon, the priest recites the Little Litany, and the chanter (*ψάλτης*), after **"Help us, save us"**, chants: **"The world (*τὴν οἰκουμένην*), Alleluia"**. Symeon of Thessalonica connects 'the world' grammatically with 'Help us, save us'; yet the analogy with the first antiphon compels us to perceive in this word a fragment of the psalm that constituted the 2nd Antiphon [^1587]. The Jerusalem manuscript makes no mention of this remnant of the 2nd Antiphon and indicates after the 1st Antiphon not the entire Little Litany, but only from **"Remembering our all-holy, immaculate…"** After the Little Litany, according unto Symeon, 'the chanter chants according unto the day the prokeimenon, which is called likewise the final (*τελευταῖον*) antiphon on account of the other antiphons read formerly, yet now omitted; on Saturday at Vespers (as such a prokeimenon) there is said: **"Let God arise"** (*ἀναστήτω ὁ Θεός*)'. In the Jerusalem manuscript in place of this 'prokeimenon' there is indicated: **"Unto the saints that are in His earth hath the Lord been wonderful"** (that is, Ps. 15:3 [16:3]), **"Alleluia, Glory..."** *(Orig. p. 342)* **"Now and ever..."**; perhaps this 'prokeimenon' is not for Sunday (although taken from a psalm containing a prophecy of the Resurrection of Christ, and the entire psalm might have been chanted with this refrain), but for ordinary Vespers and adapted unto the commemorations of diverse saints. All these antiphons constitute the introductory portion of Vespers, after which follows its principal part: Psalm 140, **"Lord, I have cried"**, with the refrain (*ὑπόψαλμα*) on one Sunday: **"Thy life-bearing Resurrection, O Lord, do we glorify"**, and on another: **"Thy saving Resurrection, O Lord, do we glorify"**; in the Jerusalem manuscript there is indicated the refrain: **"An evening sacrifice do we offer unto Thee, O Christ, which do Thou receive through Thy saints and save us"**—a refrain evidently adapted (like the preceding prokeimenon) not unto Sunday, but unto the commemoration of saints. At the verse of Psalm 140: **"For unto Thee, O Lord"**, the Entrance with lamps and censers took place (according unto St. Symeon), for which reason this verse according unto Symeon was pronounced by the chanter (according unto the Jerusalem manuscript, by the domestikos), turned toward the west, bowing unto the priest and 'as it were summoning him as one bearing the image of the Lord'; after the Entrance, accompanied by the prayer, as at present: **"Evening and morning and at noon"**, and by the exclamation: **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"**, according unto St. Symeon 'hymns of the Resurrection' are chanted upon the ambo, while according unto the Jerusalem manuscript from the verse: **"If Thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities…"**, stichera are chanted, first one set, and then another. During these hymns or stichera censing is performed, according unto Symeon by the priest or deacon, and according unto the Jerusalem manuscript by the deacon. The psalm concludes with *Glory... Now and ever...* According unto the 'Order' of the Athos manuscript, the Entrance takes place at *Glory...*, and the exclamation **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"** is made at the conclusion of the stichera (as at present). There follows the prokeimenon of the day (according unto Symeon: **"The Lord is King"**), the Litany: **"Let us all say…"** (according unto the Jerusalem manuscript; according unto Symeon: 'for all the faithful, emperors, and priests'), and the Little Litany with the exclamation, according unto Symeon: **"For Thine it is to have mercy…"**, and according unto the Jerusalem manuscript: **"For good art Thou…"** Then follow the Small Antiphons, so named because they consist not of entire psalms, but of 4 verses. The 1st Antiphon hath the refrain: **"By the prayers of the Theotokos…"**, with the verses of Psalm 114 [116:1–9]: **"I am well pleased, that the Lord hath heard…"** (in the Jerusalem manuscript: **"Because He hath inclined His ear…"**), **"Gracious is the Lord and righteous…"**, **"I will walk well-pleasing before the Lord…"** *Glory... Now and ever...* The Little Litany with the exclamation: **"For Thou art our God…"** The 2nd Antiphon hath the refrain: **"Save us, O Son of God, Who art risen from the dead…"** (on weekdays: **"Who art wonderful in the saints…"**), with the verses of Psalm 115 [116:10–19]: **"I believed, therefore I spoke: but I was humbled exceedingly"** [LXX Ps. 115:1], **"What shall I render unto the Lord…"**, **"I will take the cup of salvation…"** *Glory...* **"Only-Begotten Son..."** *Now and ever...* **"The all-glorious"**

units.slavonic_incipit: Божию Матерь. Малая ектения с возгласом
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: божию матер малая ектения с возгласом яко свят
units.slavonic_text: Божию Матерь. Малая ектения с возгласом «Яко свят еси…» 3-й антифон с припевом «Святый Боже…», стихи пс. 116: Хвалите Господа вси языцы… Истина Господня пребывает… Яко утвердися милость Его на нас… Слава. И ныне. При пении Трисвятого все стоят непокровены. Архиерей трижды благословляет народ с своего места. Затем по Симеону Солунскому ектения «великая» (сугубая?) и «прошения, т. е. Исполним молитву» (просительная ектения). После нее по Иерусалимской рукописи «отпустительный (т. е. тропарь) дня и отпуст». У Симеона Солунского окончание вечерни сложнее. В воскресение после просительной ектении «бывает заамвонная (не в притворе!) лития в умилостивление Бога ко всем верным; по пении воскресных (стихир) постиховно (τῶν ἀποστίχων) и слава и ныне от иерея бывает протяжное моление {с. 343} (ἐκтеνὴς δέησις) и Господи помилуй по обычаю как бы пред гробом Христа и после Услыши ны Боже отпустительный (тропарь) и отпуст. Если же день обыкновенный, литии не бывает, а отпустительный произносится, когда иерей выходит как бы на литию и становится позади амвона, при пении Богородице Дево. После этого иерей возглашает: Господу помолимся. Яко ты еси просвещение наше Христе Боже наш и Тебе славу возсылаем… Последняя из всех молитв — молитва главопреклонения и отпуста, так и на утрени и на всякой службе» [15]. Иерусалимская рукопись не говорит о молитвах священника в чине вечерни, очевидно потому что это не входило в ее задачу. Симеон Солунский указывает на протяжении вечерни три молитвы на определенных местах: на 1-м псалме, на входе и молитву главопреклонения и отпуста, а четвертую «Господи милосерде и милостиве» приводит в качестве примера того, что и «прочие молитвы вечерни имеют мысли применительно к псалмам антифонов и выражения заимствуют из них». Следовательно, и Симеон Солунский не ставил себе целью указывать всех молитв священника на вечерне. Восполнением его здесь могут быть древние Евхологии, которые, не давая чина вечерни, как и утрени, приводят только молитвы священника на той и другой службе, причем во многих из этих Евхологиев имеется в виду именно песненная вечерня и утреня, как показывают надписания молитв. Хотя большинство из этих молитв тождественны с нынешними светильничными, тайно читаемыми священником на предначинательном псалме, но надписываются они в некоторых Евхологиях IX–XIII вв. очень характерно: «молитва 1-го антифона» (нынешняя 1-я светильничная), «молитва 2-го антифона» (нынешняя 2-я), и т. д.; нынешняя молитва входа надписывается большей частью «молитва 8 антифона пред Господи воззвах». Вслед за этими 8 молитвами некоторые Евхологии имеют еще второй ряд молитв, иногда с новым счетом антифонов, причем определенно указывается на так называемые у св. Симеона Солунского (как и в списках Типикона Великой Церкви IX–X в.) «малые антифоны». Так Евхологий Барбериновой библиотеки в
units.english_text: Mother of God. The Little Litany with the exclamation: **"For holy art Thou…"** The 3rd Antiphon hath the refrain: **"Holy God…"**, with the verses of Psalm 116 [117]: **"O praise the Lord, all ye nations…"**, **"The truth of the Lord endureth forever…"**, **"For His mercy is confirmed upon us…"** *Glory... Now and ever...* During the singing of the Trisagion all stand uncovered. The hierarch blesses the people thrice from his place. Then, according unto Symeon of Thessalonica, there follows the 'Great' (Augmented?) Litany and the petitions, that is, **"Let us complete our evening prayer"** (the Litany of Supplication). Following it, according unto the Jerusalem manuscript, there follow 'the dismissory troparion of the day and the dismissal'. In Symeon of Thessalonica the conclusion of Vespers is more complex. On Sunday after the Litany of Supplication 'there takes place a behind-the-ambo (not in the narthex!) litiya for the propitiation of God toward all the faithful; after the singing of the Sunday (stichera) on the verse (*τῶν ἀποστίχων* / aposticha) and *Glory... Now and ever...*, there is made by the priest a fervent prayer *(Orig. p. 343)* (*ἐκтеνὴς δέησις*) and **"Lord, have mercy"** according unto custom as it were before the tomb of Christ, and after **"Hear us, O God"**, the dismissory troparion and dismissal. If, however, it be an ordinary day, no litiya takes place, but the dismissory troparion is recited when the priest goes forth as it were for a litiya and stands behind the ambo, during the chanting of **"O Theotokos Virgin, rejoice"**. After this the priest exclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord. For Thou art our enlightenment, O Christ our God, and unto Thee do we send up glory…"** The last of all prayers is the prayer of the bowing of heads and dismissal, thus both at Matins and at every service' [^1588]. The Jerusalem manuscript makes no mention of the prayers of the priest in the order of Vespers, evidently because this did not enter into its purpose. Symeon of Thessalonica indicates during the course of Vespers three prayers at appointed places: at the 1st psalm, at the Entrance, and the prayer of the bowing of heads and dismissal; while a fourth, **"O Lord, compassionate and merciful"**, he cites as an example that 'the remaining prayers of Vespers likewise possess thoughts adapted unto the psalms of the antiphons and borrow expressions therefrom'. Consequently, Symeon of Thessalonica did not set for himself the goal of indicating all the prayers of the priest at Vespers. A supplementation of him here may be found in ancient Euchologia, which, without providing the order of Vespers, as of Matins, cite only the prayers of the priest at either service, wherein in many of these Euchologia it is precisely the Sung Vespers and Matins that are had in view, as the titles of the prayers indicate. Although the majority of these prayers are identical with the present prayers of the lighting of lamps (Lucernarium prayers), read secretly by the priest during the Introductory Psalm, they are inscribed in certain Euchologia of the 9th–13th centuries very characteristically: 'Prayer of the 1st Antiphon' (our present 1st Lucernarium prayer), 'Prayer of the 2nd Antiphon' (our present 2nd), and so forth; our present Prayer of the Entrance is inscribed for the most part 'Prayer of the 8th Antiphon before **"Lord, I have cried"**'. Following these 8 prayers certain Euchologia possess yet a second series of prayers, at times with a new numbering of the antiphons, wherein explicit reference is made unto the so-called 'Small Antiphons' in St. Symeon of Thessalonica (as likewise in the copies of the Typikon of the Great Church of the 9th–10th centuries). units.slavonic_stem_tier2: риме 77 в криптоферратский так называемый
units.slavonic_text: Риме № 77 VIII–IX в., Криптоферратский так называемый Виссарионов IX в., Синайской библ. № 958 X в., Парижской Национ. библ. № 213 XI в., Барбериновой № 88 XIII в. и Требник Моск. Синод. библ. № 675/371 XIV–XV вв. имеют «после прокимна и Господи помилуй» следующие молитвы: 1) «молитва (1-го) антифона, на котором поется «Молитвами Богородицы»: «Благословен еси Господь Боже наш, просветивый день светом солнечным…». (тождественная с одной из нынешних молитв Пятидесятницы): с возгласом «Твое бо есть еже миловати…»; 2) Молитва антифона (2-го), на котором поется Единородный Сыне: «Господи избавлей нас» (тождественная с молитвою Пятидесятницы и Великого повечерия) с возгласом «Благоволением и благостию…»; 3) Молитва антифона (3-го) Трисвятого: «Боже великий, вечный…», (заключающая и прошение о достойном воспевании Трисвятого), с возгласом: «Яко свят еси…»; {с. 344} 4) Молитва оглашенных по Трисвятом: «Боже тайная сведый…» с возгласом «Да и тии с нами…»; 5) Молитва верных 1-я «Господи Боже наш и ныне…» с центральным прошением об облечении нас во всеоружие Духа Святаго на духов злобы и с возгласом: «Яко тебе подобает…»; 6) Молитва верных 2-я «Господи Боже в неприступнем обитаяй свете…» с прошением о просвещении очей душ наших и с возгласом «Яко Твоя держава»; 7) Молитва или отпуст «Боже великий и вышний…», тождественная с нынешней 7-й светильничной с возгласом «Яко благ и человеколюбец…»; 8) Молитва главопреклонения нынешняя с возгласом «Буди держава…». К этому ряду молитв некоторые памятники (Илитарий или Кондакион Синайск. библ. № 956 X в., упомянутые Евхологий Париж. национ. библ. № 213 XI в. и Требник Моск. Синод. библ. № 371/675 XIV–XV вв.) присоединяют еще три: а) «молитва, глаголемая в скевофилакии склада (καταγύρων — в ризнице)», которую указано произносить после возгласа «С миром изыдем», заключающая прошение соделать нас сосудами священными, с возгласом «Яко свят еси…»; б) «молитва, глаголемая в великом баптистерии (крещальне) по конце вечерни», заключающая благодарение Богу, сподобившему нас жребия святых, избавившему от власти тьмы и поставившему в царство любви своей; после «Мир всем», «Главы ваша…»; еще в) молитва, заключающая благодарение за возрождение водою и Духом и прошение охранить в нас благодать крещения с возгласом «Яко ты еси Бог наш, Бог еже миловати…» [16]. Таким образом верующие сопровождались молитвами при выходе из церкви до самой паперти; замечательно, что и по Амвросианскому чину есть на вечерне и утрени особые молитвы и респонсории in baptisterio (см. выше, стр. 317). О молитве за оглашенных Криптоферратский Евхологий замечает: «должно знать, что оглашенные (т. е. молитвы за них) на вечерне не всегда бывают, но только в четверг и вторник, и в эти дни не безусловно, но когда в церкви нет литургии или литии».
units.english_text: Rome, No. 77 (8th–9th c.), the Cryptferratan [Grottaferrata] so-called Bessarion codex (9th c.), Sinai Library No. 958 (10th c.), Paris National Library No. 213 (11th c.), Barberini No. 88 (13th c.), and the Trebnik of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 675/371 (14th–15th c.) have 'after the prokeimenon and **"Lord, have mercy"**' the following prayers: 1) 'Prayer of the (1st) Antiphon, upon which is chanted **"By the prayers of the Theotokos"**': **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord our God, Who hast enlightened the day with the light of the sun…"** (identical with one of our present prayers of Pentecost), with the exclamation: **"For Thine it is to have mercy…"**; 2) 'Prayer of the (2nd) Antiphon, upon which is chanted **"Only-Begotten Son"**': **"O Lord, Who hast delivered us"** (identical with the prayer of Pentecost and of Great Compline), with the exclamation: **"By the favor and goodness…"**; 3) 'Prayer of the (3rd) Antiphon of the Trisagion': **"O God, great and eternal…"** (containing likewise a petition for the worthy chanting of the Trisagion), with the exclamation: **"For holy art Thou…"**; *(Orig. p. 344)* 4) 'Prayer of the Catechumens after the Trisagion': **"O God, Who knowest secret things…"**, with the exclamation: **"That they also with us [may glorify Thine all-honorable and majestic Name]…"**; 5) 'First Prayer of the Faithful': **"O Lord our God, even now…"**, with its central petition that He clothe us with the whole armor of the Holy Spirit against the spirits of wickedness, and with the exclamation: **"For unto Thee is due [all glory, honor, and worship]…"**; 6) 'Second Prayer of the Faithful': **"O Lord God, Who dwellest in light unapproachable…"**, with a petition for the enlightenment of the eyes of our souls, and with the exclamation: **"For Thine is the majesty…"**; 7) Prayer or Dismissal: **"O God, great and highest…"**, identical with our present 7th Lucernarium prayer, with the exclamation: **"For good art Thou and the Lover of mankind…"**; 8) our present Prayer of the Bowing of Heads, with the exclamation: **"Blessed and glorified be the majesty of Thy Kingdom…"** Unto this series of prayers certain monuments (the Ilitarion or Kondakarion of Sinai Library No. 956 of the 10th c., the aforementioned Euchologion of Paris National Library No. 213 of the 11th c., and the Trebnik of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 371/675 of the 14th–15th c.) append yet three more: a) 'Prayer said in the skeuophylakion of the vestry (*καταγύρων*, in the sacristy)', which is appointed to be pronounced after the exclamation **"Let us depart in peace"**, containing a petition to make us sacred vessels, with the exclamation: **"For holy art Thou…"**; b) 'Prayer said in the Great Baptistery after the conclusion of Vespers', containing thanksgiving unto God Who hath made us worthy of the lot of the saints, delivered us from the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of His love; after **"Peace be unto all"**, **"Bow your heads…"**; and furthermore c) a prayer containing thanksgiving for regeneration by water and the Spirit and a petition to preserve within us the grace of baptism, with the exclamation: **"For Thou art our God, a God Who hath mercy…"** [^1589] In this manner the faithful were accompanied by prayers upon departing from the church unto the very portico; remarkable it is that according unto the Ambrosian rite as well there are at Vespers and Matins special prayers and responsories *in baptisterio* (see above, p. 317). Concerning the prayer for the catechumens the Grottaferrata Euchologion observes: 'it must be known that the catechumens (that is, prayers for them) at Vespers do not always take place, but only on Thursday and Tuesday, and on these days not unconditionally, but when in the church there is no Liturgy or litiya'.

units.slavonic_incipit: Следовательно, в IX в. хотя молитвы
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: следовательно в в хотя молитвы за оглашенных
units.slavonic_text: Следовательно, в IX в. хотя молитвы за оглашенных и особые за верных существовали еще на вечерне (и утрене, как увидим), но уже близки были к исчезновению. Молчание о них Симеона Солунского говорит о том, что к его времени они были отменены. — По «Чину» Афонско-Андреевской рукописи пред отпустом вечерни «поют все вместе: «Утверди Боже царей наших, ей (ναὶ), Господи, на многие лета сохрани святое царство их», а также: Τὸν δεσπότην καὶ ἀρχιρέα ἡμῶν Κύριε φύλαττε»; по исполнении этого славить (должно быть, произносит «слава Отцу…» «Слава Тебе Христе Боже») патриарх, и бывает отпуст от иерея, затем по обычаю клирики опять поют велегласно «Долговременным (πολυχρόνιον) [17] соделай Боже св. царство из на многая лета», и {с. 345} «Τὸν δεσπότην»; патриарх благословляет народ при пении Εἰς πολὰ ἔτη; его провожают со светильниками до келии, где он опять благословляет при пении Исполла [18].
units.english_text: Consequently, in the 9th century, although the prayers for the catechumens and the distinct prayers for the faithful still existed at Vespers (and Matins, as we shall see), they were already near extinction. The silence concerning them in Symeon of Thessalonica indicates that by his time they had been abolished. — According unto the 'Order' (*Taxis*) of the Athos-St. Andrew manuscript, before the dismissal of Vespers 'all chant together: **"Establish, O God, our sovereigns; yea (*ναί*), O Lord, unto many years preserve their holy empire"**, as likewise: *Τὸν δεσπότην καὶ ἀρχιερέα ἡμῶν, Κύριε, φύλαττε* ["Preserve, O Lord, our master and hierarch"]'; upon the fulfillment of this, the patriarch glorifies (in all probability, he pronounces **"Glory to the Father…"**, **"Glory to Thee, O Christ God"**), and the dismissal is given by the priest; then, according unto custom, the clerics again chant aloud: **"Prolong (*πολυχρόνιον*)"** [^1590] **"O God, their holy empire unto many years"**, and *(Orig. p. 345)* **"The Master…"** (*Τὸν δεσπότην*); the patriarch blesses the people during the singing of *Εἰς πολλὰ ἔτη* ["Unto many years"]; they escort him with lamps unto his cell, where he blesses again during the singing of *Ispolla* [^1591].

units.slavonic_text: ### Песненная утреня
units.english_text: Matins in Hagia Sophia of Constantinople in the 12th century, according unto the testimony of a Russian traveler, 'is chanted first before the royal doors in the narthex; and going forth, they chant in the midst of the church; and they open the paradise doors, and chant thirdly at the altar' [^1592]. According unto the description of Symeon of Thessalonica, the Sung Matins began with the exclamation: **"Blessed is the Kingdom…"**, which was followed by *τὰ εἰρηνικά* (the 'peaceful' petitions), that is, the Great Synapte; during it the chanter (*ψάλτης*) begins, just as at Vespers, the singing of the 1st of the three opening psalms of Matins, Psalm 3: **"Lord, why are they multiplied that afflict me?"**, specifically after **"Help us, save us…"** The chanter sings a fragment of verse 6 of this psalm, expressing its theme, with the refrain of the psalm: **"And I slept. Glory to Thee, O God!"** Following the litany the psalm is chanted by verses, beginning with verse 6: **"I laid me down and slept"**, with the designated refrain; unto Psalm 3 are joined Psalm 62 [63]: **"O God, my God, unto Thee do I rise early…"**, and Psalm 133 [134]: **"Behold now, bless ye the Lord…"**, with the same refrain, which on feasts and on the Sundays of the Forefathers and Fathers is replaced by 'Trinitarian' refrains (*τὰ τριαδικά*): **"Glory to Thee, O Father; Glory to Thee, O Son; Glory to Thee, O Holy Spirit"**, and 'similar' hymns (*καὶ τὰ ὅμοια*). The refrain is repeated at *Glory...*, at *Now and ever...*, and in conclusion (*περισσήν*) with an elevated voice. During the singing of this Three-Psalm sequence, which replaces our present Six Psalms (Hexapsalmos), the priest reads the Morning Prayers. The Three-Psalm sequence concludes with the Little Litany, following which begins the singing of Psalm 118 [119]; it begins in the same manner as the other psalms, that is, with the proclamation by the chanter of its theme and refrain: **"Blessed are the undefiled in the way. Alleluia"** (it is noteworthy that this proclamation is not inserted into the preceding Little Litany). **"Alleluia"** serves as the refrain only for the 1st and 3rd staseis of the psalm, whereas for the 2nd stasis the refrain is: **"Give me understanding, O Lord"**, which is proclaimed at the Little Litany between the 1st and 2nd staseis; at the next Little Litany before the 3rd stasis there is proclaimed: **"The world [unto the ends of the world].
