units.slavonic_stem_tier2: утреня по ктиторским студийским типиконам
units.slavonic_text: ### Утреня по ктиторским Студийским Типиконам
units.english_text: At Matins on weekdays one kathisma was appointed from Antipascha until the Exaltation of the Cross, two from the Exaltation until Great Lent (except Cheesefare Week, when one was read), and three during Great Lent; on Saturday and Sunday according unto some Typika one kathisma was read (San Nicola di Casole), according unto others two (the *Hypotyposis*, Studite-Alexis, Evergetis), wherein on Saturday there was unfailingly read **"Blessed are the undefiled"** (the *Amomos* / Psalm 118 [119]), and on Sunday the 2nd, or the 2nd and 3rd Kathismata [^1634]; thus the Psalter was chanted through at times in less than *(Orig. p. 365)* a week, at times in more than a week (compare the Ambrosian rite, p. 317), for example being chanted through only once during the entire period from Antipascha until Mid-Pentecost [^1635]. The kathismata were always chanted in the appointed tone of the week, furthermore, at least according unto the Studite-Alexis Typikon, with certain 'alleluiaria'—it is unclear whether with special verses resembling current alleluiaria, or with a simple **"Alleluia"** set unto diverse melodies—the latter being more probable; of these alleluiaria St. Theodore the Studite 'instituted' 9 for each tone, 72 in total [^1636]. In this arrangement, the evening kathisma **"Unto the Lord in mine affliction"** was chanted with the first three alleluiaria of the presiding tone, while of the morning kathismata the first was chanted with the 3rd, 4th, and 5th alleluiaria, and the second with the 7th, 8th, and 9th (for this purpose there were 9 alleluiaria; three kathismata at Matins for some reason are not provided for). Yet certain kathismata—or rather, sections thereof—constituted an exception unto this rule by reason of the particular solemnity of their execution, for which purpose, in addition unto the aforementioned alleluiaria, there existed special alleluiaria: two in Tone 4, three in Tone 6, and one in Tone 8. Specifically, the first stasis (*slava*) of the 19th Kathisma, termed 'Many-Mercied' (*Polyeleos* / *Πολυέλεος*) because of the repeated refrain unto Psalm 135 [136]: **"For His mercy (*ἔλεος*) endureth forever"**, and consisting of Psalms 134, 135, and 136 [135, 136, 137], into whatever tone among the first four it fell, was always chanted in Tone 4 with the special alleluiaria of that tone (likewise termed 'Many-Mercied' or 'Polyeleos'), and into whatever tone among the remaining four tones it fell, was chanted in Tone 6 with the 1st alleluiarion among the special ones of that tone; wherein in the first case (when the *Polyeleos* was chanted in Tone 4), Psalm 135 [136] had two **"Alleluia"** refrains after each of its verses and one after the refrain **"For His mercy endureth forever"** (**"O give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good: Alleluia, alleluia; for His mercy endureth forever: Alleluia"**—as at present in the Kyiv Caves melody); in the second case, however, under Tone 6, **"Alleluia"** was sung once in both instances. (In all this lies the embryo of the later Polyeleos). The 2nd and 3rd staseis of the 19th Kathisma were chanted with the alleluiaria of the prevailing tone. If this kathisma occurred also at the Hours, it was chanted in the same manner, whereupon a transfer of this kathisma unto another Hour took place if the general tone of the Hour (that is, the tone of its troparion) did not correspond unto its chant. In addition unto the 'Polyeleos' psalms, there were distinguished from the ordinary chanting of the Psalter at Matins the 2nd stasis of the 7th Kathisma: **"God standeth in the congregation of gods…"** (Psalm 81 [82]), and the final (3rd) stasis of the last, 20th Kathisma: **"Praise the Lord from the heavens…"** (Psalms 148–150). The former was chanted with the 2nd of the special alleluiaria of Tone 6, the latter with the 3rd of them (yet the final Psalm 150, instead of **"Alleluia"**, had the refrain **"Glory to the Father…"**). Finally, a special alleluiarion of Tone 8 existed specifically for the festal **"Blessed is the man…"**, that is, for the 1st stasis of the 1st Kathisma; while its 2nd and 3rd staseis were chanted with the 2nd and 3rd alleluiaria of the prevailing tone [^1637]. With such solemn chanting of both ordinary and especially certain appointed *(Orig. p. 366)* kathismata (an influence of the Sung Office), the Studite-Alexis Typikon does not distinguish feasts with special kathismata, but distinguishes them, as also Sundays, only by the 'Hymns of Ascent' (*Stepenny* / *Anabathmoi*) [^1638], our present ones, yet chanted with the verses of the Gradual Psalms (Psalms 119–133 [120–134] = the 18th Kathisma) and alleluias with *nenenaiki* (melismatic vocables) [^1639]. Yet all other Typika of the Studite type appoint special kathismata for feasts. All Western Typika for every Feast of the Lord appoint before the Gradual Antiphons a three-antiphon, that is, three-psalm kathisma composed of psalms specially selected for the commemorated event, for example, for the Nativity of Christ: Psalms 134, 109, and 86 [135, 110, 87] (in the Grottaferrata Typikon; others have different ones), wherein unto certain verses of the final psalm appropriate unto the feast there was a refrain (*ekphōnēsis* or *hypakoē*), strongly reminiscent of our present Magnification (*velichanie* / megalynarion), for example, in the Grottaferrata Typikon for the Nativity of Christ unto verse 5 of Psalm 86 [87]: **"Mother Sion saith: A man, yea, a man was born in her"**, the refrain: **"We glorify the Nativity in the flesh of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, and faithfully we venerate His holy icon in the likeness of His holy countenance"** [^1640]; thus the 1st and 2nd time, and the 3rd time: **"We magnify thee, Mary Theotokos, and faithfully we venerate thy holy icon in the likeness of thy holy countenance"**; **"Glory..."**: **"We praise the Lord of glory and faithfully…"**; **"Now and ever..."**: **"We magnify thee, all-pure Virgin, and faithfully…"** Psalm 135 [136] in general is frequently placed in these Typika and other liturgical books of the same epoch and provenance (Southern Italian) as a festal antiphon at Matins, and for the most part is termed 'Polyeleos' (*πολυέлеος*) either alone (the Sicilian Typikon) or in combination with Psalm 134 [135] (San Nicola di Casole, December 25), wherein at times it is appointed for chanting in all 8 tones; in an Horologion unto verses 13–15 of this psalm there are appointed such refrains: **"All generations magnify thee, who art ever-blessed, and most blameless, and the Mother of our God"**; **"It is truly meet to magnify thee, the Theotokos, more honorable than the Cherubim, and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim, and the Mother of our God"**; **"Proclaiming thee to be the Theotokos, all generations magnify thee as the Mother of our God"** [^1641]. (An echo of the struggle against Nestorianism?). In the Evergetis Typikon the term *ho polyeleos* (*ὁ πολυέλεος*) = Polyeleos is already set down without further explanation and evidently in the sense of the current Typikon (perhaps composed, in addition unto Psalms 134 and 135 [135, 136], of Psalm 136 [137] as well, as in the Studite-Alexis Typikon); yet for Feasts of Christ and the Dormition, in addition unto one or two 'daily' kathismata with the sessional hymns of the feast, there is appointed also a special festal kathisma, with a sessional hymn or hypakoe following it, for example, for the Nativity of Christ and Theophany—Kathisma 16: **"The Lord said unto my Lord"** (Psalm 109 [110])—'slowly and with great alleluiaria' *(Orig. p. 367)*; on the Dormition—the *Amomos* (Psalm 118 [119]) with the alleluiaria of the tone (on other feasts alleluiaria are not mentioned) [^1642]. — Thus the execution of kathismata in the Studite Typika bears a clear resonance of the Sung Office. No mention is made in the Typika under consideration of any troparia or refrains unto Psalm 50 [51], which together with Psalm 50 [51] occupied a prominent place in the Sung Matins. — At the canon, concerning the number of troparia per ode of which the *Hypotyposis* is silent, and for which the *Diatyposis* appoints 8 troparia [^1643] for weekdays of Pentecostarion, 10 for its Sundays and feasts, and 10 or more for the remaining days of the year [^1644] (under Symeon of Thessalonica: 8, 6, or 4; see above, p. 346), the simplest practice is provided by the Grottaferrata Typikon, which does not indicate the number of troparia for the canon and only occasionally mentions the doubling of the heirmoi (for example, at the Nativity of Christ the second heirmoi **"He saved the people"** were doubled) [^1645]; the Typika of the Sicilian redaction likewise frequently omit the number of troparia (for example, for the Nativity of the Theotokos); they also provide for the canon the lowest number of troparia—8 (for example, for the Exaltation of the Cross) [^1646]; next in the number of troparia at the canon comes the Studite-Alexis Typikon, appointing them frequently at 10, maximum 12 (on great feasts, even the Nativity of Christ, and at concurrences) [^1647]; the Typika of the Calabrian redaction take a step further, appointing for great feasts, such as the Nativity of Christ, 14 troparia and regulating the number of troparia with particular precision [^1648]; finally, the Evergetis Typikon appoints for the most part 12 or 14 troparia, and for great feasts even 16 [^1649]. — At the Praises (*Ainoi* / *Laudes*), following the *Hypotyposis*, which requires for Sunday the doubling of the (four) Sunday stichera [^1650], the Western Typika and the Studite-Alexis Typikon appoint for Sundays stichera at 8, the Evergetis at 6; for feasts, among the Western Typika some appoint 4, others 6, the Studite-Alexis—6, the Evergetis—6, yet for saints the latter appoints 4, and for the Nativity of Christ—8 [^1651]. — As regards the Great Doxology and the conclusion of Matins, in the heart of the most ancient Studite Typika a significant transformation of this part of Matins took place, namely, that a different form was imparted unto it for weekdays and for feasts; clear traces of the gradual implementation of this reform have been preserved. The Studite-Alexis Typikon at festal and Sunday Matins, in addition unto the stichera at the Praises, indicates also stichera at the aposticha (*stikhovny*) [^1652]. If one adds unto this *(Orig. p. 368)* that the Great Doxology even in its current form, especially on weekdays, consists of two purely mechanically joined parts—the Doxology proper and the morning prayer **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day"**, corresponding unto the evening **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**; if, further, one takes into consideration that our present Sunday stichera at the Praises represent an analogous mechanical combination of the stichera of the Praises proper (with the verses of the Psalms of Praise) and stichera with special Sunday verses, in other words 'aposticha' (*stikhovny*), then it becomes indubitable that the conclusion of every Matins in the most ancient Typika had the same form as the second part of festal Vespers at present from **"O Gladsome Light"**: following the stichera of the Praises (corresponding unto the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**) there followed the 1st tier of the Great Doxology (unto which the Latin *Gloria in excelsis* used at Mass is limited), corresponding unto **"O Gladsome Light"**; then followed the Augmented Litany (in the most ancient, in all likelihood, the Litany of Peace), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day"**, the Litany of Supplication, the stichera at the aposticha, a verse corresponding unto **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart…"**—in all probability **"It is good to give praise unto the Lord…"**, the Trisagion, and the troparion. Thus according unto the Mili (Sicilian) Typikon during Great Lent (which preserves even now the greatest number of traces of ancient practice) Matins has the following conclusion: **"Glory to God in the highest"** without **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day"**, the Augmented Litany (*ektenē*), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day"**, the Litany of Supplication (*tēn synaptēn tōn aitēseōn*), the stichera at the aposticha, **"It is good to give praise"**, the Trisagion through the **"Our Father"**, and the dismissory troparion of the day; Lenten Vespers has an identical conclusion: **"O Gladsome Light"**, the Augmented Litany, **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, the Litany of Supplication, **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"**, the Trisagion, and the Lenten troparia [^1653]. Yet it is remarkable that already the Western Studite Typika, beginning with that of Grottaferrata, do not know such a type of Matins; thus on the Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee the Grottaferrata Typikon indicates only the stichera of the Praises, while the Calabrian and Sicilian redactions provide here the following detailed order for the conclusion of Matins: following the stichera of the Praises and **"Most blessed art thou"**: 'the *to Doxa megalōs* (**"Glory"**—greatly), the Trisagion, the Sunday troparion, then the litany, the petitions (the Litany of Supplication), and the rest, and the dismissal'. It is remarkable that according unto the Mili Typikon exactly the same order governs also the conclusion of festal Vespers: 'stichera at the aposticha, the Trisagion, the litany (that is, the Augmented Litany), the petitions (that is, the Litany of Supplication), and the rest, and the dismissal' [^1654]. The very term 'Great Doxology' is already employed by the Grottaferrata Typikon [^1655], not to speak of the Evergetis. Yet Nikon of the Black Mountain (11th century) considers the absence of the Great Doxology and the separation of the aposticha stichera from the stichera of the Praises at Matins on the greatest feasts to be a general peculiarity of all Studite Typika [^1656].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: начиная с криптоферратского не знают такого типа утрени
units.slavonic_text: начиная с Криптоферратского, не знают такого типа утрени; так, в Неделю мытаря Криптоферр. Тип. указывает лишь хвалитные стихиры, а Калабрийская и Сицилийская редакции дают здесь следующий подробный чин конца утрени: после хвалитных стихир и Преблагословенна «τὸ Δόξα μεγάλως (Слава — велико), Трисвятое, тропарь воскресный, затем ектения, прошения (просительная ектения) и прочее и отпуст». Замечательно, что по Милийскому Типикону такой же точно порядок имеет и конец вечерни праздничной: «стихиры стиховны, Трисвятое, ектения (т. е. сугубая), прошения (т. е. просительная ектения) и прочее и отпуст» [81]. Самый термин «славословие великое» употребляется уже Криптоферратским Типиконом [82], не говоря об Евергетидском. Но Никон Черногорец (XI в.) считает отсутствие великого славословия и отделение стиховных стихир от хвалитных на утрени в самые великие праздники общею особенностью всех Студийских Типиконов [83].

units.english_text: Almost the most prominent peculiarity of the Typika under consideration is constituted, following the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* [^1657] and under the influence of the Typikon of Hagia Sophia, by the omission of the Hours on Sundays and feast days, even minor ones. The Studite-Alexis Typikon is interspersed with the remark *porozn' chasom* ('the Hours are omitted' / individual celebration of the Hours), for example, on September 1, 5, 6, 7, etc. [^1658]; the Western Typika and the Evergetis simply maintain silence concerning the Hours, yet the Grottaferrata Typikon takes a step toward Jerusalem practice when, for example, on the Nativity of the Theotokos, and consequently on other feasts likewise, it instructs to chant after Matins the 'dismissory' (troparion) thrice in place of the First Hour, and to celebrate the Hour itself individually (*katamonas*), while the Third and Sixth Hours with the Beatitudes of the feast the presbyters 'chant while vesting' for the procession before the Liturgy [^1659]. The Sicilian Typikon during Great Lent possesses single-psalm Sung Hours with a Great Litany following the psalm, three Little Litanies at the antiphons of the kathisma, and a Litany of Supplication following the troparion and reading—and with prayers of the priest [^1660]. — With respect unto Compline the Studite Typika exhibit the same diversity and vacillation as the Jerusalem Typika, and possess this service in general of an identical type with the latter (for which reason the history of this office is common unto both—see below, 'Compline'); yet the Evergetis Typikon, following the *Diatyposis* [^1661] and under the influence of the Typikon of the Great Church, in addition unto Compline—which it mentions only on the eves of Sundays, the Nativity of Christ, and Theophany—appoints during Great Lent a daily pannychis consisting of one or two canons with sessional hymns after the 3rd ode and a kontakion (for the most part **"O Protection of Christians…"**) after the 6th ode, preceded by Psalm 50 [51] and followed by the Trisagion, troparion, and litany (as among us on the eve of Pascha); during Great Lent, and perhaps in general on weekdays, this pannychis was joined unto Vespers; on the eves of feasts it preceded Matins and, having after itself also a reading, together with it and with Matins constituted a single 'vigil' (*agrypnia* / ἀγρυπνία) [^1662]; in this the Evergetis Typikon drew close unto the Jerusalem Typikon, toward which it inclines in other cases as well.

units.english_text: From the 11th century we possess the first report regarding the existence and dissemination in the East of more or less complete texts of Typika in the strict sense according unto the order of the Palestinian Lavra of St. Sabas (near Jerusalem). This report belongs unto Nikon of the Black Mountain, who was at first a certain official ('instructor' / *nastavnik*), and later hegumen in the monasteries of Rhaithou on *(Orig. p. 370)* Sinai and of St. Symeon the Wonderworker of the Admirable Mountain upon the Black Mountain near Antioch during the reign of Emperor Constantine Doukas (1059–1067), and who personally did much both in general for the development of the church Typikon and, in particular, for the replacement of the Studite Typikon by the Jerusalem Typikon [^1663]. Prompted by disorders in the monasteries of that era (disobedience toward superiors, striving toward idiorrhythmic / kellion living as granting greater freedom, discord among liturgical orders), Nikon resolved to provide a written manual for monastics, a consolidated typikon or *Taktikon*, through the collation of diverse typika. During the preliminary work for this composition, there was revealed unto Nikon not only the existence of a multitude of diverse typika—such as that of the Great Church, the Studite, the Jerusalem, the Hagiorite (Athonite), the typikon of the Patriarchate of Antioch, of the Monastery of St. Auxentius, and others (not to mention the ancient rules of St. Pachomius, Basil the Great, and Cassian)—but also a significant discrepancy among them, even between the different recensions of one and the same typikon: 'I read and collected diverse Typika, Studite and Jerusalem, and they did not agree one with another, neither a Studite with another Studite, nor a Jerusalem with another Jerusalem' (in all likelihood, Nikon had at hand ktetorial typika) [^1664]. For the resolution of his perplexities, Nikon turned unto the 'experienced fathers' in the monastery of St. Sabas, and upon their counsel 'took care concerning the ancient Jerusalem' Typikon [^1665]; the hegumen of this monastery directed him for an accurate manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon unto Laodicea (evidently in the Lavra of St. Sabas they were guided, as in part at present upon Mount Athos, by an unwritten Typikon), and lo, 'at the Savior in Laodicea,' recounts Nikon, 'we found preserved in the library an ancient Jerusalem Typikon, which the blessed Nicodemus, former hegumen of St. Sabas (chronology unknown), set forth for the Metropolitan of Laodicea from the beginning; and that one I took, as thou knowest, and I have it here at St. Symeon the Wonderworker (upon the Black Mountain), so that those who wish copy from it. All the others, as we have said, were found incorrect and do not equate unto the ancient one. Likewise did I find the Studite typika diverse, and neither do they equate one with another; and on account of this inequality, and still more because they possessed not any testimonies from the Divine Scriptures, but merely spoke thus: that we perform this and that' [^1666].

units.slavonic_text: неисправлени обретошася и не сравняются в древним. Такожде и студийския обретох типики различны, и ниже тии сравняются друг другу; и ради несравнения сего и паче же яко ни от Божественных писаний имеяху свидетельства некая, но точию глаголюще сице: яко сотворяем се и се» [93].
units.english_text: *(Orig. p. 371)* Thus Nikon accords preference unto the Jerusalem Typikon over the Studite: (a) on account of the possibility of utilizing its ancient and complete manuscript; (b) because the Jerusalem Typikon substantiates its prescriptions upon the 'Divine Scriptures' and does not impart them, like the Studite, without motivation—an example of which Nikon points out further in the stricter rules of fasting according unto the Jerusalem Typikon, which are consonant with the canons of the holy Apostles, councils, and ancient ascetics (for example, regarding the non-mitigation of the fast on Wednesday and Friday on account of feasts, and regarding the hour of breaking the fast on Great Saturday). In view of such advantages of the Jerusalem Typikon, Nikon also labored for its dissemination, and composes his consolidated rule ('Typikon', *Taktikon*) in its spirit, noting nevertheless in places also the Studite practice, and occasionally borrowing prescriptions from the Hagiorite Typikon. (The disciplinary portion of this *Typikon* of Nikon was subsequently incorporated into the Slavonic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon and exists in our present Typikon).

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: с 371 таким образом никон отдает преимущество иерусалимскому
units.slavonic_text: {с. 371} Таким образом Никон отдает преимущество Иерусалимскому уставу пред Студийским а) из-за возможности пользоваться его древним и полным списком, б) из-за того, что Иерусалимский устав обосновывает свои предписания на «Божествнных писаниях», и не дает их, подобно студийским, без мотивировки, пример чего Никон указывает далее в более строгих правилах поста по Иерусалимскому уставу, согласных с правилами св. апостолов, соборов и древних подвижников (например, о неразрешении поста в среду и пяток для праздников, о часе разрешения поста в Великую субботу). В виду таких преимуществ Иерусалимского Типикона Никон и заботился о его распространении и свой сводный устав («Типик», «Тактикон») пишет в его духе, отмечая все же по местам и Студийскую практику, а иногда заимствуя предписания из Святогорского Типикона. (Дисциплинарная часть этого Никонова «Типика» впоследствии внесена в славянские списки Иерусалимского устава и существует в нынешнем нашем Типиконе).
units.english_text: Thus in the 11th century and earlier, the Jerusalem Typikon enjoyed dissemination not only in Palestine [^1667], but also in the Patriarchate of Antioch and Asia Minor. Around this time, if not earlier, the Jerusalem Typikon was adopted upon Sinai, as is evident from its manuscripts [^1668] and other liturgical books arranged according unto this Typikon in the Sinai Library, occasionally dating back unto the 10th century and earlier [^1669], although the Jerusalem Typikon that developed upon Sinai exhibits certain peculiarities in comparison with the genuine Jerusalem one [^1670]. Somewhat later (in the 12th century), in all probability, the Jerusalem Typikon was adopted in the Diocese of Constantinople, judging by the fact that Nikon says nothing regarding its dissemination there. Yet Patriarch Nicholas III Grammatikos of Constantinople (1084–1111), in his 'Epistle unto the Protos of the Holy Mountain' [^1671], resolves the perplexities of the Athonite monastics—arising upon the grounds of the conflict between the less strict Studite practice concerning fasts and the stricter Jerusalem practice—in the spirit of *(Orig. p. 372)* the latter. The ktetorial Typikon given by Empress Irene, consort of Emperor Alexios Komnenos († 1183), unto the Monastery of the Mother of God, Full of Grace (*Kecharitomene*), founded by her in Constantinople—which in its liturgical portion refers in general unto the 'Synaxarion' (generally accepted), presupposes Jerusalem practice: *agrypniai* (vigils) and inter-hours (*mesoria*) are mentioned [^1672]. Unto the Palestinian Typikon the Typikon of Neilos, Hegumen of the Monastery of the Mother of God of Machairas, likewise refers [^1673]. The Typikon of the Monastery of the Archangel Michael upon Mount St. Auxentius near Chalcedon, given unto it by its founder, Emperor Michael Palaiologos (1250–1282), requires that psalmody be celebrated according unto the ancient custom of the Palestinian monasteries 'or according unto the Jerusalem Typikon,' except for Sunday vigils, as being exceedingly burdensome [^1674]. The consolidation of the Jerusalem Typikon in Constantinople was, in all likelihood, facilitated by the devastation of the Studion Monastery by the Crusaders, from which it was restored only by Emperor Constantine Palaiologos in 1298. Around this same time, in the 12th century, the Jerusalem Typikon found dissemination upon Mount Athos. Even if at the beginning of this century the Jerusalem regimen of fasting still seemed strange unto the Athonites, in this very century there appear upon Mount Athos Menaia of Jerusalem liturgical structure, several copies of which were brought from there by Arseny Sukhanov unto Russia and are preserved at present in the Moscow Synodal (former Patriarchal) Library (MSS Nos. 446–451: Jan., Mar., June, Aug., Oct., Dec.). As upon Sinai, the Jerusalem Typikon upon Mount Athos acquired certain local peculiarities, retaining at times the Studite practice deeply rooted there (for example, regarding fasts) and forming a distinct form of the Hagiorite Typikon [^1675]. — From the 12th century is likewise known the first manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon *(Orig. p. 373)* for Georgia, namely written for the monastery of St. Shio of Mghvime (near Tiflis) in 1172, in all probability from an original of the Wonderworking Mountain Monastery, and preserved in a 13th-century copy bearing the title: 'Typikon of the Church Office of the Well-Ordered Lavra of the Holy and God-Bearing Sabas; Such Also Occurs in All Other Monasteries of Palestine.' Among published manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon this is the most ancient (there is no Little Vespers; the Markian Chapters are without the name of Mark and are exceedingly brief; there are no commemorations of: the Holy Mandylion [*Ubrus*], established in 944; Athanasius of Athos, † 1000; Lazarus of Mount Galesios, † 1053; Michael Choniates, † 1266 [read 1222]; or even George the Chozebite of the 7th century) [^1676]. In the 13th–14th centuries the Jerusalem Typikon attains the widest dissemination throughout the entire East, as is evident from a series of its Greek manuscripts preserved from these centuries, such as, for example, its most ancient manuscript in Russia, yielding little unto the Shiomghvime manuscript, in the Moscow Public (Rumyantsev) Museum from the Sevastyanov Collection No. 35/491 (13th c.); the Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library, Greek Department No. 381, written, judging by the names in the diptychs, under Patriarch Athanasius of Constantinople (1289–1332); the Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 456 with the dubious date 1298, more likely 14th century; and the Typikon of the Vatican Library No. 784, written in 1317 in *Tēphrei tēs chōras Rōsias* (in Russia, in Tver?) [^1677]. How *(Orig. p. 374)* widely disseminated in Greece the Jerusalem Typikon had become by the 14th century is attested by the so-called *Diataxis tēs hierodiakonias* (Order of the Holy Ministry / *Chin svyashchennosluzheniya*), attributed unto

units.slavonic_incipit: Константинопольскому патриарху Филофею, известному литургисту XIV
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: константинопольскому патриарху филофею известному литургисту в но
units.slavonic_text: Константинопольскому патриарху Филофею, известному литургисту XIV в., но появившийся возможно и ранее [105]; назначенный, очевидно, для самого широкого повсеместного применения, он дает иерусалимский чин всенощной, стараясь договорить недомолвки древних списков Иерусалимского устава о действиях священника и диакона при богослужении [106]. В Сербии первым полным списком Иерусалимского устава был перевод его в 1319 г., сделанный архиеп. Никодимом, бывшим архимандритом Хиландарского монастыря, с греч. подлинника, взятого у Константинопольского патриарха (не с Афона, где был Иерусалимский устав не в его чистом виде) из монастыря Предтечи (должно быть, Студийского, где следовательно был введен уже Иерусалимский устав) [107]. До этого же времени Сербия руководилась Хиландарским уставом, на что есть глухое указание в предисловии Никодимову Типикону. В 1331 г. Никодимов устав переписывается и для Хиландаря неким Романом [108]. После Никодимова устава в Сербии явился ряд других Типиконов, большей частью близких к нему [109]. — К XIV же веку принадлежат и древнейшие славянские переводы Иерусалимского устава, сделанные в России, каковы Моск. Синод. библ № 328/383 XIV в. (русское происхождение их видно из наличности нескольких русских святых и отсутствия южно-славянских), очень близкие и по составу, тем более по строю суточного богослужения, к древне-греческим и сербским. Появлению в России полных списков Иерусалимского устава предшествовало постепенное проникновение практики его из Греции, начавшееся с XIII века. Владимирскому Собору 1274 г. и Константинопольскому 1276 г. русские епископы выражают уже недоумения по поводу некоторых студийских обычаев (например, относительно литургии Преждеосвященных в среду и пяток сырные и в Великий пяток) и получают ответ в духе Иерусалимского устава [110]. Но еще в XV в. студийская практика держится в России, как показывают списки Студийского устава от этого века и вопросы псковского духовенства св. митроп. Фотию (1410–1431 г.) [111]. Распространению в России Иерусалимского устава много содействовал {с. 375} св. митроп. Киприан (1380–1406 г. с перерывом), своими изданиями (рукописными) «Часословца по уставу иже во Иерусалиме лавры прп. отца нашего Саввы» (Следованная Псалтирь) и «Служебника» 1397 г., в который внесен Διάταξις патр. Филофея [112]. При Киприане же сделана первая попытка русской переработки Иерусалимского устава в лице «Ока Церковного» игумена Афанасия Высотского, переведенного им в Константинопольском монастыре Перивлепто и снабженного дополнениями, между прочим, дисциплинарными статьями из Никона Черногорца. [113] Этот опыт положил начало целому ряду русских редакций Иерусалимского устава, закончившихся лишь с появлением печатного издания его [114].
units.english_text: Patriarch Philotheus of Constantinople, the celebrated 14th-century liturgist, yet having appeared possibly even earlier [^1678]; appointed, evidently, for the widest universal application, it provides the Jerusalem order of the All-Night Vigil, striving to supply the omissions of ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon concerning the liturgical actions of the priest and deacon during divine worship [^1679]. In Serbia, the first complete text of the Jerusalem Typikon was its translation in 1319, executed by Archbishop Nicodemus, former archimandrite of the Hilandar Monastery, from a Greek original obtained from the Patriarch of Constantinople (not from Mount Athos, where the Jerusalem Typikon existed not in its pure form), from the Monastery of the Forerunner (in all probability the Studion, where consequently the Jerusalem Typikon had already been introduced) [^1680]. Prior unto this time, Serbia was guided by the Hilandar Typikon, unto which there is an implicit reference in the preface unto Nicodemus's Typikon. In 1331, Nicodemus's Typikon was transcribed also for Hilandar by a certain Roman [^1681]. Following Nicodemus's Typikon, there appeared in Serbia a series of other Typika, for the most part close unto it [^1682]. — Unto the 14th century likewise belong the most ancient Slavonic translations of the Jerusalem Typikon made in Russia, such as Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 328/383 of the 14th century (their Russian origin is evident from the presence of several Russian saints and the absence of South Slavonic ones), exceedingly close both in contents and still more in the structure of the daily office unto ancient Greek and Serbian codices. The appearance in Russia of complete manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon was preceded by the gradual penetration of its practice from Greece, beginning from the 13th century. Unto the Synod of Vladimir in 1274 and that of Constantinople in 1276, Russian bishops already express perplexities concerning certain Studite customs (for example, regarding the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts on Cheesefare Wednesday and Friday and on Great Friday) and receive an answer in the spirit of the Jerusalem Typikon [^1683]. Yet even in the 15th century Studite practice persists in Russia, as shown by manuscripts of the Studite Typikon from that century and the queries of the Pskov clergy unto St. Metropolitan Photius (1410–1431) [^1684]. Unto the dissemination of the Jerusalem Typikon in Russia, *(Orig. p. 375)* St. Metropolitan Cyprian (1380–1406 with interruption) contributed greatly through his (manuscript) editions of the 'Horologion according unto the Typikon of the Lavra of our Venerable Father Sabas in Jerusalem' (the Sequenced Psalter / *Sledovannaya Psaltir*) and the *Sluzhebnik* of 1397, into which was incorporated the *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus [^1685]. Under Cyprian as well, the first attempt at a Russian recension of the Jerusalem Typikon was made in the form of the *Tserkovne Oko* (*Oko Tserkovnoye*) by Hegumen Athanasius of Vysotsky, translated by him in the Peribleptos Monastery at Constantinople and furnished with additions—among others, disciplinary articles from Nikon of the Black Mountain [^1686]. This endeavor laid the foundation for an entire series of Russian recensions of the Jerusalem Typikon, concluding only with the appearance of its printed edition [^1687].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: характер суточного богослужения по иерусалимскому уставу
units.slavonic_text: ### Характер суточного богослужения по Иерусалимскому уставу
units.english_text: In contrast unto the Studite Typika, the Jerusalem Typika present a uniform structure of Vespers and Matins, identical with our present one. Although this is explained partly by the later date of these Typika, yet if one takes into consideration that this structure coincides also with that given by the Holy Sepulchre Typikon of the 9th century (the century unto which belong also the earliest monuments of the Studite Typikon) and at times remains truer than the Studite unto the ecclesiastical practice of the 4th–5th centuries (litiyas, as in Silvia/Egeria; vigils, which in the 4th–5th centuries occurred at least several times a year), then we may recognize as the first valuable characteristic in this domain—and one that contributed unto the ascendancy of the Jerusalem Typikon over the Studite—a greater stability, immutability, and fidelity unto antiquity in the daily office in comparison with the Studite Typikon. Another equally advantageous characteristic (from a Christian-ascetic perspective) of the Jerusalem Typikon was the greater duration of church services according unto it, which depended upon the greater proximity of this Typikon (both geographical and spiritual) and its fidelity unto the traditions of ancient asceticism (a characteristic manifested still more vividly in the comparatively greater strictness of this Typikon in its fasting regimen); most noticeably regarding the daily office, this characteristic revealed itself in the indispensable celebration of the Hours, which were not omitted for any feasts whatsoever. In relation unto the most important daily services—Vespers and Matins—this characteristic of the Jerusalem Typikon was manifested above all in a greater number of kathismata: at Matins there was always one kathisma more than according unto the Studite Typikon, except during Great Lent, Saturdays, Sundays, and feast days, when the number of kathismata according unto both Typika was identical. If one recalls that among Eastern monasticism there once existed a tendency *(Orig. p. 376)* to chant the entire Psalter every twenty-four hours (see above, pp. 294–295, the narrative of the visit unto Nilus of Sinai by John and Sophronius, and p. 299, 'Armenian Liturgy'), then in this characteristic of the Jerusalem Typikon as well one cannot fail to perceive its greater fidelity unto the traditions of asceticism, which attributed such paramount significance unto the Psalter (see above, pp. 189 ff.). Connected with this is likewise the greater number of stichera and troparia according unto the Jerusalem Typikon: the latter permits at **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Gospodi vozzvakh*) 10 stichera, and at the canon usually 14 and sometimes 16 verses, heirmoi, and troparia, whereas in the Studite Typika the maximum for the former was 9, and for the latter 14, usually 12. The same must be said regarding vigils: under the influence precisely of ascetic practice, with its customary all-night prayers, the Jerusalem Typikon, in place of the pre-dawn Matins customary in antiquity for Sundays and feast days, introduced all-night vigils (*agrypniai*) for both. Not unconnected with that same spirit of asceticism was the melodic simplification of divine worship in the Jerusalem Typikon: here drop away the requirements of the Studite Typikon, which constituted within it the heritage of the Sung Office (*asmatike akolouthia*), regarding the special, melodic execution of kathismata [^1688], hypakoai, and the like. — Other characteristics of the Jerusalem Typikon depended upon its place of origin: the Holy Land. From this perspective an explanation is provided for the litiyas which this Typikon requires, as was the case in Jerusalem practice as early as the 4th–5th centuries (see above, pp. 140 ff.), for every Vespers and Matins. The homeland of this Typikon, which compelled a more intense reliving of the celebrated sacred events, manifested itself also in the fact that the Jerusalem Typikon establishes a far sharper distinction between weekday and festal worship than does the Studite. This distinction is achieved—leaving aside vigils—on the one hand by the addition unto festal services of the Polyeleos (*Polyeleos*), whereas the Studite Typikon in such cases merely substituted certain (likewise chanted) kathismata for others; and on the other hand by the so-called 'Great Doxology,' which constitutes a technical term designating a completely different conclusion of Matins for feasts in comparison with weekdays: it signifies the transposition of the prayer **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Spodobi, Gospodi*) into direct conjunction with the Great Doxology, and the fusion of the aposticha stichera with the stichera at the Praises for feast days.

provenance.verbatim_source: In contrast unto the Studite Typika, the Jerusalem Typika present a uniform structure of Vespers and Matins, identical with our present one. Although this is explained partly by the later date of these Typika, yet if one takes into consideration that this structure coincides also with that given by the Holy Sepulchre Typikon of the 9th century (the century unto which belong also the earliest monuments of the Studite Typikon) and at times remains truer than the Studite unto the ecclesiastical practice of the 4th–5th centuries (litiyas, as in Silvia/Egeria; vigils, which in the 4th–5th centuries occurred at least several times a year), then we may recognize as the first valuable characteristic in this domain—and one that contributed unto the ascendancy of the Jerusalem Typikon over the Studite—a greater stability, immutability, and fidelity unto antiquity in the daily office in comparison with the Studite Typikon. Another equally advantageous characteristic (from a Christian-ascetic perspective) of the Jerusalem Typikon was the greater duration of church services according unto it, which depended upon the greater proximity of this Typikon (both geographical and spiritual) and its fid

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: вечерня и утреня смешанного типа
units.slavonic_text: ### Вечерня и утреня смешанного типа
units.english_text: All these, although characteristic, are not exceedingly significant peculiarities in the structure of the daily office, more specifically in the order of Vespers and Matins. In general, these two services in both Typika possess one and the same order and structure, diverging with almost equal *(Orig. p. 377)* sharpness from the so-called 'Sung Office' (*asmatikos typos*), or the court-cathedral Typikon of Constantinople. This latter order not only persisted intact in many churches until the 15th century, but also strove to assimilate unto itself the monastic, Studite-Jerusalem Vespers and Matins. The imprint of such a tendency is borne by the orders of Vespers and Matins in certain Euchologia of the 12th–16th centuries. Vespers in them exhibits the following peculiarities: According unto the Euchologia of the 12th century (1153) of the Sinai Library No. 973 and of the 13th century of the Patmos Library No. 105, Vespers begins with the exclamation **"Blessed is the Kingdom..."** (*Evlogēmenē hē basileia...* / *Blagoslovenno Tsarstvo...*). According unto the Euchologion in a 16th-century manuscript of the Tiflis Ecclesiastical-Archaeological Museum No. 450, at the beginning of Vespers the Introductory Psalm is not indicated; it begins with three 'antiphons' with Little Litanies and special prayers at each of them. Following **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Kyrie ekekraxa* / *Gospodi vozzvakh*), prior unto the stichera, there is again a Little Litany, yet of a distinctive type, similar unto the Second Litany of the Faithful at the Divine Liturgy ('In peace let us pray unto the Lord... For the peace from above... For the peace of the whole world... For this holy temple... Help us, save us... And for all who require aid from God. Calling to remembrance our all-holy, immaculate... For unto Thee is due...'). The Augmented Litany **"Let us all say"** (*Rtsem vsi*) is appointed in its present place—following the prokimenon and before **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**—yet possesses a distinctive composition, identical, except for the first four petitions, with our present Great Litany; consequently it represents the Augmented Litany and the Great Litany still in the period of their union. According unto the aforementioned Patmos Euchologion of the 13th century, which provides fully our present order of Vespers in its festal form, after the exclamations of the Great Litany and the three Little Litanies there is appointed **"Peace be unto all,"** so that in the course of Vespers it is repeated six times (and before the prokimenon it is pronounced by the deacon) [^1689]; compare the Milanese (Ambrosian) and Mozarabic order of Vespers (see above, pp. 353 and 355). According unto the aforementioned Sinai Euchologion of the 12th century, the Litany of Supplication is appointed after **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** (*Nyně otpushchayeshi*) and the troparion; whereas according unto the Euchologion of the Tiflis Ecclesiastical-Archaeological Museum, in this place at festal Vespers there is indicated the litany **"Have mercy on us, O God..."** (*Pomiluy nas, Bozhe...*), and the Litany of Supplication before **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** (consequently, the conclusion of Vespers is as at present on weekdays). All the indicated Euchologia distribute the evening prayers throughout the entire course of Vespers at all its litanies. — No fewer variations in comparison with our present order are presented by the Euchologia of the same era for Matins. According unto the Sinai Euchologion of the 12th century, it begins with the exclamation **"Blessed is the Kingdom..."** Following the Hexapsalmos and the Great Litany, the Sinai and Patmos Euchologia indicate: the former prior unto the *kathisma* (sessional hymn) and Polyeleos, and the latter prior unto the Anabathmoi / Antiphons of the Degrees (*stepenny*—the Studite type of festal Matins) and the Gospel, the prayers of the 'three antiphons' with a Little Litany following the 2nd (Sinai) or 3rd (Patmos) among them, beginning **"Again and again"** (*Paki i paki*) or **"Help us, save us"** (*Zastupi, spasi*—Sinai, in accordance with the Sung Office), and with the exclamation **"Peace be unto all"** before it (Patmos) and after it (Patmos; Tiflis No. 450). In place of these 'antiphons,' the Tiflis Euchologion and the Georgian manuscript *(Orig. p. 378)* of the Imperial Public Library No. 208 of the 16th century indicate prayers and Little Litanies following each of the three 'psalms' of the kathisma (in all probability, there is presupposed a single sung-festal three-psalm kathisma, as in the Italo-Sicilian branch of the Studite Typika); after the kathisma there follow: the sessional hymn, reading (both Georgian monuments), Anabathmoi / Degrees (MS No. 208), the Blameless / Amomos (Psalm 118 [119]), the Evlogetaria / **"The Assembly of Angels"** (*Angelskiy Sobor* / *Ton angelōn ho dēmos*—No. 450), the Gospel, and Psalm 50 [51]. The most ancient of the aforementioned Euchologia, the Sinai manuscript, indicates Psalm 50 [51] after the 'kontakion,' that is, after the 6th ode of the canon (or a triodion with the kontakion at the beginning is presupposed—see below), and the Gospel after the Great Doxology (in accordance with the Sung Office). This same Euchologion indicates after the 'kathisma' the 'Prayers of the Sunday Polyeleos in Holy Lent' (a hint at the original use of the Polyeleos exclusively in Lent), wherein it further apparently cites these prayers: the first having no heading whatsoever, and the subsequent ones designated: 'Prayer of the 5th Antiphon' (consequently the preceding was of the 4th), 'of the 6th Antiphon,' '7th Prayer'—four in all; after the last (8th) follows the rubric: 'Then the kontakion, the 50th (Psalm), and immediately the deacon: **"In peace let us pray unto the Lord,"** the 9th prayer..., **"Help us, save us..."** **"The morning and..."** (*tēn orthrinēn kai tēn...*), **"An angel of peace..."** **"Pardon..."** and immediately the odes, and after the 9th ode: **"Again and again..."** with the prayer.' Thus, after the antiphons of the Polyeleos or of some festal kathisma, this Euchologion indicates immediately the kontakion, Psalm 50 [51], the Litany of Supplication with an opening taken from the Litany of Peace and the Little Litany, and only then the canon ('the odes'), yet a canon evidently of exceedingly brief composition (since there is no mention of the customary inter-ode hymnody), perhaps a diodion or triodion; moreover, earlier in this Euchologion, prior unto the discussion of the Polyeleos prayers, occurs the rubric: 'after the 6th ode the kontakion'; perhaps at weekday Matins, in place of the Polyeleos, there was a full canon (precious vestiges of the ancient structure of Matins at the transition from the kontakion-based system unto the canon-based system). All other aforementioned Euchologia, after Psalm 50 [51], presuppose the customary full canon; yet the Georgian manuscripts place before it, after Psalm 50 [51], a Litany of Peace of a distinctive composition differing in both manuscripts (one of 6 petitions, the other of 9), and with our present exclamation (which precedes the canon). The Georgian monuments appoint a litany with prayer also at the 7th ode of the canon, and a prayer at the 8th ode. (It is possible that litanies formerly occurred at every ode, and here we have a survival of this practice, as at present at Paschal Matins and in the Cryptaferrata / Grottaferrata Typikon at Nativity Matins [^1690]). The order of litanies at the conclusion of Matins is in all of them of our present festal type, yet in the Patmos codex it is of our present weekday type (although Matins is presupposed to be festal). The Georgian codices do not name the Augmented Litany, but indicate only its prayer, the first with a ninefold **"Lord, have mercy"** [^1691].

units.english_text: If the Studite and Jerusalem Typika possessed so much in common in the structure of the most important services of the daily cycle—Vespers and Matins—then in the secondary services, such as the Hours, Compline, Midnight Office, and Typika (*Izobrazitelnye*), *(Orig. p. 379)* they were rendered completely uniform. These services possessed their own distinct history, taking no account of the peculiarities of the one or the other Typikon.

units.slavonic_incipit: Если Студийский и Иерусалимский уставы имели
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: если студийский и иерусалимский уставы имели так много
units.slavonic_text: Если Студийский и Иерусалимский уставы имели так много общего в строе важнейших суточных служб — вечерни и утрени, то во второстепенных службах, каковы часы, повечерие, полунощница и изобразительные, {с. 379} они совершенно обезразличивались. Эти службы имели свою особую историю, не считавшуюся с особенностями того и другого устава.
units.english_text: As regards the Hours, we have seen that already in the 9th century their order had developed up unto the Trisagion, where the order of the Hour concludes both according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon and according unto the Sinai Horologion of the 8th–9th century according unto the order of the Lavra of St. Sabas (see above, p. 298), which represent in general a complete coincidence in the order of the Hours. The latter Horologion provides likewise all our present psalms of the Hours, and both monuments provide our present troparia of the Hours (their first series following the psalms) and the 'verses' of the Hours (**"Order my steps..."** / *Stopy moya...* and the like). If in this Horologion and certain subsequent ones (for example, Sinai No. 864 of the 9th century), other psalms are joined unto our present three psalms of the Hours, this is because these Horologia, evidently, were intended for cell use rather than for church celebration. For this reason, one must suppose, these Horologia do not contain the priestly element in the service of the Hours. A supplement unto them may be found in the ancient Euchologia, which provide—as, for example, the Greek Sinai MS No. 958 of the 10th century, Paris National Library MS No. 213 of the 11th century (1027), and the Slavonic *Trebnik* of the Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 371/675—the priestly prayers of the Hours. Of such prayers at each Hour there are indicated here six: 'Prayer of the 1st Antiphon,' 'of the 2nd Antiphon,' 'of the 3rd Antiphon,' 'Prayer of the Dismissal,' 'of the Bowing of Heads,' and a special concluding prayer without title; each with an exclamation (it is not everywhere marked: 'exclamation'); before the 5th, **"Peace be unto all,"** **"Bow your heads..."**; before the concluding prayer, the deacon: **"Wisdom."** In their contents the prayers are adapted unto the time of day and the sacred commemorations of the Hour, frequently containing expressions from our present psalms and verses of the Hours; in the prayer of the Third Hour commemoration is made of the Descent of the Holy Spirit; of the Sixth Hour, of the Crucifixion; of the Ninth Hour, of the going up unto prayer at that hour of the Apostles Peter and John [^1692]. Judging by the fact that these prayers are located in Euchologia that presuppose the Sung Office structure of Vespers and Matins, they were intended, in all probability, for Sung Hours. Such Hours are appointed for Lent by the Western ktetorial Typika of the Sicilian recension (see above, p. 402). Their order was as follows: a single psalm of the Hour was chanted, followed by the Great Litany; the priest recited the prayer lying prostrate before the altar; then the 'stichology' (*stichologia* / στιχολογία), that is, a kathisma, at each antiphon of which a Little Litany was said (prayers are not mentioned); then the troparion of the Hour (Lenten) with its Theotokion; a reading; the Litany of Supplication; the verse of the Hour (**"Order my steps..."** and the like); the Trisagion through the **"Our Father"**; **"Lord, have mercy"** 12 times on each choir; **"Glory to the Father..."**; **"In the Name of the Lord, bless, father"**; the priest: **"O Lord Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy on us"**; three great prostrations; the prayer **"Unto all who lie prostrate"**; and the dismissal [^1693] (in this same manner, as we have seen, the Ninth Hour was chanted according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon during Passion Week). *(Orig. p. 380)* It is possible that in churches where the Sung Office was maintained, such Hours—arising, in all probability, under the influence of the *trithekte*—were chanted outside of Great Lent as well, or at least that ordinary Hours there possessed priestly prayers in such or a smaller number.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: чтение просительная ектения стих часа стопы моя и
units.slavonic_text: чтение, просительная ектения, стих часа («Стопы моя…» и т. п.), Трисвятое по Отче наш, «Господи помилуй» по 12 раз на каждом клиросе, Слава Отцу…, «Именем Господним благослови, святый»; иерей: «Господи Иисусе Христе, Боже наш, помилуй нас»; 3 великих поклона, молитва «Всем ниц лежащим» и отпуст [120] (так же пелся, как мы видели, по Святогробскому уставу 9-й час на Страстной седмице). {с. 380} Возможно, что в церквах, где было песненное последование, такие часы, возникшие, вероятно, под влиянием тритекти, пелись и вне Четыредесятницы или же по крайней мере, что там обыкновенные часы имели священнические молитвы в таком или меньшем количестве.
units.english_text: In addition unto the indicated series of prayers, the Paris Euchologion in separate rubrics provides yet another prayer, rather lengthy, for each Hour—perhaps precisely for the occasion when the Hours were celebrated with less solemnity. This latter practice—of only a single priestly prayer at each Hour—prevailed; yet this priestly prayer of the Hour was gradually abbreviated unto the brief exclamation **"God be bountiful unto us..."**, borrowed from Psalm 66:1 [67:1] and recalling the Old Testament priestly blessing, or unto the exclamation **"O Lord Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy on us"** (see above), later augmented by the addition at the beginning of **"Through the prayers of our holy fathers."** That these exclamations replaced the former (lengthy) prayer of the priest at the Hours is evident from the fact that in ancient Typika they are customarily accompanied by the note: 'and the priest prays' (*euchetai* / εὔχεται), and at times are even directly replaced by this note or designated the 'prayer of the Hours' or 'of Compline' [^1694]. Yet the memory of the former practice prompted the introduction, in place of the priestly prayers that had disappeared from the Hours, of prayers recited by the reader—originally one for each Hour and brief, in the manner of a troparion [^1695], and later several (two or three), among which appears the prayer **"Thou Who at all times"** (*Hō en panti kairō* / *Izhe na vsyakoye vremya*) [^1696]. The latter, on account of its universal contents, was in the course of time appropriated unto each Hour, which received in addition unto it another specialized prayer as well [^1697]. Beside the transformation of the prayer element in the Hours, the present era brought unto the service of the Hour certain additions as well. Such above all was the repeated **"Lord, have mercy,"** which was an echo of ascetic practice (see above, p. 190) [^1698]. *(Orig. p. 381)* Later than other parts, there entered into the composition of the service of the Hours the troparia after the Trisagion, concerning which ancient Horologia and Typika not only exhibit, but also expressly state [^1699], a great vacillation.

units.slavonic_incipit: Кроме указанного ряда молитв Парижский Евхологий
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: кроме указанного ряда молитв парижский евхологий в отдельных
units.slavonic_text: Кроме указанного ряда молитв Парижский Евхологий в отдельных рубриках дает еще по одной молитве, довольно длинной, для каждого часа, — может быть именно на тот случай, когда часы служились с меньшею торжественностью. Последняя практика — одной лишь священнической молитвы на каждом часе — возобладала; но эта священническая молитва часа постепенно сократилась до краткого воззвания «Боже ущедри ны…», заимствованного из пс. 66, 1 и напоминающего ветхозаветное священническое благословение, или до воззвания «Господи Иисусе Христе Боже наш помилуй нас» (см. выше), осложнившегося впоследствии добавлением в начале «Молитвами св. отец наших»; что эти возгласы заменяли собою прежнюю (длинную) молитву священника на часах, видно из того, что они в древних Типиконах обычно сопровождаются замечанием: «и молится (εὔχεται) священник», иногда даже прямо заменяются этим замечанием или называются «молитвою часов» или «повечерия» [121]. Но память о прежней практике побудила ввести взамен исчезнувших с часов священнических молитв молитвы, произносимые чтецом, — первоначально одну для каждого часа и краткую в роду тропаря [122], потом по несколько 2–3, среди которых появляется молитва «Иже на всякое время» [123]. Последняя за свое общее содержание с течением времени усвояется каждому часу, получающему кроме нее и другую специальную молитву [124]. Кроме преобразования молитвенного элемента в часах настоящая эпоха принесла в службу часа и некоторые добавления. Таким прежде всего было многократное «Господи помилуй…» которое являлось отзвуком подвижнической практики (см. выше, стр. 190) [125]. {с. 381} Позднее других частей в состав часовой службы вошли тропари по Трисвятом, относительно которых древние часословы и уставы не только представляют, но и констатируют [126] большое колебание.
units.english_text: Besides the Hours, the Jerusalem Typikon from its most ancient manuscripts (at least among those published) possessed also the inter-hours (*mesoria*) or intermediate hours (*pochasiya*). Them is indicated already by the Shio-Mgvime Typikon (which possesses no Little Vespers), wherein their order is literally identical with the present one—only the concluding prayer is lacking; even the selection of psalms and troparia coincides almost entirely with the present one (the sole difference in psalms being that at the Inter-Hour of the Ninth Hour there is a superfluous psalm: Psalm 50 [51]). Yet Horologia from the 12th century, in which the order of the Inter-Hours first appears, although likewise presenting their present structure, exhibit great vacillation in the selection of psalms and prayers for the Inter-Hours; moreover, it is remarkable that in the most ancient Horologia there are more coincidences with the present order: thus, the Horologion of the Sinai Library MS No. 865 of the 12th century contains all the present psalms (only at the First and Third Hours with the additional Psalm 50 [51]); in the Sinai Horologion MS No. 870 of the 13th century, only two psalms coincide with the present ones; while in the Horologia of the Athos-Vatopaidi Library MS No. 350/984 of the 13th century, the Sinai MS No. 868 [printed: 8686] of the 13th–14th centuries, and the Novgorod-Sophia Library (at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy) MS No. 1052 of the 13th–14th centuries, not a single psalm coincides with the present cursus; evidently these Horologia, being manuals of the kellion-skete rule (see below), do not take into account the generally accepted and ancient order of the Inter-Hours; according unto some of them, certain Hours even possess more than one inter-hour: thus, in the Sinai Horologion MS No. 870 of the 13th century, the First Hour has one inter-hour, the Third and Sixth have two each, and the Ninth has three inter-hours [^1700] (corresponding, in all probability, unto the importance of the commemorated events).

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: указывает уже и шиомгвимский типикон не имеющий малой
units.slavonic_text: указывает уже и Шиомгвимский Типикон (не имеющий малой вечерни), причем чин их здесь буквально тождественен с нынешним, нет только заключительной молитвы, даже состав псалмов и тропарей почти во всем совпадает с нынешним (разница в псалмах только та, что на междочасии 9 часа лишний псалом — 50-й). Но часословы с XII в., в которых впервые появляется чин междочасий, хотя дают тоже нынешний строй их, представляют большое колебание в подборе псалмов и молитв для междочасий; при этом замечательно, что в древнейших часословах более совпадений с нынешним чином; так часослов Синайской библ. № 865 XII в. все псалмы имеет нынешние (только на 1 и 3 часе добавочный 50-й пс.); в Синайском часосл. № 870 XIII в. уже только два псалма совпадают с нынешними; в часословах же Афоно-Ватопедской библ. № 350/984 XIII в., Синайской № 8686 [868] XIII–XIV и Новгор. Софийской (при Спб. Дух. Акад.) № 1052 XIII–XIV в. уже ни один псалом не совпадает с нынешним; явно, что эти часословы, как руководства келейно-скитского устава (см. ниже) не считаются с общепринятым и древним чином междочасий; по иным из них некоторые часы имеют и более одного почасия; так в Синайск. Часосл. № 870 XIII в. 1-й час имеет одно почасие, 3 и 6 по два, а 9 — три почасия [127] (сообразно, должно быть, важности воспоминаемых событий).
units.english_text: Subject unto no fewer modifications than the Hours was the order of Compline (*apodeipnon* / повечерие), and in like manner the particularities of the diverse Typika exercised no influence upon the development of this office: in both the Studite and Jerusalem Typika it shared a common history. The earliest notices concerning this office lead us to understand that in both branches of the Typikon it possessed a very similar, if not identical, composition. Thus the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis*, distinguishing two forms of Compline (*ta apodeipna* / τὰ ἀπόδειπνα)—complete (*holoklēra* / ὁλόκληρα) and abbreviated for festal days—direct that the second be commenced from **“God is with us”** (*Hypotyposis*) or from **“He that dwelleth in the help of the Most High”**, that is, Psalm 90 [91] (*Diatyposis*) [^1701]. If one compares with these rubrics the order of Compline in the most ancient Horologion according unto the rule of the Lavra of St. Sabas, Sinai Library *(Orig. p. 382)* MS No. 863 of the 8th–9th centuries, one cannot fail to notice that in both instances approximately one and the same office is intended. And in this Horologion, Compline, as we have seen (see above, p. 298), not yet possessing even this title, but designated “Prayer at the 1st Hour of the Night,” has a structure very close unto our present Great Compline in its first part, namely: Psalms 4, 12 [13], 26 [27], **“Glory,”** Psalms 30 [31], 90 [91], 6 (at present: 4, 6, 12 [13], 24 [25], 30 [31], 90 [91]), **“God is with us,”** Alleluia with the verses **“Look down and hear me, O Lord...”** and **“In peace in the selfsame...”** (the present verses unto the troparia **“Mine unseen enemies”**), then the troparia **“Mine unseen enemies...”** or others according unto the day, **“Lord, have mercy”** thrice, **“Deliver not unto beasts the soul that confesseth Thee...”** (a verse or a prayer?)—thereafter the manuscript breaks off. A similar composition, yet somewhat more complex and closer unto the present one, is exhibited by Compline in the Studite-Alexis Typikon:

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: молитва далее рукопис обрывается такой же состав
units.slavonic_text: молитва?), — далее рукопись обрывается. Такой же состав, но немного сложнее и ближе к нынешнему имеет повечерие в Студийско-Алексиевском уставе: «6 псалм отпевше, тажь С нами Бог и Бесплотное И верую и Пресвятая Владычице и Отче наш и Господи помилуй 30, таже покланяются триждь….. и паки такожь и на 3-м поклонении рещи: Приидите поклонимсь, таже псалм 7 Господи да не яростию. и Святый Боже и Отче наш и Господи помилуй 12 и молитве от попа бывши идут в келия своя» [129].
units.english_text: “Having chanted the 6 psalms, then **‘God is with us’** and **‘The Bodiless Nature’** and the Creed (**‘I believe’**) and **‘All-Holy Sovereign Lady’** and **‘Our Father’** and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 30 times, then they make 3 prostrations... and likewise again at the 3rd prostration to say: **‘Come, let us worship,’** then Psalm 7, **‘O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine anger,’** and the Trisagion and **‘Our Father’** and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 12 times, and a prayer having been said by the priest, they depart unto their cells” [^1702].

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: такая павечерница называется исполн полно полная и между
units.slavonic_text: Такая «павечерница» называется «исполнь» (полно, полная) и, между прочим, поется от понедельника Антипасхи до Вознесения. Но замечательно, что даже для Петрова поста указывается повечерие короче: «6 псалм и С нами Бог и Бесплотное и Верую и Пресвятая Владычице и Святый Боже и Отче наш и Господи помилуй 12 и коньчают» [130]. В первом повечерии явно две части, второе не делится на части. Так как невероятно, чтобы в пост повечерие было короче, чем в полупраздничный период Пятидесятницы, особенно в виду того, что Студийско-Алексиевский устав требует сокращенного повечерия не только для воскресных и праздничных дней, но и, например для попразднества Вознесения, то должно быть, там и здесь имеется в виду один чин повечерия и второй вид его — представитель его древнейшего типа, случайно оставшегося на страницах устава не поправленными, после осложнения его новыми вставками. Этот буднично-постный чин повечерия по Студ.-Алекс. уставу сокращался для праздников и других льготных дней путем урезок начальных псалмов его; именно: «в субботу вечером и в Господский праздник павечерница от С нами Бог и прочая и Господи помилуй 15, а от Вознесения Господня до всех святых от Живый в помощи и прочее». В первом случае следовательно опускались все начальные псалмы, и место их занимала песнь Исаии, во втором опускался ряд псалмов до 90 пс., который неизвестно, какое занимал место в их числе, последнее ли как ныне, или предпоследнее, как в Синайском Часослове VIII–IX в. Первого рода, т. е. более сокращенное, повечерие полагалось кроме воскресения и праздников в Великую пятницу, на Вознесение вечером и должно быть, в других аналогичных случаях; второе кроме попразднества Вознесения, под 1-ю субботу поста «праздника ради св. Феодора», под субботу ваий, в первые три дня Преполовения и должно быть, в подобные полупраздничные {с. 383} дни [131]. Неизвестно, существовал ли кроме этих трех видов повечерия еще особый вид его для Великого поста; данные для решения этого вопроса заключаются только в следующем замечании о службе великого понедельника: «мефимон же поется великый якоже и в пост» [132]; судя
units.english_text: Such a Compline (*pavechernitsa*) is termed *ispoln* (complete, full) and, among other times, is chanted from the Monday of Thomas Week (Antipascha) until Ascension. Yet it is remarkable that even for the Apostles’ (St. Peter’s) Fast a shorter Compline is indicated: “The 6 psalms and **‘God is with us’** and **‘The Bodiless Nature’** and the Creed (**‘I believe’**) and **‘All-Holy Sovereign Lady’** and the Trisagion and **‘Our Father’** and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 12 times, and they finish” [^1703]. In the first Compline there are clearly two parts; the second is not divided into parts. Since it is improbable that during a fast Compline would be shorter than during the semi-festal period of Pentecost, especially in view of the fact that the Studite-Alexis Typikon requires an abbreviated Compline not only for Sundays and feast days, but also, for instance, for the afterfeast of Ascension, it must be that in both places one and the same order of Compline is intended, and its second form is a representative of its most ancient type, accidentally left uncorrected on the pages of the Typikon after its complication with new insertions. This daily-furious/lenten order of Compline according unto the Studite-Alexis Typikon was abbreviated for feasts and other alleviated days by means of curtailing its initial psalms; namely: “on Saturday evening and on a Feast of the Lord, Compline from **‘God is with us’** and the rest and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 15 times; and from the Ascension of the Lord until All Saints, from **‘He that dwelleth in the help’** and the rest.” In the first case, consequently, all initial psalms were omitted and their place was taken by the canticle of Isaiah; in the second case, a series of psalms up unto Psalm 90 [91] was omitted, concerning which it is unknown what place it occupied among them—whether the last, as at present, or penultimate, as in the Sinai Horologion of the 8th–9th centuries. The first kind, that is, the more abbreviated Compline, was appointed, besides Sunday and feast days, on Great Friday, on Ascension evening, and in all probability in other analogous cases; the second, besides the afterfeast of Ascension, on the eve of the 1st Saturday of Lent “for the sake of the feast of St. Theodore,” on the eve of Lazarus Saturday (Palm Saturday), on the first three days of Mid-Pentecost, and in all probability on similar semi-festal *(Orig. p. 383)* days [^1704]. It is unknown whether, besides these three forms of Compline, there existed also a special form of it for Great Lent; the data for resolving this question consist solely in the following remark concerning the service of Great Monday: “and the great *methimon* [great compline / μεθέορτον/меθύμνον] is chanted even as in the fast” [^1705]; judging from the fact that “Great Compline” (*Velikaya pavechernitsa*) was appointed in Great Lent and on the eves of Saturdays [^1706], when “there is no fasting,” it is to be supposed that Lenten Compline did not differ from the daily office (*ispoln*), even as at present the Compline of the lesser fasts does not differ from that of Great Lent.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: тому что великая павечерница полагалас в великий
units.slavonic_text: по тому, что «Великая павечерница» полагалась в Великий пост и под субботы [133], когда «пост не бывает», надо полагать, что великопостное повечерие не отличалось от будничного («исполнь»), как ныне не отличается повечерие малых постов от великопостного.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: ночные часы и чин 12 псалмов
units.slavonic_text: ### Ночные часы и чин 12 псалмов
units.english_text: “It is needful to know that after the feast of Thomas Week (Antipascha), immediately after Compline, we begin the *pannychis*; and until All Saints we perform only the canon (such a composition was possessed by one form of the sung pannychis) and after it the Blameless (the *Amomos* / Psalm 118 [119]); from that time until Ascension we append 6 psalms, at which there are 3 prostrations and standings (*staseis* / στάσεις); after the Exaltation (of the Holy Cross), however, we perform 12 psalms and the other offices until the Great Forty Days; for then at every Trisagion we perform bows (*metanoiai*) with standings” [^1708].

units.slavonic_incipit: Дальнейшее развитие повечерия, в котором оно
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: дальнейшее развитие повечерия в котором оно получило кроме
units.slavonic_text: Дальнейшее развитие повечерия, в котором оно получило, кроме наметившихся уже здесь двух частей, и третью, и обогатило заключительную свою часть, обусловливалось с одной стороны слиянием его с песненным чином великой панихиды, но особенно включением в него последования так называемых «ночных часов» [134], чина, стоявшего в свою очередь в связи с древним, упоминаемым еще у прп. Кассиана «Чином 12 псалмов» (см. выше, стр. 216) и помещавшимся в Часословах и Псалтирях Следованных в качестве самостоятельной службы. Указание на тот и другой (ночные часы и 12 псалмов) чины находится и в Диатипосисе: «надобно же знать, что после праздника Антипасхи сейчас по повечерии начинаем паннихиду; и до Всех святых творим только канон (такой состав имел один из видов песненной панихиду) и после него Непорочны; с этого же времени до Вознесения присоединяем 6 псалмов, на которых поклонов и стояний (στάσεις) 3; по Воздвижении же псалмов 12 и прочие творим последования до великой Четыредесятницы; ибо тогда на каждом Трисвятом творим метания со стояниями» [135].
units.english_text: The most ancient complete order of the 12 Psalms and Nocturnal Hours is provided in the Sinai Horologion MS No. 864 of the 9th century. The manuscript, preserved in a fragment, commences with the psalms of the Ninth Hour, wherein the sequence of psalms is interrupted by a special division sign, after which follow 12 psalms, divided by three **“Glories”** into 4 parts, three psalms in each. There follow next two Theotokia, two “nocturnal canons” with special penitential refrains and troparia adapted in their contents unto the midnight hour; and then is set forth a special “office of the Midnight Office.” The psalms here are the following: 83 [84], 84 [85], 85 [86], 68 [69], 112 [113], 110 [111], 120 [121], the division sign, 74 [75], 20 [21], 54 [55] + 5, 7, 40 [41] + 31 [32], 80 [81], 81 [82] + 93 [94], 104 [105], 56 [57]. All these psalms, with slight variations in composition, enter into the *kanones nykterinōn psalmōn* (κανόνες νυκτερινῶν ψαλμῶν / canons of nocturnal psalms) of the 10th-century Psalter of the Athos University Library MS No. 7/67, where such an order of psalmody is set forth: *Kanones hēmerinōn* *(Orig. p. 384)* *psalmōn* (Κανόνες ἡμερινῶν ψαλμῶν / canons of diurnal psalms).
