units.english_text: Fidelity unto the monastic rule is maintained under St. Theodore, on the one hand, by a system of monastic hierarchy, and on the other, by a penal code for infractions thereof—epitimias (*penances*). In the monastic administration, after the hegumen, the second rank was occupied by the *deuterarios* (cf. in the Pachomian monasteries, above, p. 211), *ho ta deutera pheron* (*ὁ τὰ δεύτερα φέρων*), *ho deutereuon* (*ὁ δевτερεύων*) [^1793], his closest assistant and deputy—almost identical with the ecclesiarch of subsequent Typika. The third rank was occupied by the oikonomos (*steward*) [^1794]. Next followed the epistemonarchs—who examined offenses and assigned penances; according unto the *Hypotyposis*, 'unto them lesser transgressions are reported, and they apply measures of correction' [^1795]; taxiarchs assigned places unto all in assemblies; according unto the *Hypotyposis*, they reminded the brethren to stand decorously in the choirs; under St. Theodore there were four of them, while the *Hypotyposis* appoints two for the two choirs [^1796]; overseers (*epiteretai / ἐπιτηρηταί*)—supervised the fulfillment of the monastic rule [^1797]; according unto the *Hypotyposis*, two are appointed every evening; 'after the striking of the wooden semantron (*bilo*), they urge the slothful to go to Vespers and Compline, and upon the conclusion of the latter they inspect the hidden places in the monastery, and with due severity disperse those who gather for unseasonable assemblies' [^1798]; the awakener (*aphypnistes / ἀφυпνιστής*), according unto St. Theodore, awakens the brethren for Matins [^1799]; according unto the *Hypotyposis*, during the readings at Matins, quietly making the rounds of the brethren, he awakens those who have fallen asleep [^1800]. There are likewise mentioned in St. Theodore the *kellarites* (*κελαρίτης*)—the cellarer, in charge of provisions, and the *aristetarios* (*ἀριστητάριος*), literally the supervisor of morning collation, the refectorian [^1801]. The *Diatyposis*, of these officials (beginning from the epistemonarch), does not indicate taxiarchs, but defines the duties of epistemonarchs as the *Hypotyposis* defines those of the taxiarchs: unto them it likewise assigns the first half of the overseers' duties—to dispatch unto church after the bell-ringing those who have tarried, adding that from those remaining (in their cells during the service) they demand an explanation, and if they remained there not by order and not of necessity, they urge them unto diligence with moderate penances; furthermore, the *Diatyposis* speaks of only a single overseer, who 'day and night making the rounds of the cells, workshops, and other places of the Lavra with due severity and appropriate penance, disperses those who indulge in chatter and unseasonable strolls'; finally, the *Diatyposis* likewise indicates the office of the doorkeeper (*porter / thyroros / θυρωρός*), who, having charge of the entrance into the church, demands from those who did not arrive before the beginning of the service an account of their tardiness, and forbids those who leave unseasonably from exiting after one or two occurrences. Concerning penances (*epitimias*), although the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* mention them repeatedly, they do not specify their types and degrees, *(Orig. p. 420)* silently referring thereby unto the specialized instructions concerning them by St. Theodore in the *Monastic Epitimias* [^1802] and the *Great Catechesis* (§§ 60, 69). In penances St. Theodore is exceedingly close unto Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople († 828 AD), in his *Penitential Canons* [^1803]; from Basil the Great St. Theodore is distinguished by granting less discretion unto superiors in assigning penances [^1804]. The degrees of penance under St. Theodore are: 1) excommunication (*aphorismos / ἀφορισμός*)—that is, exclusion for a certain time from communion with the brethren at meals, in prayer, and in work [^1805]; it is appointed under St. Theodore in 23 cases: for example, for theft, inciting the brethren against the superior, evasion of confession and Holy Communion, negligence in service duties, idle wandering through the monastery, concealment of others' misdeeds (inter alia, also for reciting from memory unto the brethren from a book that was being transcribed); 2) xerophagy (*dry-eating / xerophagia / ξηроφαγία*)—subsistence upon bread and water, probably for a single day each time, for less important omissions in duty, and for tardiness unto divine services; 3) prostrations (*metanoiai / μετάνοιαι*) in varying numbers in church or in the cell; 4) standing (*parastasis / παράστασις*) during meals or in church at the departure of the brethren (the latter in a bowed posture—for slight tardiness unto the service); if the former was assigned for breaking dishware, the guilty brother stood holding the potsherds.

units.slavonic_text: «Монастырских епитимиях» [229] и «Большом Катихизисе» (§ 60, 69). В епитимиях прп. Феодор очень близок к патр. Константинопольскому Никифору († 828 г.) в его «Епитимийных канонах» [230]; от Василия Великого прп. Феодор отличается предоставлением меньшего усмотрения начальствующим в назначении епитимий [231]. Степени епитимьи у прп. Феодора: 1) отлучение, ἀφορισμός — т. е. удаление на некоторое время от общения с братией в трапезе, молитве и работе [232]; оно назначается у прп. Феодора в 23 случаях, например за кражу, возбуждение братии против настоятеля, уклонение от исповеди и причастия, нерадение по службе, праздношатание по монастырю, утайку чужих проступков (между прочим, и за чтение на память братиям из списывавшейся книги); 2) сухоядение (ξηροφαγία) — питание хлебом и водою, должно быть, один лишь день каждый раз, за менее важные упущения по службе, за опоздание к богослужению; 3) поклоны (μετάνοιαι) в разном количестве в церкви или келии; 4) стояние (παράστασις) за трапезой или в церкви при выходе братии (последнее — в согбенном положении — за незначительное опоздание к службе); если первое назначалось за разбитие посуды, то виновный стоял с черепками. Не говоря определенно ни об одном из этих видов епитимьи, Ипотипосис и Диатипосис указывают один лишь, но более суровый вид ее — заключение в особое помещение (ἀφοριστηρία) на сухоядение для непокорных и упрямых, причем первый замечает, что «исправление посредством бичей (διὰ μαστίγων, ср. выше, стр. 195 о Нитрийском монастыре IV–V в.), идущее мирянам, справедливо отвергнуто нашими св. отцами» (Ипотипосис § 25). При недействительности епитимий прибегали к удалению из монастыря (по Диатипосису). Из проступков с особым негодованием говорит Диатипосис о краже: «производящие какую бы то ни было покражу вещей обители заслуживают смерть Анании и Сапфиры; но те телесно, а эти душевно наследуют смерть с проклятием» (§ 33). Из внутренней жизни монастыря оба памятника касаются следующих сторон. Ищущий поступления в монастырь 2–3 недели должен жить в монастырской странноприимнице, знакомясь с порядками, и поучаясь игуменом; после этого «оглашения принимаемый вводился в собрание братий, делал им поклон, а они молились за него (Ип. § 24, Диат. § 11). От монахов требуется полная нестяжательность: нельзя иметь и собственной мебели (Диат. § 30). Наиболее внимания уделяется богослужению. Из служб в Ипотипосисе указываются часы только для литургии в пост: когда трапеза в 9 ч. (= 3 ч. дня), литургия в 6 (12) ч., в непостные дни в 3 (9) ч. (§ 27); по Диатипосису утреня будничная в 7 ч. (1 ч. ночи), воскресная в 6 (12 ч. ночи), праздничная в начале 5 (10 ч. § 7). В Четыредесятницу 1-ый час указывается совершать отдельно от утрени на рассвете (Ипотипо{с. 421}сис, § 14). Запрещается стоять в церкви с жезлами и даже входить туда с ними, пользоваться при коленопреклонениях скамейками (σκαμνίοις Диат. § 13). По Ипотипосису
units.english_text: Without speaking definitively of any of these types of penance, the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* indicate only one, but more severe form thereof—confinement in a special chamber (*aphoristeria / ἀφοριστηρία*) upon dry-eating for the insubordinate and stubborn, wherein the former observes that 'correction by means of scourges (*dia mastigon / διὰ μαστίγων*, cf. above, p. 195 concerning the Nitrian monastery in the 4th–5th centuries), which is suited unto laymen, is justly rejected by our holy fathers' (*Hypotyposis*, § 25). Upon the inefficacy of penances recourse was had to expulsion from the monastery (according unto the *Diatyposis*). Of offenses, the *Diatyposis* speaks with special indignation concerning theft: 'those who commit any theft whatsoever of the monastery's property deserve the death of Ananias and Sapphira; but whereas they died bodily, these inherit death of the soul with a curse' (§ 33). Of the internal life of the monastery, both documents touch upon the following aspects: He who seeks admission into the monastery must dwell for two to three weeks in the monastic guest-house (*xenodocheion*), becoming acquainted with the order and being instructed by the hegumen; after this 'catechesis', the candidate was introduced into the assembly of the brethren, made a prostration before them, and they prayed for him (*Hypotyposis*, § 24; *Diatyposis*, § 11). Complete poverty (*non-acquisitiveness / ne-styazhanie*) is required of the monks: they may not possess even their own furniture (*Diatyposis*, § 30). The greatest attention is accorded unto the divine services. Among the offices, the *Hypotyposis* specifies the hours only for the Liturgy on fast days: when the meal is at the 9th hour (= 3:00 PM), the Liturgy is at the 6th hour (12:00 noon); on non-fast days, at the 3rd hour (9:00 AM) (§ 27); according unto the *Diatyposis*, weekday Matins is at the 7th hour of the night (1:00 AM), Sunday Matins at the 6th (12:00 midnight), festal Matins at the beginning of the 5th (10:00 PM) (§ 7). In the Great Fast, the First Hour is appointed to be celebrated separately from Matins at dawn (*Hypoty*(Orig. p. 421)*posis*, § 14). It is forbidden to stand in church with staves and even to enter therein with them, or to use stools (*skamnia / σκαмνίοις*, *Diatyposis*, § 13) when kneeling. According unto the *Hypotyposis*, daily at the beginning of the 4th Ode of the Canon the hegumen departs from the choir and, sitting down, receives the brethren for confession; according unto the *Diatyposis*, he does this whenever he desires, and may entrust confession unto another (*Hypotyposis*, § 22; *Diatyposis*, § 29). On the eve of Palm Sunday at *Lord, I have cried*, the choirs were exchanged, evidently for the entire year: the right choir became the left and vice versa—naturally in view of the greater difficulty and greater quantity of chanting upon the right choir (for which reason this is treated in the chapter 'On Proportion in the Services', *Hypotyposis*, § 34). In the Great Fast an elderly (according unto the *Diatyposis*—a 'discreet') brother is designated, who from the 3rd hour (9:00 AM) makes the rounds of all the work-places, and in each, having made a metania, proclaims: 'Brethren and fathers, let us take heed unto ourselves, for we die, we die, we die'; according unto another manuscript, there is added: 'let us call to mind also the Kingdom of Heaven'; according unto the *Diatyposis*: 'concerning eternal torment'; according unto the *Diatyposis*, in response unto this the brethren 'cease work, arise, recite the Trisagion, and sit down again' (*Hypotyposis*, § 23; *Diatyposis*, § 9). In a special article 'On Proportion in the Services' both documents regulate manual labor and furnish the schedule for the monastic day. According unto the *Hypotyposis*, the brethren all engage in bodily labors from sunrise or after the chanting of the First Hour, when the hours are appointed, until the 6th hour (12:00 noon); from the 6th unto the 8th hour (12:00–2:00 PM) rest is appointed for the brethren, whether there is dinner or not; from the 8th hour (2:00 PM) until Vespers there is work again: after Vespers, 'each retires into solitude as he desires' (§ 33). The *Diatyposis* indicates days when there is no labor: these are the first and Great Week of the Fast and the week of Pascha (*Bright Week*), especially until Wednesday; other great feasts are likewise understood. The *Diatyposis* does not speak of midday rest, but occupies itself in detail with the table for those performing heavy labors—blacksmiths, muleteers, boatmen, carpenters, vinedressers, and bakers; unto these workers before the common meal there is given at the 3rd hour (9:00 AM) in the great fasts bread, and on minor fasts and ordinary days wine also, and at the refectory an additional cup (*krasobolion*) of wine is granted them; on days free from labor they are content with the common allotment (*Diatyposis*, §§ 25, 26). On feasts when there is no labor, reading of books from the monastic library is recommended unto the brethren; the *Diatyposis* gives general counsel concerning this, while the *Hypotyposis* defines also the order for distributing books: the librarian strikes the wooden semantron (*bilo*) once, the brethren proceed unto the library, there each receives a book, and before Vespers, again upon the stroke of the semantron, returns it (*Hypotyposis*, § 26; *Diatyposis*, § 28). Those who had not learned the Psalter by heart presented themselves for Matins only at the Canon upon the threefold stroke on the semantron by the canonarch, employing the beginning of Matins (the Kathismata) for the study of the Psalter (*Hypotyposis*, § 36). Both documents determine in detail the quality and quantity of clothing (see ch. 39 of the Typikon) and of food throughout the entire year, principally during fasts (see chs. 32 and 33 of the Typikon). Here a distinguishing feature of these documents, in comparison with the Jerusalem Typika, is the permission throughout the entire Pentecostarion, on great feasts occurring on Wednesday and Friday and during the minor Quadragesimas, as well as for the evening of Great and Holy Saturday, of cheese and eggs; for Great and Holy Saturday this permission is not granted *(Orig. p. 422)* by later manuscripts of the *Hypotyposis* (*Hypotyposis*, §§ 28, 29; *Diatyposis*, §§ 14–18). This chapter of the *Hypotyposis*, although it entered into the Studite-Alexis Typikon in a softened form, provoked great disputes in Russia during the 12th–13th centuries in view of its discrepancy with the ancient canons and the Jerusalem Typikon (see below). In both monuments, comportment at the refectory table is defined in agreement: "When the brethren assemble to dine (*Diatyposis*: 'at the sound of the bell,' *kodonos*), in their mouths must be a verse" (a prayerful verse, according unto later monuments: **"Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us"**); according unto the *Diatyposis*, likewise: "and when they rise from the table, until such time as, having departed into the narthex, they offer thanksgiving for that which they have eaten"; they sit at the tables nine men each (*Diatyposis*), according unto the direction of the overseer watching that there be no vacant places; they sit at the refectory in hoods (*koukoulia*; *Hypotyposis*); there is also a reading, "which (*Diatyposis*) is directed by the ecclesiarch, who takes care that whatever they did not manage to read in church should be read at the refectory and nothing should be omitted"; "the signal for the conclusion of the reading is the clatter of spoons cast simultaneously into the bowls at the final dish; likewise for the pouring of wine and the serving of courses a signal is given by means of a strike" (*Diatyposis*: by a bell; *Hypotyposis*, § 28; *Diatyposis*, § 14). Finally, the *Diatyposis* also provides for a brother's departure from the monastery, "if he has no spiritual peace in our lavra"; it must not be a clandestine flight, but must occur upon forewarning the 'spiritual guide,' "so that departure from the monastery may also take place with prayer and blessing, and not with prohibition, nor with a curse, nor with excommunication by the Holy Fathers" (§ 31).

units.slavonic_text: рукописями Ипотипосиса (Ипот. § 28, 29, Диат. § 14–18). Эта статья Ипотипосиса, хотя вошла в Студийско-Алексиевский устав в смягченном виде, вызвала большие споры в России XII–XIII в. ввиду разноречия ее с древними канонами и Иерусалимским уставом (см. ниже). В обоих памятниках согласно определяется поведение за трапезою. «Когда братия сходятся обедать (Диат.: «по звуку колокольчика», κώδονος) в устах у них должен быть стих» (молитвенный, по поздн. памятн. — «Господи Иисусе Христе сыне Божий помилуй нас»), по Диатипосису — так же, «и когда встанут из-за стола, до тех пор, пока отошедши в притвор, не принесут благодарение за то, что покушали» садятся за столы по 9 человек (Диат.), по указанию надзирателя наблюдающего, чтобы не было пустых мест; сидят за трапезою в кукулях (Ип.); бывает и чтение, «которым (Диат.) распоряжается екклисиарх, заботящийся «о том, чтобы чего не успели прочитать в церкви, то было прочтено за трапезою и ничего не было опущено»; «знаком окончания чтения бывает стук ложек, бросаемых одновременно в тарелки при последнем кушанье; равным образом и к наливанию вина и к подаче кушаний дается знак посредством ударения» (Диатипосис — звонком. Ипот. § 28. Диат. § 14). — Наконец Диатипосис предусматривает и оставление братом монастыря, «если он не имеет душевного покоя в нашей лавре»; оно должно быть не тайным бегством, а происходить с предупреждения об этом «духовного вождя», «чтобы и удаление из монастыря было с молитвою и благословением, а не с запрещением, не с проклятием, не с отлучением от св. Отцев» (§ 31).
units.english_text: The Great Synaxarion of the Athonite Iviron Lavra of the 11th century (see above, p. 372, n. 4), the exemplar of Holy Mountain Typika, in its disciplinary portion represents an abridgment and slight modification of the *Diatyposis*; from it are retained here the sections concerning the hour of services, food, proportion in services, non-acquisitiveness, the order of leaving the monastery, imprisonment, clothing, and non-working days. The hours of service are appointed for Matins: throughout the year, weekday Matins is at the 8th hour (2:00 AM; an hour later than in the *Diatyposis*); on Sundays at the beginning of the 7th hour, and festal Matins at the beginning of the 5th hour (slightly later than in the *Diatyposis*); during the Twelve Holy Days [from the Nativity of Christ unto Theophany], Cheesefare Week, and the second days of the Great Feasts of the Lord, toward the beginning of the 9th hour (around 2:00 AM); in Great Lent, toward the beginning of the 6th hour (around 11:00 PM). Concerning fasts, the dispensation of the *Diatyposis* for cheese during Pentecost and for feasts occurring during multi-day fasts is abrogated, and this dispensation is preserved for feasts falling upon ordinary Wednesdays and Fridays. Unto those occupied with heavy labors during a fast, food is given at the 6th hour (not at the 3rd). Monks are forbidden to acquire money (concerning furniture nothing is said). Of the penances, imprisonment is preserved with the observation: "punishment by blows or other means appropriate in the world is condemned by our fathers, although in case of extreme necessity it is permissible to resort unto them also." In the event of a desire to leave the monastery, "the hegu-*(Orig. p. 423)*-men shall entrust the departing brother unto another hegumen, or undertake whatever other measures." Feast days are divided into non-working days for all, including laborers, and non-working days only for the brethren; unto the former, besides the Twelve Great Feasts, belong September 13 and 26; November 8 and 14; December 6, 9, and 26; January 1; April 23; May 8 and 24 (Symeon the Wonderworker); June 24 and 29; August 29; unto the latter: September 20; October 18, 23, and 26; November 1 and 13; December 4, 13, and 27; January 17, 20, and 25; February 17 and 24; March 9; June 8; July 1, 8, 20, and 27; August 31; the small number of 'secular' feasts (for the laborers) the *Synaxarion* explains by the small number of laborers in the monastery (only four) and their high wages [^1806].

units.slavonic_incipit: На основе Ипотипосиса выработана дисциплинарная часть
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: на основе ипотипосиса выработана дисциплинарная част в студийско алексиевском
units.slavonic_text: На основе Ипотипосиса выработана дисциплинарная часть в Студийско-Алексиевском уставе (XI–XII в.), который был так долго регулятором монашеской жизни в России. Но первоисточник здесь подвергся и большим изменениям, чем, например, в Иверском «Синаксаре», и значительно расширен: из 281 листов древнейшей рукописи этого устава дисциплинарная часть занимает более трети: 85 листов. Позднейшие рукописи оставляют без изменения эту часть устава. Из должностных лиц Ипотипосиса не упоминаются таксиархи и надзиратели; их обязанности, по-видимому, передаются епитсимонархам, наименование которых переведено по-славянски «хитрьцяначальника» [234]; их было двое (л. 215). Первым лицом после игумена был эконом («иконом»); но в церкви, если эконом не имел священного сана, первым после игумена считался старейший из священников (л. 266 об.). Затем такие «служьбьници» (служебницы): «коутьник» — главный начальник над трапезою (то, что у св. Феодора — келарь и трапезарь); «иже стареи на обою сторону церкви», т. е. два хитрецяначальника, хотя они (по другому месту устава) в церкви ставятся непосредственно после игумена и эконома (л. 266); «пономарь — съсудохранильник; житници ключарь; иже о больных стоит (больничный); иже въспоминае (будильщик?) [235]; деместик церковный (= канонарх); книжный хранитель; келарь (заведующий одеждой?) и старейший странноприимец». Игумен увольняет (а след. и назначает) всех должностных лиц (л. 225 об., 226). Повиновение игумену должно быть такое же, как военачальнику. Пред разговором с ним, или завидя его, кланяются «вельми» («Мнишескии заповеди живущих в киновии рекъше вкупе жити», л. 216 об.). Одна из главных обязанностей игумена — почаще наставлять монахов и всех вместе и каждого отдельно («О том, еже чясто оглашати мнихы» л. 223). Денежные дела
units.english_text: Upon the foundation of the *Hypotyposis*, the disciplinary portion was elaborated in the Studite-Alexis Typikon (11th–12th centuries), which was for so long the regulator of monastic life in Russia. But the primary source here underwent greater modifications than, for example, in the Iviron *Synaxarion*, and was significantly expanded: out of the 281 folios of the most ancient manuscript of this Typikon, the disciplinary portion occupies more than one third: 85 folios. Later manuscripts leave this portion of the Typikon unaltered. Of the officials of the *Hypotyposis*, taxiarchs and overseers are not mentioned; their duties, apparently, are transferred unto epistemonarchs, whose title is translated in Slavic as *khitretsyanachalnika* [^1807]; there were two of them (fol. 215). The first person after the hegumen was the oeconomus (*ikonom*); but in church, if the oeconomus lacked holy orders, the senior among the priests was considered first after the hegumen (fol. 266v). Next follow such 'servitors' (*sluzhbnitsi*): the *kutnik*—chief superintendent over the refectory (that which under St. Theodore was the cellarer and refectorian); "those who are senior on both sides of the church," that is, the two *khitretsyanachalnika*, although they (according unto another passage of the Typikon) are placed in church immediately after the hegumen and oeconomus (fol. 266); "the paramonarios—sacristan (*ssudokhranilnik*); the granary key-bearer; he who attends unto the sick (infirmarian); he who awakens (the awakener?) [^1808]; the church domestikos (= canonarch); the keeper of books; the cellarer (supervisor of clothing?), and the senior hospitaller." The hegumen discharges (and consequently appoints) all monastic officials (fols. 225v, 226). Obedience unto the hegumen must be the same as unto a military commander. Before speaking with him, or catching sight of him, they bow "greatly" (*"Monastic commandments of those living in a cenobium, that is to say, living together,"* fol. 216v). One of the chief duties of the hegumen is to instruct the monks more frequently, both all together and each individually (*"Concerning this, that monks should be frequently catechized,"* fol. 223). Financial affairs of the monastery the hegumen is advised to conduct with the knowledge and mediation of other monastic officials; money is to be kept in a chest sealed by him, the oeconomus, and the *kutnik* (fol. 226v). The order for the election of a hegumen is indicated: after the death of a hegumen, the brethren, "having performed common prayer and fasting for three days, fervently entreat the Godhead to appoint one who is worthy"; "thereafter, with the Holy Gospel lying before them, they elect whom they know"; the elected candidate must be not younger than 33 years of age, from among the tonsured monks of the monastery, and not those who en-*(Orig. p. 425)*-tered from another monastery, so as not to grieve the local brethren by the necessity "to be pastured by an outsider," and lest the hegumen destroy "the rule of our divine fathers Elias and Theodore"; it is also necessary to elect one who is "by no means partaker of marital intercourse" (neither a widower nor one who has abandoned a wife), lest "love for kindred" distract him from the monastery; it is recommended to elect from among the "consecrated" [priests] or "great schema-monks"; if the election is not unanimous, they elect three candidates and present them unto the Patriarch (*"Concerning hegumens,"* fols. 238v–241). Regarding the spirit of monastic governance itself, the founder wishes, as we have seen, that the principles of St. Theodore be observed here, which is why at the conclusion of the Typikon there is appended a translation (unfinished) of the Penitential of St. Theodore under the title *"Concerning the remnants of church canons"* (fol. 280). The Typikon devotes much space unto admission into the monastery. The establishment of the monastery is fixed at 40–50 or more monks, "besides those who are in the villages" (*"Concerning the number of monks,"* fol. 231v). Unknown persons must be tested for a year before admission; those from other monasteries are to be received only with good recommendations; priests and deacons from other monasteries are admitted unto celebrating only after three months upon learning all the customs of the monastery. It is forbidden to demand from incoming applicants a contribution unto the monastery (*"Concerning priests and deacons,"* fols. 232–234v). Those who make large contributions dare not claim any privileges in the monastery (*"Concerning offerings,"* fol. 234); to receive someone into the monastery upon such conditions is worse than contracting a loan. In case of a deficiency of funds in the monastery, it is better to pawn something or borrow from the patriarchate or its monastery (*"Concerning renunciation,"* fols. 235v–237). In connection with this, the Typikon likewise forbids burying anyone in the monastery, "even if he should give something on that account"; at this, the founder-patriarch observes that even for himself he prepared a tomb in the monastery not by his own will, but at the request of the monks; he himself had the desire to be buried in the Studite monastery, where as a youth he received tonsure and labored until the patriarchate itself (*"Concerning this, that no one should be buried in the monastery,"* fol. 237v). The founder wishes to make the monastery, after the model of the great ancient ones, as isolated from the world as possible: leaving the monastery is permitted only with the hegumen's permission; visitors are received initially only in the hospice, and are reported unto the hegumen for further directions. To oversee this, at the outer 'hospice' gates of the monastery there is one monk, and at the inner gates three, "from men aged, chaste, and borne witness by all"; they may alternate in attending divine services, and at their post it is recommended to read the Psalter and other soul-profiting books. Women are unconditionally forbidden entry into the monastery; permission is granted only unto the empress with a single maidservant; while for the ladies of her court, "as many of the women as follow after her," it is permitted to enter the monastery only through the "bath-house" (the bath or refuse) gates into the small church; and it is forbidden for all to meet the empress, but only the hegumen, oeconomus, protopresbyter, paramonarios, and other elders (*"Concerning hospices,"* fols. 229–231). During Great Lent, however, from Vespers of Cheesefare Sunday until Friday of the sixth week, the monastery was locked unconditionally, except in case of deliveries or dispatching someone, for which purpose *(Orig. p. 426)* they open the rear gates (*"How it is proper to lock the monastery during holy Great Lent,"* fol. 215v) [^1809]. With the aim of greater isolation from the world, the monastery was required to maintain within itself (as was practiced also by ancient monasteries of high ascetic discipline) such necessary institutions as an infirmary with a physician and pharmacy, and a special hospice for elderly monks, placed under the charge of eight elders, where the means for its maintenance by the monastery in food, firewood, oil, and candles are defined in detail; into this hospice Christ-loving laymen were also received at their own expense, where it is likewise determined in detail for what payment is taken from them—not forgetting payment for soap in the bath-house and "the washing of their garments by one of the neighboring women" (*"Concerning the infirm and the aged,"* fols. 241–244). The means of sustenance the monastery was obliged to acquire for itself chiefly through the labors of the monks; therefore no one in the monastery is exempt from manual labors, not even the hegumen. In particular, kneading dough was also performed by all in rotation, for which purpose the brethren are divided into three 'ranks' (*chiny*): the first is called ("styled") the rank of the hegumen, the second of the oeconomus, and the third of the *kutnik*; each of these supervisors had assistants: the hegumen the *kutnik*, the oeconomus the sub-oeconomus, and the *kutnik* the sub-*kutnik*; alongside them, one of the brethren (a specialist?) was placed at the head of each rank; his duty included calling to the kneading. Following the Six Psalms at the beginning of the kathismata, this brother, having naturally prepared everything in the bakehouse, entered the church and, having made a bow in the center, approached first on the right side of the temple, then on the left, each brother of his rank, and with a bow said: **"Lord, bless, unto the bakehouse"** (*Gospodi blagoslovi v peklnitsyu*); those summoned in this manner assembled before the Royal Doors and, together with that brother, at the conclusion of the first antiphon, approached the hegumen and bowed unto him to the ground; the caller said: **"Bless. Pray for us, holy father"**; the latter replied: **"God save you"**; in the bakehouse, part of them kneaded the dough, while part chanted "the Six Psalms, one canon, and the remainder of Matins"; upon conclusion of the work they return unto the church and chant with the rest, "and the first manages according to the readiness of the dough"; prosphora were kneaded by a single baker (*"Concerning kneading,"* fols. 227v–228). "Just as kneading the dough is established for the brethren themselves, so also burdens brought into the monastery from without, such as firewood or wine and the like, they themselves we command to carry up from the shore into the monastery, and no one out of pride ought to be ashamed of such labor, but before all others let the venerable father hegumen labor with zeal and joy, providing an example unto his spiritual children" (*"Concerning the carrying of heavy burdens,"* fol. 229) [^1810]. The Typikon exhor-*(Orig. p. 427)*-ts the monks to perform all commissions given them, especially oversight of labors outside the monastery (where work must have been executed chiefly by hired hands under the supervision of monks), with constant thought of the unslumbering eye and to fear, as the sin of Ananias and Sapphira or as sacrilege, any dishonesty (*"Concerning those sent upon obediences,"* fol. 219). In free time they may not assemble for conversations, nor enter the cell of another even under the pretext of study. Those wishing to study assemble for this in the 'refectory' after Matins. The hegumen takes care that each monk know the Psalter by heart and chant it in church according to the "living book of the soul," and not search for a book here and there (*"That it is not fitting for monks to congregate with one another,"* fols. 220–221). In connection with the external life of the monastery, the Typikon speaks *"Concerning monastic vesture"* (fols. 223v–224) in greater detail than the present Typikon (see ch. 39 of the Typikon), and concerning the bath-house: they go to it by tickets ("seals") from the hegumen, apparently once a month (the place is abraded in the manuscript), and the sick according unto the direction of the physician (fol. 225). Extensive sections of the Typikon under the headings: *"Chapters of the church rule, similar unto the first rule-book (that is, the rule concerning food) of various chapters extending into church service"* (fols. 245v–249), *"Concerning this, with what great attentiveness monks must stand at divine doxologies"* (fols. 249–250), *"Concerning the standing of monks in church"* (fol. 253), interspersed with purely liturgical paragraphs (concerning how to chant the triadika [Trinity hymns], concerning the number of kathismata at Matins, concerning the chanting of kathismata on Saturday, concerning the chanting of **"God of gods"** [Ps. 49:1], that is, the second antiphon of the 7th kathisma, and **"Praise the Lord"** [Ps. 148], that is, the third antiphon of the 20th kathisma, with special alleluiaria, concerning the refrains unto the Psalms of Praise and **"Lord, I have cried"**), these sections are dedicated unto the comportment of monks in church. Here, first of all, the time for Matins is defined: during Pentecost it begins at the start of the 9th hour (3:00 AM) [^1811]; from Pentecost unto Great Lent, as also on Sundays and Feasts of the Lord throughout the year, at the 7th hour (1:00 AM); on Monday through Thursday of Great Lent at half-past the 4th hour (9:30 PM); on Friday and Saturday of Great Lent at the beginning of the 7th hour (2:00 AM). Upon the arrival of the hour, the awakener (*ubuzhayay*) rises and goes first of all unto the cell of the hegumen, bows unto the ground, and says outside the door: **"Bless and pray for me, holy father"**; the latter replies from within: **"God save thee"**; then the awakener, still by the cell, proclaims very loudly: **"Bless, holy fathers"** (*Blagoslovite svyatii*), and repeats this likewise loudly, passing by all the cells. Meanwhile, the striking of the *klepalo* begins, first upon the "upper sounding-board (*bilo*) at the guestmaster's," then upon the great *bilo*, and finally upon the small *bilo* (fols. 246v–247). Upon entering the church they make a prostration before the Royal Doors, yet without approaching the icon screen for this purpose; he whose place is near the hegumen makes a prostration unto him also; unto the brethren no bow is made (fols. 253v–254). Matins begins in the narthex, and in winter (from the Exaltation) *(Orig. p. 428)* in the church. In the church the brethren stand along the walls, in front the priests in order of their ordination, next the deacons, and so forth; in front of all on the right side stands the hegumen, on the left the oeconomus. They are required to stand erect, vigilantly, feet together, hands joined beneath the mantle, not scratching themselves ("for if a flea, gnat, louse, or something else falls upon one, immediately to turn one's thought unto it and scratch, this one his head, that one his feet, and another some other part of his body, or thrusting hands inside one's garment, is not the conduct of a steadfast man, but of one exceedingly negligent and impatient," fols. 245v–249). Beginning the chanting, concluding it, and making a bow after it must take place simultaneously with the senior (fol. 254). It is indicated what character the chanting of the Six Psalms, the triadika, and **"God is the Lord"** must possess (see below, ch. 2 of the Typikon). The reader during the reading must have his head uncovered, and likewise during the refectory reading (fol. 213). From the epistemonarchs ("the elders of both sides") is required careful preservation from damage of liturgical books (to keep them under lock, not allowing them to be touched with bare fingers, nor wax to drip, nor to bespatter them with saliva; fol. 261). In particular, among the disciplinary-liturgical aspects of monastic life, the Typikon defines in detail the order of kissing after Compline (fol. 265), the order of the Exaltation of the Cross (fol. 261), the order of monastic burial (fol. 273v); it indicates when the brethren are to stand in church with candles: at the consecration (patronal feast) of the church or narthex, at the Theophany blessing of waters, on Palm Sunday, on Great and Holy Tuesday at the chanting of the stichera of the Holy Passions, and on Great Week (*"How many times monks will take candles,"* fols. 271v–273). It is appointed on Great and Holy Thursday to clean, and on Great and Holy Friday to wash the church, and it indicates at this how to illuminate it on Great and Holy Saturday and Pascha (*"Concerning church illumination,"* fols. 278–279; see below under "Great and Holy Saturday"). In close connection with divine services, Eastern Typika have always placed fasting, for which reason the Studite-Alexis Typikon begins its disciplinary portion with the section on fasts (*"The rule-book examining concerning the food and drink of monks..."* fols. 196–212) and defines the monastic table for the entire year with even greater detail than the present Typikon. In this regard, the Studite-Alexis Typikon first of all indicates the order at the refectory table, providing what was subsequently called the 'elevation of the Panagia' (*chin o panagii*) with a ritual no less complex than the present one, only instead of the Panagia (the prosphoron of the Mother of God) a dish with morsels of bread (*ukrukhi*) is elevated (fols. 196v–201); an observation is made concerning the order of dining for those who did not dine together with all—the cellarer and those who served (*"Concerning the second table,"* fol. 201), concerning the evening meal (*"Concerning Vespers [supper],* fol. 202), concerning reading at the refectory and attentiveness unto it, a prohibition against being dissatisfied with the food [^1812] (fols. 203–204), and, finally, a detailed distribution of foods for all fasts (fols. 205–211; see chaps. 32 and

provenance.verbatim_source: Upon the foundation of the *Hypotyposis*, the disciplinary portion was elaborated in the Studite-Alexis Typikon (11th–12th centuries), which was for so long the regulator of monastic life in Russia. But the primary source here underwent greater modifications than, for example, in the Iviron *Synaxarion*, and was significantly expanded: out of the 281 folios of the most ancient manuscript of this Typikon, the disciplinary portion occupies more than one third: 85 folios. Later manuscripts leave this portion of the Typikon unaltered. Of the officials of the *Hypotyposis*, taxiarchs and overseers are not mentioned; their duties, apparently, are transferred unto epistemonarchs, whose title is translated in Slavic as *khitretsyanachalnika* [^1807]; there were two of them (fol. 215). The first person after the hegumen was the oeconomus (*ikonom*); but in church, if the oeconomus lacked holy orders, the senior among the priests was considered first after the hegumen (fol. 266v). units.slavonic_stem_tier2: 33 тип эта статья заключается особым чином коляды
units.slavonic_text: 33 Тип.). Эта статья заключается особым чином (коляды», т. е. исполнения певцами за трапезою пасхальною, успенскою, рождественскою и Богоявленского тропаря, кондака, икоса и ипакои, после чего певцам вручалось от игумена вознаграждение — {с. 429} «благословение по предании от кута» [240] («Коляда», л. 211 об.). Запрещается держать в келье пищу или посуду для приготовления ее; если иноку нужно предложить пищу посетителю или гостю своему, то это можно сделать только за общею трапезою с разрешения игумена (л. 213–214). Отдел о трапезе заключается указанием, «како подобает возжягати огнь, идеже пекуть и в поварници» (л. 216): повар входит в храм, трижды кланяется до земли «пред чистыми преградами» (иконостасом) и просит огня от церковника; тот омакает рогоз в светильник и зажигает от св. света [241]. В другом месте устава определяется в цифрах праздничное довольство монастыря (включая конечно и посетителей): 8 сент., 21 ноября, 6 янв., 2 февраля, 25 марта — «хлеба спуды (неизвестная мера сыпучих тел) 3, вина меры 3»; 29 июня, 6 авг., Вознесение, Пятидесятница и Нед. всех свв. — хлеба спуды 3, вина меры 2; 14 сент. и 6 дек. — хлеба сп. 3 и вина 1 м.; 23 апр. хлеба сп. 1 и вина 1 м.; в храмовые же праздники монастыря это довольство значительно увеличивалось: 15 авг. хлеба сп. 10, вина мер 10, кутии и пшеницы сп. 4, сочива сп. 4, воды 2; 11 ноября на св. Феодора Студита — хлеба сп. 6, вина м. 8, кутии сп. 6, сочива сп. 6; 17 марта на св. Алексия — 4 + 6 + 3 + 2; 24 июня 4 + 4 + 4 кутии; 27 июля — 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 («О издаянии», л. 244 об.).
units.english_text: 33 of the Typikon). This chapter concludes with a special rite of the 'carol' (*kolyada*), that is, the performance by the chanters at the Paschal, Dormition, Nativity, and Theophany refectory meals of the troparion, kontakion, ikos, and hypakoe, after which there was handed unto the chanters by the hegumen a recompense—*(Orig. p. 429)* "a blessing according to tradition from the corner (*kut*)" [^1813] (*"Kolyada,"* fol. 211v). It is forbidden to keep food in the cell or utensils for preparing it; if a monk needs to offer food unto a visitor or guest of his, this may be done only at the common refectory table with permission of the hegumen (fols. 213–214). The section concerning the refectory concludes with the instruction *"how it is proper to kindle fire where they bake and in the kitchen"* (fol. 216): the cook enters the temple, bows thrice unto the ground "before the pure screens" (the iconostasis), and asks for fire from the sacristan; the latter dips a reed into the lamp and kindles it from the holy light [^1814]. In another place of the Typikon, the festal allowance of the monastery (naturally including visitors) is defined in figures: September 8, November 21, January 6, February 2, March 25—"of bread 3 *spudy* (an unknown dry measure), of wine 3 measures"; June 29, August 6, Ascension, Pentecost, and the Sunday of All Saints—of bread 3 *spudy*, of wine 2 measures; September 14 and December 6—of bread 3 *spudy* and of wine 1 measure; April 23—of bread 1 *spud* and of wine 1 measure; on the patronal feast days of the monastery, this allowance increased significantly: August 15—of bread 10 *spudy*, of wine 10 measures, of kolyva and wheat 4 *spudy*, of boiled grain (*sochivo*) 4 *spudy*, of water 2; November 11, on the feast of St. Theodore the Studite—of bread 6 *spudy*, of wine 8 measures, of kolyva 6 *spudy*, of *sochivo* 6 *spudy*; March 17, on the feast of St. Alexis—4 + 6 + 3 + 2; June 24—4 + 4 + 4 of kolyva; July 27—3 + 3 + 3 + 2 (*"Concerning distribution,"* fol. 244v).

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: дисциплинарная част древний ктиторских типиконов
units.slavonic_text: ### Дисциплинарная часть древний ктиторских Типиконов
units.english_text: Not a little space is allotted unto the disciplinary side of monastic life by all the other extant founder (*ktitoral*) Typika as well. The majority of them even have exclusively such content, referring for liturgical practice unto other Typika (see above, pp. 362–363). But these Typika exerted no influence upon our present Typikon: not one of them is older than the Studite-Alexis Typikon, which was preserved in an immutable form in Russia until the introduction of the Jerusalem Typikon. Nevertheless, a comparison of these Typika with the Studite-Alexis Typikon can demonstrate the distinctive character of the latter and explain why precisely unto this Typikon fell such a broad and enduring sphere of operation. In none of the currently known founder Typika does the administrative section touch unto such a degree upon all aspects of monastic life as in the Studite-Alexis Typikon. They occupy themselves more with the auxiliary institutions of the monastery—hospitals, hospices—than with the internal life of the monastery. At times, noticeable deviations from the counsels of asceticism are also made. Thus, for example, the organization of the Pantokrator Monastery in Constantinople resembles rather the staff of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople than the great lavras of antiquity; here are the same ecclesiastical ranks, including even four women who clean the temple and correspond unto the 'myrrh-bearers' of Hagia Sophia and *(Orig. p. 430)* of the Church of the Resurrection [^1815]; menial labors fall upon four permanent persons, and not upon the whole brotherhood in rotation [^1816]. Remarkable is the peculiarity in the election of the hegumen presented by certain of these Typika: they elected three candidates and determined the final choice by lot, wherein parchments with the names of those elected were placed upon the holy table and prayer was offered that God might reveal the one who was worthy; a priest, an illiterate monk, or a boy drew the parchment from the holy table [^1817]. Remarkable likewise is the requirement of certain of these Typika, for example the Evergetis Typikon, that the Typikon should be read at the beginning of each month at the refectory.

units.slavonic_stem_tier2: константинопольского пантократорского монастыря напоминает скорее штат св софии
units.slavonic_text: Константинопольского Пантократорского монастыря напоминает скорее штат св. Софии Константинопольской, чем великие лавры древности; здесь те же церковные чины, включая и четырех женщин, убирающих храм и соответствующих «мироносицам» св. Софии и {с. 430} храма Воскресения [242]; черные работы лежат на четырех постоянных лицах, а не на всей братии по очереди [243]. Замечательна особенность в выборе игумена, представляемая некоторыми из этих Типиконов: избирали трех кандидатов и окончательное избрание решали жребием, причем хартии с именами избранных полагались на престоле и возносилась молитва, чтобы Бог явил достойного; хартию брал с престола священник, неграмотный монах или мальчик [244]. Замечательно также требование некоторых из этих Типиконов, например Евергетидского, чтобы Типикон прочитывался в начале каждого месяца за трапезою.
units.english_text: Among these Typika, the Typikon of Empress Irene deserves attention as the first (and almost unique) experience of a female monastic rule. The difference from male rules consists in: a lighter fasting regimen: on Wednesday and Friday usually oil; daily not two, but two or three dishes; yet of wine not two or three cups, but one, with permission also for an addition at the discretion of the abbess; all sleep in one or two rooms, so that "all might be visible unto all"; meeting with male relatives is permitted only at the monastery gates in the presence of the abbess or a most honorable nun; no exception is made even for sick nuns, who are carried unto the gates upon stretchers. Priests must be monks and eunuchs. They likewise serve as oeconomoi of the monastery in view of the inconvenience for nuns of external relations outside the monastery. The officials are the same as under St. Theodore with minor additions and modifications: there is a 'granary mistress,' a 'wine-pourer,' two 'docheiariai' (one for financial accounting, the other supervising clothing), and two 'ergodotriai'—labor-givers, that is, supervisors of handiwork [^1818].

units.slavonic_incipit: Из этих Типиконов заслуживает внимания Типикон
units.slavonic_stem_tier2: из этих типиконов заслуживает внимания типикон имп ирины
units.slavonic_text: Из этих Типиконов заслуживает внимания Типикон имп. Ирины, как первый (и почти единственный) опыт женского монашеского устава. Разница от мужских уставов: легче постный режим: в среду и пятницу обычно елей; ежедневно не два, а два или три блюда; но вина не по 2 или 3 чаши, а по 1, с дозволением и прибавки по воле игумении; спят все в одной или двух комнатах, чтобы «все были явны всем»; видеться с родственниками мужчинами дозволяется только в воротах монастыря в присутствии игумении или честнейшей монахини; исключения не делается и для больных монахинь, которые приносятся к воротам на носилках. Священники должны быть монахи и евнухи. Они же являются экономами монастыря в виду неудобства для монахинь внешних сношений за монастырем. Должностные лица те же, что у прп. Феодора с небольшими дополнениями и изменениями: есть «житничная», «виночерпия», две «дохиарии» (одна для денежной отчетности, другая заведует одеждою), две «ергодотрии» — работодательницы, т. е. заведующие рукоделием [245]. {с. 431} ### Дисциплинарная часть в Иерусалимском Типиконе по грузинским и древнегреческим рукописям
units.english_text: In contrast unto the Studite Typika, the ancient Jerusalem Typika possess a very small disciplinary portion. In the most ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, for example, the Georgian Shiomghvime MS of the 13th century and the Greek MS of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection No. 35/491 of the 13th century, the disciplinary sections are inserted here and there among the liturgical material into the first general part of the Typikon, preceding the Menologion and the Triodion and setting forth the order of Sunday and weekday daily services, so that these sections not only do not form an independent part of the Typikon, but are scarcely noticeable within it; while the rules of comportment in church, which in the Studite Typika constitute the most prominent disciplinary section, are here for the most part situated within the order of the service itself, for example, the observation concerning silence during the Six Psalms, concerning the choir convergence. Thus the disciplinary portion proper in the mentioned two copies of the Jerusalem Typikon possesses the following uncomplicated composition. At the end of the exposition of the weekday service, such observations are made: "It is necessary to know that the monk appointed to chant the prokeimenon, following its intonation, bows unto the holy doors, then turns toward the west and stands with hands crossed upon his chest until the brethren recite the last verse; thereafter he bows and goes unto his place. If paroemias are appointed, he reads them also, as well as the Acts of the Apostles at the Vigil, and **\"God is the Lord\"**. He likewise intones **\"Let every breath\"** and the kontakion after the 6th ode of the canon. After the 9th ode the priest says: **\"Holy is the Lord our God\"** and the beginning of **\"Glory to God in the highest\"** at the Great Doxology. The aforementioned monk intones the prokeimena at the Divine Liturgy; he reads also the Epistle with the Alleluia, if he happens to know this. But if not, the ecclesiarch invites another who is skilled; after the prokeimenon, the two of them together make a bow. It is necessary to know that at Matins **\"God is the Lord...\"** and the Alleluia, and at the Divine Liturgy the prokeimena and the Epistle, we chant and read standing; during the reading of the Gospel, at the Cherubic Hymn, at the **\"Our Father...\"**, and at **\"Let our mouths be filled...\"**, we uncover our heads." During chanting it is forbidden to converse at the service, as well as to leave the church, but one must wait until a reading is offered; nor is it permitted to enter during the chanting of that choir in which someone stands, but to wait until the other choir begins to chant; having entered into his stasidion, he must bow unto the brethren. According unto the Greek MS, oversight of this is entrusted unto the ecclesiarch; while the Georgian MS demands here of the ecclesiarch oversight that no one stand without a partner, alone. The ecclesiarch must arrange that the brethren standing in the narthex allow no one into the temple, neither monk nor layman, "when the church is chanting, which is a sign of disorder" (later MSS: "but let them await the dismissal," that is, latecomers stand in the narthex until the end of the service). Next is indicated the order for the alternation of choirs during chanting: "The choir that began the psalmody (kathisma) at Vespers must begin it also at Matins; it begins the odes (canon) as well; from it also must be the chanter for the prokeimenon, **\"God is the Lord\"**, and the exapostilarion; at the Divine Liturgy *(Orig. p. 432)* (the same choir begins) the Typika [^1819], at Compline—**\"God is with us\"**, **\"All-Holy Lady Theotokos\"**, and **\"O Lord of hosts\"**; in holy and Great Lent the Hours are recited with psalmody thus: the choir that began at Matins **\"Praise the Lord\"** begins also the psalmody of the First Hour, that is, the Alleluia in Tone 6 (the tone of the troparion of the First Hour); at the Third Hour the other choir begins the Alleluia of the second kathisma in Tone 6; at the Sixth Hour the other choir begins the first Alleluia of Tone 2; while the monk who makes the beginning chants the prokeimenon of prophecy, reads the prophecies, and also performs the reading from the *Ladder* [of St. John Climacus]; at the Ninth Hour the other choir begins the first Alleluia of Tone 8; the same choir makes the beginning of the Beatitudes; while from Vespers onward there is again an alternation (of choirs)" [^1820]. The Typikon returns again unto discipline following the exposition of the service of the Hours and Mid-Hours: after the First Hour and its Mid-Hour, "those wishing to be saved do not leave the cell until the time of the church bell tolling (*chrousmatos*), but some occupy themselves with handiwork, others with reading, and others with psalmody with the knowledge of the superior; while the servers (*diakonetai*) attend unto (*scholazousi*) their service. It should be known that when we are present at church offices, the ecclesiarch directs (*tassei*) the right choir, while the epistemonarch directs the left." Next is cited the chapter concerning the awakener in the recension of the present Typikon (cf. the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis*) [^1821]. Finally, and this is already for the third time, the most ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon touch upon monastic discipline at the end of their first general part, before the Menologion; here an observation is made that at Compline "at Psalm 50 the candle-lighter (according unto the Georgian MS, the canonarch) gives water unto the brethren"—this in view of the fact that after Compline, as the last prayer of the day, partaking of any food is already forbidden on account of the morrow's Liturgy (on days of Vigils it is forbidden to drink water after partaking of the blessed bread and wine at Vespers); furthermore, it is required right here to conclude Compline before dark (*epiouses hemeras*, "while daylight yet remains"); after Compline "it is not permitted for monks to engage in conversations (*syntychias*) with one another, but each departs unto his cell, to occupy himself a little with the Trisagion which we have received (evidently, the cell rule, as is explicitly stated in the Georgian MS) and with reading, so that with attentiveness they may rise for Nocturns and the remaining office and church assembly (*synaxei*)" [^1822].

units.slavonic_text: же начало монах поет прокимен пророчества, читает и пророчества; творит же чтение и из Лествицы; на 9 часе начинает другой хор 1-е аллилуиа гл. 8; тот же хор творит начало Блажен; с вечерни же опять бывает перемена (хоров)» [247]. Снова Типикон возвращается к дисциплине по изложении службы часов и междочасий: после 1-го часа и его междочасия «желающие спастись не выходят из келии до времени церковного благовеста (χρούσματος), но одни занимаются рукоделием, другие чтением, иные псалмопением с ведома настоятеля: прислуживающие же (διακονηταὶ) занимаются (σχολάζουσι) служением своим. Должно знать, что когда мы находимся на церковных (чино)последованиях, правым хором управляет (τάσсей) екклисиарх, на левом же епистимонарх». Далее приводится статья о будильщике в редакции нынешнего Типикона (ср. Ипотипосис и Диатипосис) [248]. Наконец, и это уже в третий раз, древнейшие списки Иерусалимского Типикона касаются монастырской дисциплины в конце своей первой общей, части, пред месяцесловом; здесь делается замечание, что на повечерии «на пс. 50-м кандиловжигатель (по груз. ркп. — канонарх) дает братии воды», — это ввиду того, что после повечерия, как последней молитвы дня, уже запрещается вкушение всякой пищи из-за завтрашней литургии (во дни бдений воду запрещается пить после вкушения благословенных хлеба и вина на вечерни); затем здесь же требуется повечерие оканчивать засветло (ἐπιούσης ἡμέρας, «еще сущу дню»); после повечерия «монахам нельзя творить бесед (συντυχίας) друг с другом, но отходит в свои келии, заняться немного Трисвятым, которое мы приняли (очевидно, правилом келейным, как и сказано в груз. ркп.) и чтением, чтобы со вниманием встать на полунощницу и прочее последование и службу (συνάξει) церковную» [249].
units.english_text: This all too meager disciplinary material subsequent Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon expand, chiefly by insertions from the *Hypotyposis*. Following the exposition of the daily cursus with the aforementioned *(Orig. p. 433)* disciplinary insertions, some of which are at times omitted (for example, in MS of the Moscow Synodal Library, Greek No. 391 of the 13th–14th centuries, the observation concerning the awakener is omitted), certain Greek MSS have the following sections: 1) an exhortation unto the superior not to despise that which is contained in the Typikon and not to spend much time outside the monastery, neglecting the souls entrusted unto him; especially not to leave the monastery during the three holy Forty-Day Fasts, and not to permit others to leave the monastery during this time; 2) an exhortation unto the brethren to care only for the heavenly, intensely to seek the kingdom of heaven, and to strive that all things be conducted among them in good order, especially in church, to preserve the mind unenticed by anything worldly, to go unto church at the first bell-ringing (*blagovest*), to stand there attentively from the very beginning; with particular reverence and attentiveness must one stand during the Six Psalms; entering into the church at that time is strictly forbidden; those unable to stand throughout it thus—the elderly and the sick—let them stand in the narthex; attentive, slow chanting with a meek, even, and clear voice is required; conversations are forbidden upon the cliroi, as well as at the refectory: at the latter it is likewise forbidden to look about or where one should not, for example, at how others eat; it is forbidden also to murmur against the quality of the food served [^1823]. Then, under the special title: "Of the Monastery of Stoudios," a series of disciplinary excerpts from the *Hypotyposis* is given: concerning the monastic officials, concerning confession unto the hegumen at the 4th ode of the canon, concerning an elder-brother appointed during the Forty-Day Fast to remind of death, concerning a two-to-three-week trial prior unto admission into the monastery, concerning the reading of books from the library on feast days, concerning the hour of the Divine Liturgy during fasts, concerning proportion in the services, concerning a penance for one who breaks dishware at the refectory, and concerning the quantity of clothing [^1824]. Following the exposition of the order of the Divine Liturgy, the aforementioned MSS of the Typikon contain two further disciplinary articles: concerning the three ranks of feasts from Nikon of the Black Mountain (see above, p. 408) and the following "Canons" (*κανόνες*) of Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople: dispensation for an ailing monk during the Forty-Day Fast to take cooked food, oil, and wine; prohibition against traveling on Sunday except under necessity and constraint; prohibition against receiving Communion from a priest who does not fast on Wednesday and Friday; rejection of apocryphal books: the Apocalypses of Paul, Ezra, and Zosimas, the "Two Martyrdoms" of St. George, of Cyricus and Julitta, and the books of Macarius and Diadochus; permission for laboring monks during the Forty-Day Fast to eat bread at the 9th hour [3:00 PM] and to sup in the evening, with a prohibition against relaxing unto oil and wine under pretext of labor; permission for hired workmen to partake of food on non-fasting days from the 3rd hour [9:00 AM], and during fasts at the 6th hour [12:00 PM] (according unto the Holy Mountain Typikon, see above, p. 422). In Slavic copies of the Jerusalem Typikon, almost all these disciplinary rubrics disappear, at least as specialized sections; but in place of this, as we have seen, there appear in these Typika our present disciplinary excerpts from Nikon of the Black Mountain (in MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 329/384 of the 14th century, still in a separate gathering sewn unto the front; in later MSS, for example No. 678/386 of the 15th century, already in the very *(Orig. p. 434)* text: apparently, these excerpts were introduced into the Typikon by Athanasius of Vysotsk; see above, p. 375).

units.slavonic_text: у них по чину, особенно же в церкви, соблюдать ум неувлекаемым со стороны чего-либо мирского, идти по первому благовесту в церковь, стоять там внимательно с самого начала; с особенным благоговением и вниманием нужно стоять на шестопсалмии; входить тогда в церковь безусловно запрещается; кто не может так выстоять — старые, больные, — пусть стоят в притворе; требуется пение внимательное, медленное, кротким, ровным и ясным голосом; запрещаются разговоры на клиросах, а также на трапезе: на последней также запрещается глядеть по сторонам и куда не нужно, например, как другие едят; запрещается и роптать на качество предложенных снедий [250]. Затем с особым заглавием: «Монастыря Студийского» дается ряд дисциплинарных выдержек из Ипотипосиса: о должностных лицах, об исповеди игумену на 4 песни канона, о старце-брате, назначаемом в Четыредесятницу для напоминания о смерти, о 2–3 недельном испытании пред приемом в монастырь, о чтении книг из библиотеки в праздничные дни, о времени литургии в пост, о соразмерности в службах, об епитимьи разбившему посуду на трапезе, о количестве одежды [251]. После изложения чина литургии вышеупомянутые ркп. Типикона имеют еще две дисциплинарные статьи: о трех разрядах праздников из Никона Черногорца (см. выше, стр. 408) и следующие «Правила» (κανόνες) Никифора, патр. Константинопольского: разрешение болящему монаху в Четыредесятницу на варение, елей и вино; запрещение путешествовать в воскресенье кроме нужды и насилия; запрещение причащаться от иерея, не постящегося в среду и пятницу; не должно принимать книг: Апокалипсисов Павла, Ездры, Зосимы, «двух мучений» св. Георгия, Кирика и Иулиты, книг Макария и Диадоха; позволение трудящимся монахам в Четыредесятницу в 9 час вкушать хлеб, а вечером ужинать, с запрещением под предлогом работы разрешать на елей и вино; дозволение работникам вкушать пищу в непост с 3 ч., а в пост в 6 ч. (по Святогорск. уст., см. выше, стр. 422). В славянских списках Иерусалимского устава почти все эти дисциплинарные указания исчезают, по крайней мере специальные отделы их; но взамен этого, как мы видели, в этих уставах появляются нынешние дисциплинарные выдержки из Никона Черногорца (в ркп. Моск. Синод. библ. № 329/384 XIV в. еще в особой тетради, пришитой спереди; в позднейших, например № 678/386 XV в. уже в самом {с. 434} тексте: по-видимому, эти выдержки внесены в устав Афанасием Высотским (см. выше, стр. 375).
units.english_text: Thus, by the 13th–14th centuries, all the most essential parts of the Typikon had gradually taken shape: besides the fundamental Menologion-Triodion section, there was also the general liturgical section (the daily cycle of services) and the disciplinary section. Later than these parts, there entered into the Typikon as an independent and separate section yet another part: liturgical rubrics for the coincidence of fixed feasts with Sundays or movable feasts. In the most ancient Typika, these rubrics are very brief and indefinite, being provided in the Menologion under the corresponding days of the month. Thus, already in the Studite-Alexis Typikon under September 8, the observation is made that if it fall upon a Sunday, "the Sunday service is chanted first," and that one must act likewise if the memory of an apostle or evangelist fall upon a Sunday; of the details of the service, an instruction is given only regarding the troparia at the conclusion of Vespers and at the Divine Liturgy. Under March 25, the identical observation (in the Studite-Alexis Typikon) is very extensive; it provides for the coincidence of the Annunciation with an ordinary Saturday and Sunday, with Lazarus Saturday, Palm Sunday, all days of Holy Week, and with the Sunday and Monday of Holy Pascha, providing rubrics regarding all stichera, troparia, and canons. This exhausts the material in the Studite-Alexis Typikon corresponding unto the content of our present Markian Chapters. These observations are not inscribed here under the name of Mark. The identical form and scope are possessed by these observations in the Western Studite Typika and in the Evergetis Typikon; here too the name of Mark does not appear over them, which is particularly characteristic for the Western Studite Typika in view of their proximity unto the place of activity of Mark, Bishop of Otranto. The identical scope and form are possessed by the rubrics concerning the coincidence of fixed feasts with movable ones in the most ancient copies of the Jerusalem Typikon, the Greek MS of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection No. 35/491, and the Georgian Shiomghvime MS; here these rubrics are very close unto the Studite ones, with the exception, naturally, of the peculiarities of Jerusalem practice, and likewise do not bear the name of Mark. In later Greek copies of the Jerusalem Typikon, as already in MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 381 of the 13th–14th centuries, these rubrics are supplemented by marginal annotations, so that around the Annunciation the margins of several pages are covered with them. But in such an ancient copy of the Jerusalem Typikon as the Greek MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 456, probably of the 13th century, all observations of this kind are gathered into one place, divided into 95 chapters, and inscribed: "Compendium (*σύνταγμα*) of Mark, sinful hieromonk, compiled concerning the doubtful matters (*ἀποῤῥούμενα*) of the Typikon" (fol. 165). Thereafter, in the most ancient Slavic Typika, MSS of the Moscow Synodal Library Nos. 328/383 and 329/384 of the 14th century, there is an identical compendium of these observations with the heading (in the first): "Of Mark the sinful hieromonk concerning the omissions of the Typikon" (fol. 189). Subsequently, in many subsequent Slavic and Greek MSS, such a compendium is found with varying numbers of chapters and *(Orig. p. 435)* with an identical name in the inscription, for example: "Of the most sacred Mark of Hydrous [Otranto]," "Of Mark, most holy oeconomos," and the like. units.slavonic_stem_tier2: типикона здес получили возможност значительно расшириться и обобщит
units.slavonic_text: Типикона, здесь получили возможность значительно расшириться и обобщить свое содержание — дать указания на случай совпадения с воскресеньями и подвижными праздниками не только отдельных праздников, но и целых родов их, как-то Христова праздника вообще или Богородичного с воскресеньем, пред-, попразднества или отдания великого праздника с воскресеньем, великого (бденного), полиелейного или шестеричного святого с воскресеньем, с субботой и т. п. Это мы и видим уже в самых древних редакциях Марковых глав, носящих его имя (например, греч. Тип. Моск. Синод б. № 456 XIII в., в слав. уставе Моск. Синод библ. № 328/383 XIV в.). В позднейших славянских рукописях, так уже и в № 678/386 XV в., эти сводки разбиваются на две части: первая, содержащая общие указания о господских и Богородичных праздниках и их пред- и попразднствах в неделю, о святых в неделю и субботу, ставится отдельно в 1-ой общей части устава, излагающей суточные службы, и имя Марка большей частью не надписывается над ней, а вторая с именем Марка распределяется по числам месяцев (т. е. принимает свой первоначальный вид). Так и в нынешнем Типиконе, но общая часть сокращена: только о святых в неделю и субботу. В еще позднейших слав. рукописях, с XVI в., например, Музея Киевск. Акад. Аа 194 и 196 прибавляются указания о совпадении храмовых праздников с подвижными («Главы о храмах» нынешнего Тип.). В греч. же ркп. вплоть до печатного издания греч. Типикона и в этом печатном издании Марковы главы помещены в одном отделе, хотя повторяются потом и под числами месяцев (в более короткой, древнейшей редакции), а храмовых нет.
units.english_text: Typikon, acquired here the capacity to expand significantly and to generalize their content—to provide rubrics for the coincidence with Sundays and movable feasts not only of individual feasts, but of entire classes thereof: such as a feast of Christ in general or of the Theotokos with a Sunday; the forefeast, afterfeast, or Apodosis of a Great Feast with a Sunday; a great (vigil-rank), polyeleos, or six-stichera saint with a Sunday, with a Saturday, and the like. This we observe already in the most ancient recensions of the Markian Chapters bearing his name (for example, the Greek Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 456 of the 13th century, and the Slavic Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 328/383 of the 14th century). In later Slavic manuscripts, as already in No. 678/386 of the 15th century, these compendia are divided into two parts: the first, containing general rubrics concerning feasts of the Lord and of the Theotokos and their forefeasts and afterfeasts on a Sunday, and concerning saints on Sunday and Saturday, is placed separately in the first general part of the Typikon setting forth the daily services, and the name of Mark is for the most part not inscribed over it; while the second, bearing the name of Mark, is distributed according unto the days of the months (that is, it assumes its original form). So it is likewise in our present Typikon, though the general part is abridged: treating only of saints on Sunday and Saturday. In yet later Slavic manuscripts from the 16th century onward, for example MSS of the Museum of the Kyiv Theological Academy Aa 194 and 196, rubrics are added concerning the coincidence of temple feasts with movable feasts (the "Temple Chapters" of our present Typikon). In Greek manuscripts, however, up unto the printed edition of the Greek Typikon, and within that printed edition itself, the Markian Chapters are placed in a single section, though they are subsequently repeated under the days of the months (in a shorter, more ancient recension), while the temple chapters are absent.

units.english_text: Yet even this is not all that entered into the composition of ancient Typika and enters into our present one. Already the most ancient Studite-Alexis Typikon in MS of the Moscow Synodal Typography Library No. 285/142/1206 of the 11th–12th centuries places upon its pages, alongside rubrical observations, also the most essential and most frequently employed brief hymns, such as: prokeimena, alleluiaria, kontakia, and troparia. Such material, in greater or lesser volume, enters likewise into all subsequent copies of the Typikon. Other sections of more or less related content also find their way into it: for example, notices concerning the lives of commemorated saints (in the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th–10th centuries), the order of the Divine Liturgy (MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 381), expositions of essential dogmas, and the Paschal Tables (in late Greek copies).

units.slavonic_text: С такою же постепенностью, с какою слагалось содержание и рос объем Типикона, вырабатывался и план его. Простейший план — в Типиконе {с. 436} Великой Константинопольской церкви IX–V в., имеющем только уставные замечания на разные дни годы (месяцеслова и Триоди). Но прототипом плана нынешнего Типикона послужили — Ипотипосис, приписываемый прп. Феодору Студиту и его переработка — Диатипосис прп. Афанасия. Начинаясь изложением пасхальной службы (особый отдел с заглавием: «Как поступаем в собраниях св. и славного тридневного воскресенья»), эти памятники на первом месте дают ряд чисто литургических отрывочных замечаний — о богослужении в Пятидесятницу, в пост св. апостолов и далее на важнейшие неподвижные праздники и периоды церковного года, затем на Четыредесятницу (особый отдел «О св. Четыредесятнице»); в следующей затем дисциплинарной части речь сначала о должностных лицах, о поведении за богослужением, и после нескольких мелких замечаний дисциплинарного характера памятники переходят к монастырскому столу (в отделах «О количестве и качестве пищи и питья и о благочинии на трапезах», «О св. вел. Четыредесятнице» и «О благовещении», последний § более литургического содержания), к работам монахов («О соразмерности в службах») и одежде их («О количестве одежды и об обуви и о устроении постели и о подобном» только в Ипотипосисе). Тот же план выдерживает в общем Студийско-Алексиевский устав, давая сначала триодный устав (с Недели мытаря), затем месяцеслов (в ркп. Моск. Синод. библ. № 333/381 XIV в. и 906/382 XV в. месяцеслов ранее — перестановка позднейшая, как показывает предисловие к месяцеслову во второй ркп.); следующая затем дисциплинарная часть вначале тоже, по-видимому, намерена следовать Ипотипосису, говорит сначала о столе; но затем оставляет выдержанный план, стараясь лишь располагать предметы по какому-либо сходству: как например, §§ о должностных лицах стоят почти все рядом, тоже §§ о поведении за богослужением. Типикон Великой Константинопольской церкви IX–X в. положил начало другому плану Типиконов, поставив месяцеслов ранее Триоди. Такого порядка держатся все западные Студийские Типиконы и Евергетидский. Типикон Великой церкви и западные Студийские не имеют дисциплинарной части, но Типиконы Калабрийской редакции (Николо-Касулянского монастыря (начинаются общелитургической частью, заключающей (в 28 гл.) наставления о тех или иных пунктах суточного богослужения, например, о пении Бог Господь и аллилуиа, о благовесте, о каждении, о кафисмах на утрене и вечерне в простые дни и в праздники, об отмене поклонов в некоторые дни, о кафисмах в посты и попутно о трапезе в обыкновенные дни и посты, о стихирах на службах — воскресных, будничных, праздничных, о канонах на разных службах, о чтениях, о повечерии [252].
